#6. Saudi Arabia postpones big investor conference to 2027 as Iran-backed Houthis escalate attacks on kingdom

Saudi Arabia on Monday postponed its big annual investor conference until 2027 as Iran-backed Houthi militants have escalated missile and drone attacks on the kingdom in recent weeks.

The Future Investment Initiative was originally scheduled to take place in the Saudi capital Riyadh from Oct. 26 to Oct. 29. "We will announce the new 2027 dates very soon," the conference organizers said in a statement.

The decision to postpone the conference comes after the Houthis attacked King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Oct. 10, leaving at least 12 people dead and more than 300 injured.

Some of the biggest names in business and finance were listed as speakers for the conference. They included JPMorgan Chase's Jamie Dimon, Goldman Sachs' David Solomon, Blackstone's Stephen Schwarzman, BlackRock's Larry Fink and Citigroup's Jane Fraser.

CNBC was told some participants and speakers had planned to travel to Saudi Arabia by flying first to Bahrain and then driving five hours to Riyadh.

Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund launched the Future Investment Initiative in 2017. The conference has played a key part in Riyadh's plans to diversify its oil-dependent economy. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman unveiled the ambitious megaproject NEOM at the first conference in 2017.

The decision to postpone the conference underscores the deteriorating security situation in the Middle East as the U.S-Iran war spreads across the region. Houthi militants have launched repeated waves of missile and drone strikes at Saudi Arabia since the deadly airport attack earlier this month.

The Saudi military intercepted and destroyed several drones launched at the Riyadh region on Friday and Saturday, a spokesperson from the kingdom's armed forces said.

Missiles launched over the Red Sea were also intercepted on Friday including one heading toward the port city and oil terminal Yanbu, the spokesperson said.

#7. Top Wall Street analysts are bullish on the growth potential of these 3 stocks

Fears around the artificial intelligence trade and higher pressure on oil prices are weighing on global markets, but a few stocks offer investors solid growth prospects even in choppy times.

Investors with a long-term horizon can look beyond the ongoing volatility and track the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts to pick attractive stocks with strong long-term growth potential.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Health insurer UnitedHealth delivered better-than-expected results for the third quarter of 2026. The company also raised its full-year earnings outlook, reflecting continued progress on its turnaround plan.

Following the Q3 print, Morgan Stanley analyst Erin Wright reiterated a buy rating on UNH stock with a price target of $529. "UNH's beat & raise reinforces turnaround momentum, with improving MA [Medicare Advantage]/Optum Health supporting a higher '26 EPS baseline & upside to '27 consensus," said Wright.

The five-star analyst added that better-than-expected performance in the UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health businesses supported another upgrade to the company's 2026 adjusted earnings per share outlook to at least $20.50. Wright noted that UNH raised the earnings guidance despite incremental investments planned for the fourth quarter of 2026.

Furthermore, Wright highlighted management's view that the consensus 2027 EPS of $22.63 was too conservative. Reaching even the low end of the company's 13% to 16% long-term EPS growth target would imply an EPS of $23.17.

Wright raised her 2026 EPS estimate to $20.65 from $19.82 and 2027 EPS to $23.24 from $22.54, reflecting the latest upside and an improving 2026 medical loss ratio to 87.4% from 88.1%. Overall, she believes that UNH's operational performance continues to improve, increasing her confidence in its UHC strategy and Optum Health turnaround execution.

Wright ranks No. 264 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 15%. See UnitedHealth Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Social media giant Meta Platforms has been making headlines since the launch of its Muse AI agent, which is seeing solid traction. Investors look forward to updates on the company's AI strategy when it announces its third-quarter results on Oct. 21.

Heading into Q3 earnings, Guggenheim analyst Michael Morris maintained a buy rating on Meta stock and increased his price target to $850 from $700, reflecting higher estimates for 2027. He expects Muse usage momentum and engagement levels to shape investor sentiment into the Q3 earnings call.

Specifically, Morris highlighted that, according to Apptopia, Muse reached 1.3 million daily active users in five weeks versus 300,000 in the first week. Given that Muse's current adoption represents less than 0.05% of Meta's 3.6 billion daily active user base, the analyst expects management to prioritize boosting usage over near-term monetization.

"Over time, we believe Muse monetizes primarily through businesses paying to reach consumers through their agents, consistent with the economics of Meta's core advertising business, rather than consumer wallets," said the five-star analyst. He added that the checkout integrations with Shopify and PayPal reflect this framework.

While there are concerns that a rival could overtake Muse or the recently launched Muse Wonder and push Meta into a prolonged cycle of overinvestment, Morris remains bullish due to the company's strong record in scaling WhatsApp and competing strongly with TikTok via Reels as well as free distribution to an extensive user base.

Morris ranks No. 629 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.2%. See Meta Platforms KPIs on TipRanks.

Next is semiconductor company Marvell Technology. Earlier this month, Marvell held its Investor Day, where it raised its total addressable market estimate to $400 billion by 2030, reflecting solid AI-led demand tailwinds.

After hosting a non-deal roadshow with Marvell's senior management following the Investor Day, Stifel analyst Tore Svanberg reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $370.

The five-star analyst said that a major focus of the roadshow was the XPU and XPU Attach mix, as Marvell's Custom business expands toward its FY31 revenue target of $30 billion. In this regard, management reiterated that it expects a balanced mix of XPU and XPU Attach revenue in FY31, though it noted that either segment could grow rapidly enough to shift the mix toward 60/40 or 40/60.

While XPU drove most of the nearly $1.5 billion Custom revenue in FY26, Svanberg expects Marvell's XPU Attach business to grow substantially through the end of the decade, leading to a more balanced mix in this business. At the Investor Day event, the company raised its FY29 Custom target from more than $10 billion to over $12 billion, mainly driven by strength in the XPU Attach business.

Svanberg said that another key topic in the roadshow was whether Marvell can secure enough capacity to meet its raised targets. Management said that it met with suppliers ahead of Investor Day to share its five-year goals and received commitments to support these targets. The analyst believes that Marvell's supply chain commitments give it a competitive edge over rivals as customers seek reliable partners for large-scale infrastructure buildouts.

Svanberg ranks No. 91 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 58% of the time, delivering an average return of 31.8%. See Marvell Technology Statistics on TipRanks.

#8. Cliffs (CLF) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. (CLF +15.80%) reported sequential growth in revenue and profitability during the third quarter, supported by higher average selling prices and decreased unit costs. Management attributed the recovery to domestic trade enforcement and higher facility utilization rates. The company stated it is prioritizing debt reduction using free cash flow and proceeds from contracted property sales, with a goal of reaching its leverage target by mid-2027. Strategic initiatives discussed on the call include the modernization of Middletown Works and a 25% capacity expansion for grain-oriented electrical steel production to meet growing infrastructure demand.

Operator: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. My name is Donna, and I am your conference facilitator today. I would like to welcome everyone to Cleveland Cliffs' Third Quarter 26 Earnings Conference Call. All lines have been placed on mute to prevent background noise. After the speakers' remarks, there will be a question and answer session. Lourenco Goncalves: Thank you, Donna, and good morning, everyone. 3 months ago, we told you that the earnings recovered that Cleveland Cliffs was becoming visible Today, the recovery is firmly underway. With a 25 thousand person workforce that spans some of the most important industrial communities in The United States.

What the Trump administration has done on trade is not just good for Cleveland Cliffs, it is good for America. As a consequence of the renaissance of manufacturing in The United States. We are currently selling steel under the best price environment in 3 years. And these are the prices we need to run a thriving business that grows employment, pays its workers well, reinvest in people and equipment, and protect our critical supply chains and national defense.

The most important and positive development for Cleveland Cliffs since our last call has been the strength of our 2027 round of contract negotiations with our clients. The largest portion of our steel volume consists of tons sold to service centers and end users under annual fixed price or index linked contracts. These agreements cover every segment of light flat rolled steel consumption outside automotive. All these contracts reset on January 1 of next year, and nearly all of these customers want more steel under contract in 2027 than in 2026. Suffice to say, that we have been very successful in renewing this contract. In aggregate, the improvements should generate more than $1 billion of year over year EBITDA improvement.

Before even contemplate changes of the underlying pricing index. More importantly, our customers are not fleeing to imported steel. Actually, we are finally operating within The United States with a fair commercial structure that is critical to sustaining a healthy business allowing us to reinvest in our facilities and in our people. The strong contract renewal environment and the good health of our well maintained equipment have created a compelling opportunity to maximize the value of our existing asset base. With that, we are postponing the Burns Harbor C-Blast furnace reline from mid-27 to April 2028. Our President and Chief Financial Officer, Celso L. Goncalves Jr., will be talking about that on his prepared remarks.

We have several other similar ongoing projects bigger and smaller. The most critical being the modernization of Middletown Works, This past quarter, we officially completed the rescoping of our $1 billion modernization project for Middletown. This revised project was commemorated with a visit by Vice President, JD Vance to his hometown of Middletown, Ohio. And to our flagship automotive grade steel plant Middletown Works. The new scope entails a $1 billion investment including $500 million of support from the Department of Energy. And will modernize 1 of the most important steelmaking facilities in the country. While maintaining uninterrupted production throughout the construction period.

The project includes a state of the art blast furnace rebuild, advanced material handling infrastructure artificial intelligence enabled process controls, and a new cogenerating co-generation facility that will capture blast furnace gas and convert this off-gas into electricity and steam for on-site use. Our work on this rescoped project has already begun. And we expect to be completely done in the first quarter of 30. Other notable projects on the agenda in the coming years that fit into our reinvestment master plan include the Cook plant rebuild at Burns Harbor. And the ability to produce galvanized steel. 1 more time. The domestic market for galvanized steel in Canada is not big enough to accommodate 2 Canadian producers of galvanized steel Stelco and ArcelorMittal Dofasco, and also an avalanche of imports that have not been adequately reduced by the Canada's tariff rate quota system.

Cleveland Cliffs invested C$3.4 billion less than 2 years ago to acquire Stelco, And Stelco was supposed to be an immediately accretive investment for Cleveland Cliffs. A couple of months later, and for reasons clearly beyond our control or ability to predict Stelco became a negative contributor to Cliffs' results. A situation that persisted for more than 1 year. Fast forward we found a way to steer Stelco out of trouble and into a profitable path. All while waiting as long as possible to avoid the idling of the galvanized line. I have no doubt we will get there.

And our American employees represented by the USW will be rewarded for the success we expect to have together in the coming years. With that, I will turn it over to the President and Chief Financial Officer of Cleveland Cliffs, Celso L. Goncalves Jr. for his remarks.

#15. OpenAI bugging suspect's conduct could pose danger to U.S. national security, feds warn

Federal prosecutors in a new court filing warned that the alleged bugging of an OpenAI executive conference room by a Saudi national working as an engineer at that artificial intelligence giant "could pose a danger to the national security of the United States."

Prosecutors said that in the days around the time that Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly planted a recording device in a television in that room in OpenAI's San Francisco headquarters on Sept. 28, "OpenAI executives met with government officials in that very room."

The filing came as Alfozan, 35, faces a detention hearing in U.S. District Court in San Francisco on Monday morning local time. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California is asking a judge to keep Alfozan held without bail.

The filing cites his ties to Saudi Arabia, his financial resources, and the fact that his wife and their 3-month-old baby flew there on the heels of his Oct. 9 arrest.

Prosecutors said Alfozan had been "in frequent communications via WhatsApp with a member of the Saudi Royal Family" throughout 2025 and 2026.

Alfozan communicated with the Saudi royal as recently as Oct. 5 — four days before he was arrested, prosecutors said.

Prosecutors did not identify the Saudi royal or say how Alfozan knew that person.

"Among other things, the individual [the royal family member] told the defendant [Alfozan] that an artificial intelligence initiative was being launched in Saudi Arabia and wanted the defendant to join it," the filing says.

"In May 2026, the individual told the defendant, 'Saudi needs you more then [sic] the US!' to which the defendant responded '100,' indicating he agreed," prosecutors wrote.

"The individual repeatedly tried to recruit the defendant and asked when he planned to leave OpenAI," prosecutors wrote. "At the time, the defendant said he wouldn't leave until his stock vested."

The filing does not say the Saudi royal directed Alfozan to install a recording device at OpenAI or steal information from the AI giant.

Alfozan, who lives near the San Francisco airport, is a venture partner at Raed Ventures, a Saudi venture capital firm. Prince Khalid bin Bader Al Saud, a member of the Saudi royal family, joined the firm as a venture partner in 2025. In their filing, prosecutors did not mention that prince by name, or say that the unidentified royal who communicated with Alfozan had ties to Raed.

Prosecutors in the same filing said the Saudi government and then, shortly afterward, a member of the Saudi military booked separate flights for Alfozan's wife, Lujain Alassaf, and their three-month-old son to fly out of the United States after his Oct. 9 arrest upended plans for the three of them to fly as a family to Saudi Arabia on Oct. 12.

The wife and son flew from San Francisco to Doha, Qatar, on Oct. 10 on a business-class flight paid for by the unidentified member of the Saudi military, the filing said.

Alfozan has been in jail since his arrest on a charge of using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. He faces a maximum possible sentence of five years in prison if convicted. OpenAI fired him after his arrest.

Alfozan's lawyer, William Pernik, in a separate filing asked that the defendant be released with home detention and GPS monitoring, and a bond co-signed by others, and "supported by the written undertaking of the Consulate General of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia."

The Saudi embassy in Washington, D.C., has not responded to CNBC's requests for comment on Alfozan since his arrest was announced on Oct. 13.

FBI Director Kash Patel, when Alfozan's arrest was announced, said he allegedly concealed the recording device to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company's artificial intelligence technology.

Prosecutors in their new filing also argued that Alfozan is a flight risk because of his access to "ample resources ... and what appears to be considerable support from a foreign government that has (i) no extradition treaty with the United States; (ii) limitless resources; and (iii) the ability to provide extraordinary travel assistance, including based on similar circumstances in this District," the filing said.

"He has the connections needed not only to flee, but to build a new life in Saudi Arabia. The Court should order the defendant detained pending trial," prosecutors wrote.

Alfozan has spent about 15 years in the United States, working at various tech companies, including Meta, and obtaining a master's degree from the University of California, Berkeley in 2025. He is a legal permanent resident of the United States and has applied to become a naturalized citizen.

For his most recent job, as an OpenAI engineer, Alfozan was hired in July 2025 with an annual base salary of $325,000, which was later increased to $385,000, prosecutors said in their filing. He also received a new hire equity grant of $2.2 million in profit participating units, the filing said.

Alfozan planned to take two months of parental leave after the birth of his son, according to the filing. He and his family were scheduled to fly one-way to Saudi Arabia on Oct. 12.

"On or about September 28, 2026 — about two weeks before their scheduled flight—the defendant inserted a surreptitious audio recording device into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive OpenAI conference room, where the device remained for at least multiple days," the filing said.

The conference room is frequently used for "discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, as well as nonpublic information about OpenAI's technical progress and strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements, and commercial relationships," the filing said.

The filing also says that after Alfozan's arrest, his iPhone was found to contain photographs dated Sept. 22 to 28 depicting "at least one additional concealed device as well as what appear to be the input/output panels on televisions and other electronic devices in various locations in OpenAI buildings, including another conference room where sensitive meetings frequently occurred."

"The defendant's residence contained several electronic components similar to those in thecustomized devices the defendant installed in the OpenAI conference room," the filing said.

OpenAI also found another recording device in a bag Alfozan inadvertently left behind in a printer room on Oct. 5, the same day he was seen on camera checking behind the TV where the first recording device had been left in the conference room, prosecutors have said. The camera was installed after OpenAI discovered the recording device on Sept. 30, prosecutors said.

His cellphone also contained a deleted note from September "with links to various recording devices, including devices made by Seeed Studio, the manufacturer of the devices OpenAI found in its offices and the devices FBI agents found in the defendant's residence," the filing said.

Another note, entitled "OpenAI leave," suggests that Alfozan planned early pickup "of the devices he had installed or intended to install and then extending his planned parental 'leave to full,'" the filing said.

In addition to being in contact with a Saudi royal, Alfozan "was pursuing other opportunities in Saudi Arabia, including participating in the Misk Foundation's '2030 Leaders' program, which would have required his in- person participation in Riyadh," prosecutors said.

A day before she left the U.S. with their baby, Alfozan's wife told FBI agents who interviewed her that "her U.S. visa was expiring and that she and her son were permanently moving back to Saudi Arabia — and that her husband, the defendant, eventually intended to do the same," the filing said.

Alfozan's lawyer, Pernik, in his request that Alfozan be released into home detention, said, "nationality is not evidence of flight," and that his planned travel to Saudi Arabia was for "family and immigration reasons."

Alfozan's wife's 60-day post-employment grace period for her own visa was expiring on Oct. 12, the originally scheduled date of their flight, the lawyer said.

"Mr. Alfozan was made aware of OpenAI finding the device per its own filings and OpenAI'spublic statements, approximately eight to ten days before he was arrested," Pernik wrote. "If his intention was to flee, he would have done so at that time."

The lawyer also said that Alfozan, who had booked a one-way ticket to Saudi Arabia for himself and his family, regularly bought one-way tickets because he has learned they are more cost-effective than changing his flights at the last minute.

Pernik also wrote that the Saudi Consulate General confirmed in writing to the U.S. Pretrial Services Office on Thursday that it "'will not issue any travel documents' to Mr. Alfozan during his release and that, if he requests one, it 'undertakes to promptly notify U.S. Pretrial Services.'"

The attorney argued that prosecutors have not shown that Alfozan is a serious flight risk.

"Mr. Alfozan has lived in the United States for fifteen years and in the Bay Area for roughly ten," Pernik wrote. "Fifty-four people, at least twenty-seven of them in the Bay Area, have written to the Court, and they describe someone who organizes dinners, welcomes newcomers, mentors students, and shows up for friends' weddings, birthdays, and moves."

"That is not the profile of a person with one foot out the door," Pernik said.

#16. The Austin Powers steamroller: How to trade CoreWeave's slow moving crisis

In Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery, a Virtuocon guard famously stands in front of a commandeered steamroller, screaming "No!!" three times before being run over. The joke, of course, is that the hazard moved so slowly he had ample time to step out of the way.

For months, equity traders holding CoreWeave (CRWV) have played that guard. Despite credit markets flashing warnings, equity holders essentially just stood there. Now, after a shocking 27.5% drop from last Friday's close to this Thursday morning's 52-week lows, followed by a whiplash 17% rebound, equity investors, if not squashed like Dr. Evil's henchman, are dazed and confused. Shares are down another 5% today.

With earnings just a few weeks away, massive leverage, a heavily split sell-side, and 15.4% short interest, the stock remains primed for explosive volatility.

The hazard approaching CRWV equity wasn't hidden. The AI cloud infrastructure platform essentially didn't exist five years ago and has accumulated $51.6 billion in debt (~$46 billion net of cash) against a backdrop of zero historical profitability. That was well known, but the CEO's comments that the company aspired to be investment grade so it could borrow "unlimited sums", even as investors already anticipated nearly another $60 billion in debt in the next 18months, spooked folks. (Trick or Treat!) Especially since the debt issued only in June had already fallen 20% since.

From an options trader's point of view, it was hard to reconcile deteriorating credit and rising leverage with falling options premia; as recently as last week, they were in the 6th percentile, 1.5 standard deviations below the one-year mean. At 72%, options weren't cheap in absolute terms, but given everything going on, they should have been higher. The stock also looked somewhat complacent, with the equity chopping around historical support levels dating back to May 2025. The credit side was on tilt:

Because CRWV is levered by more than 2:1, a 10% move in enterprise value translates to a nearly 22% swing in equity value.

Despite the dire credit picture, equity sentiment remains fiercely divided, driving this week's 17% bounce from the lows. For example, HSBC maintains a Sell rating with a $39 price target, essentially calling for the stock to be cut in half. Conversely, banks like BNP and Cantor Fitzgerald (my former employer) suggest these fears are overblown and the stock should more than double from here.

It's not just bankers defending the company either. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang downplayed systemic concerns, and ARK Investment stepped in to buy 192,000 shares. BofA argues that CRWV's ability to bring active power online at scale, combined with higher pricing from Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin deployments, will drive faster-than-expected revenue growth. They described execution risk as a bigger concern than financing; I'm not sure those who bought the 2032 8 1/2s at par would agree.

With CRWV's credit heavily distressed but its equity heavily defended by high-profile dip-buyers, going outright long or short into earnings carries excessive directional risk. A November/January Call Diagonal, currently trading for just under $6 per spread. Almost 9% of the current stock price. Normally, that's a lot, but given this stock has fallen 27.5% and then gained 17% in the past 5 sessions, it isn't.

#17. Why AMD Stock Popped on Monday

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +3.56%) stock jumped 3.6% through 12:30 p.m. ET Monday.

You can thank the friendly analysts at TD Cowen for that. AMD stock may have lost 16% of its value over the past two weeks as semiconductor stocks sold off, but Cowen still thinks AMD stock is a buy.

TD Cowen analyst Joshua Buchalter reiterated his buy rating and $675 price target on AMD this morning, citing "growing adoption of agentic AI and production inference workloads." Whereas AI training requires GPUs, you see, AMD's CPUs are better suited for "coordination of multi-step workflows, tool calls, API management, and sequential decision-making" in agentic AI.

AMD seems to agree. The company recently doubled the estimated size of its total addressable market to $220 billion and predicted its sales of CPUs for AI data centers will rise 70% in 2027.

At first glance, the stock still looks richly priced at more than 156 times trailing earnings. But here's the thing: That P/E ratio is based on AMD's $6.4 billion in reported net income. When valued on free cash flow, though, AMD is actually generating more than $8.4 billion in real cash profit.

And that's enough to drop the company's price-to-free cash flow ratio down to just 102x.

Mind you, a P/FCF ratio of 102x still is not obviously "cheap," but with a long-term forecast growth rate of 60%, the stock's price-to-FCF-to-growth ratio is only about 1.7 -- a lot cheap-er than its PEG ratio of 2.6.

While not an obvious bargain, AMD stock is at least a bit cheaper than it looks. While I hesitate to buy it myself, I see why Cowen might think it's a buy.

#24. Google says it can build data centers the right way. Some experts and residents are skeptical

If there's one thing most Americans can agree on, it's that they don't want a data center in their backyard.

A Gallup survey conducted in March found that 71% of Americans opposed the construction of a data center in their local area. Chief among their concerns: energy usage. Half of Americans surveyed by Pew Research Center in July and August said data centers would be mostly bad for the environment and for household energy costs.

Now Google is betting that a massive AI data center can help finance a cleaner, more reliable power grid. Its proposed deal with Xcel Energy would add more wind, solar and battery capacity than the data center is expected to use.

Under the agreement, Google would help pay for the added capacity and continue paying, even if it doesn't use all of the power.

Pine Island, Minnesota, is a small town of about 4,000 residents an hour southeast of Minneapolis. Google hopes that its new 780-megawatt data center plan will build goodwill with the Pine Island community and keep the company on track to meet its goal of operating on carbon-free energy, 24 hours a day, seven days a week by 2030.

Google — whose cloud business powers its own Gemini AI and brought in nearly $25 billion in second-quarter revenue, an 82% increase from a year earlier — says it has found a model for doing this the right way. The company plans to finance the addition of 1,400 megawatts of wind, 200 megawatts of solar and 300 megawatts of battery storage to Xcel's grid.

Those additions amount to more than the capacity of the data center itself, which Google said is because wind and solar do not generate energy at all times. Xcel Energy said the new power will serve all customers in the local area, not just Google. Xcel also said the upgrades will help advance the local grid's carbon-free energy supply.

The proposed agreement between Google and Xcel includes minimum demand charges and exit fees, which Google says will keep the company on the hook for the infrastructure being built on its behalf, even if the AI boom cools. Google will pay for at least 75% of its contracted capacity, even if it uses less, and would owe up to eight years' worth of those minimum demand charges if it terminates the agreement early.

"Nobody wants to have a big buildout and then have nowhere for that power to go and nobody to pay for that power," said Amanda Rome, executive vice president and chief customer officer at Xcel Energy. "That's where these protections come in."

The agreement between Google and Xcel Energy is pending approval by the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission.

New data centers will account for "most" of the projected increase in electricity demand over the next decade, according to the North American Electric Reliability Corporation, a nonprofit regulator.

The Department of Energy under President Joe Biden reported that more than 70% of U.S. transmission lines and power transformers were at least 25 years old and found that the cheapest ways of meeting future demand would require the nation's transmission system to more than double in size by 2050.

But hyperscalers argue that they can finance badly needed grid upgrades while also making the grid cleaner and more reliable.

"The timing of this industrial revolution couldn't be more perfect," said Amanda Peterson Corio, Google's global head of energy and power. "It's right at the time when we needed capital to fix aging infrastructure in the United States."

Jigar Shah, a partner at Multiplier, a consulting firm that helps clean energy startups go public, said data center operators could be constructing smaller facilities in places where the grid already has unused capacity. That would minimize the need to build — and pay for — new generation or transmission equipment.

"If you fit the load growth that the data centers want into the existing grid, everybody's rates go down by a lot," said Shah.

That's because the existing grid has enormous fixed costs from the infrastructure already in place: power plants, transmission lines, substations. If one new customer comes onto the grid and pays a large slice of that, everyone else's bills go down.

"And so the question really is, why are people not doing these 25-megawatt data centers? Why are they doing 1,000-megawatt data centers? And it turns out people are just lazy," Shah said. "They're like, well, it's easier for me to contract one data center that's one gigawatt in size than figuring out how to do something on the order of 40 data centers that are 25 megawatts each."

Industry watchdogs also warn of another reason that utilities often prefer to build new infrastructure, rather than make more use out of their existing grid.

"When [utilities] build something new, they fund part of that investment with dollars from their investors on Wall Street, and they enjoy incredibly high, exorbitant returns on those investments, typically around 10%," said David Pomerantz, executive director at the Energy and Policy Institute, a utility watchdog agency.

Building a data center that fits neatly into an existing grid provides little opportunity for a utility to make new money.

What if a hyperscaler offers to pay for those grid investments?

"One way to leverage data centers to lower people's bills is for data centers to provide that capital at much cheaper rates than the utility," said Pomerantz. "But that's a big problem for the utility. And this fight is actually already emerging."

Still, Shah said, the Google/Xcel project in Minnesota is a good example of a data center project acting as a catalyst for newer, greener technology.

"Google came in and said, well, here's a new way of doing things, using new technologies. How about we do it that way? And then that helps ratepayers. And the utility was like, yeah, that makes a lot of sense."

Watch the video above for the full story, including an interview with Google's global head of energy and power. — CNBC's Jeniece Pettitt and Lora Kolodny contributed to this report.

#25. Netflix's Co-CEO Ted Sarandos Just Gave Investors Bad News Before Earnings

Netflix (NFLX -1.32%) reports earnings on Tuesday, and the company's Co-CEO Ted Sarandos didn't give investors reason to be bullish about the numbers. The company is laying off approximately 6% of its workforce, and Sarandos has recently said that the business simply is "not growing as fast as I want."

These are not things that investors want to see heading into the streaming company's earnings release, as they could suggest a weak quarter is on deck. And that's bad news for a stock that's already been nosediving for much of the year.

Despite the struggles Netflix is facing right now, according to a memo that CNBC has seen, management told its employees that it's still "on track to deliver our full year forecast."

When the company last released earnings in July, it reported 13% revenue growth. It also forecasted that for the full year, its revenue will rise by around 13% to 14%, totaling approximately $51 billion. It's a decent growth rate, but one that clearly management isn't thrilled with. It also comes as Netflix has raised prices this year across all of its plans; investors may have been expecting better growth.

Netflix has been investing more in content and sporting events, and thus, there may be more of a need to show a payoff from such investments.

It's been an exceptionally bad year for Netflix, as its shares have fallen more than 25% thus far, while the S&P 500 has risen by around 13%. That's not typically what investors would expect to see from a growing business, and it signifies the worry that the market has about Netflix's future growth; a premium may be hard to justify given the uncertainty ahead.

Currently, the stock is trading at a forward price-to-earnings multiple of under 19, which is in line with the average stock on the S&P 500. Arguably, however, the stock deserves a better multiple given its growth prospects, as sports, gaming, and international expansion could still open up more potential for the business in the long run.

Its growth rate remains solidly in double digits, which is an encouraging sign that even with multiple rate hikes over the years, consumers continue to see compelling value in its streaming plans. The business may need some tweaks, but I don't think it's in as dire a situation as its sell-off this year might suggest; at a reduced valuation, now could be a great time to buy the stock, as I don’t think it’s likely to go a whole lot lower.

#26. Brian Sullivan: Why the 'real' price of oil is likely $30-$40 higher than where it is now

Oil, in reality, is $125 per barrel or higher.

That's the real cost of a barrel of oil because buying the physical commodity is a very different story from a number on traders' screens.

Oil futures are just that: paper contracts indicating a price today, tomorrow, next month or further out.  If you want to buy the physical commodity, it may be a totally different story — and price.

As I've reported, prices for oil delivery have skyrocketed. Last week, a VLCC (aka a "supertanker" in non-shipper parlance) was chartered from the U.S. Gulf Coast to China for $76 million. Another very large crude carrier went for $77 million from the U.S. to South Korea. That's 10 times more than the price of the same trip less than one year ago.

Assuming these ships hold about 2 million barrels of oil, that charter price means each barrel on the ship costs about $38 over the price of the oil itself.

I'm certainly not saying to avoid looking at oil futures prices, but you need to know that the price on the CNBC screen or CNBC.com isn't always the full price being paid. These days, any company that needs oil shipped by sea, rail or truck will pay a hefty premium over the price of the oil itself. So, while the volume of oil moving through Hormuz is closing in on pre-war levels, costs are not. And there's no sign that they're going anywhere but up.

You know what else is up? The stocks of the shipowners. Look at their moves this month and this year.

On a more serious note, I want to express my condolences for the awful attacks on the airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The cowardly strike on civilians—some of whom were religious pilgrims—took the lives of at least 14 people and injured more than 300.

The airport was attacked at least three times as travelers and energy industry professionals from around the world were flying into Riyadh for the World Petroleum Council conference. I was scheduled to fly in on Saturday, but the trip was canceled because of the strikes. The WPC went on as planned — here's one panel that took place Tuesday — and I look forward to seeing all my global energy friends again soon.

Thanks for reading—and watching. Be safe in these crazy and often scary times.

The supercap oil and gas stock to watch right now is Shell (SHEL). Shell is not a shell of its former self. It's back to being what energy investors wanted: a major player in global energy, focused on what it does best. Shareholders are being rewarded.

Shell hit a new high this week. While analysts remain bullish, the stock is getting close to its target price.

Shell may be underappreciated for its huge liquefied natural gas business. RBC analyst Biraj Borkhataria writes: "Without a sustained resumption in Qatari volumes and with European storage levels below seasonal lows heading into winter, European gas prices continued on an upward trajectory in 3Q26. With HH broadly unchanged throughout the summer, export margins have increased to the widest levels seen since 2022, on our estimates nearly double the level in 2Q26 (~$13/mmbtu vs. $7/mmbtu)."

Borkhataria expects Shell and other companies with huge U.S. LNG positions — TotalEnergies (TTE) and BP (BP) — to benefit from wider margins on exports to Europe.

Speaking of RBC and energy, the firm lists ConocoPhillips as one of its top 30 global stock ideas. The company is covered by analyst Scott Hanold, who believes it has a "returns-focused value proposition, a strong balance sheet, and peer-leading distributions." He loves its "global and diverse" asset base and management's clear "investment propositions." Hanold has a $152 target on COP. That's more than 20% upside.

In oil and gas, refiners and big energy stocks are generating cash for investors, and Morgan Stanley is optimistic more is coming.

The firm says the diesel shortage is now spilling over into gasoline, potentially marking another leg of the "golden age" for refiners. Morgan Stanley has been revising its earnings estimates higher for companies including ExxonMobil (XOM), Valero (VLO), Phillips 66 (PSX) and PBF (PBF).

Fun Fact →  While nearly every other company calls Texas home, refiner PBF is headquartered in a suburban office park just off a highway in New Jersey.

Two big calls to quickly highlight in power production.

First, Truist says you have to buy First Solar (FSLR). The analyst upgrades it to Buy with a $270 target. Tariffs should help the Phoenix-based company, giving it pricing power for at least four more years. The Section 232 tariffs—which are too complicated to detail here—should help First Solar raise solar module prices and boost earnings. We agree, having written about the company and stock back in July.

Another call on the Power Insider radar: TD Cowen is starting coverage of TeraWulf (WULF) with a Buy rating and a $21 target. That indicates about 50% upside for the stock, but it's actually one of the Street's lower price targets. TeraWulf and other AI power companies have seen their stocks hit hard following months of big gains, but Cowen analyst Michael Elias says the valuation is now attractive and a likely lease in the second half of 2027 at a Kentucky location could be a catalyst.

In the wake of the terror attacks on Saudi Arabia, we spoke with RBC Capital Markets' Helima Croft about the attacks, energy and more.

The entire energy world is watching Europe's natural gas storage levels. The question is whether the continent will have enough gas to make it safely through the winter. Power Insider wrote about the topic in the last issue.

The fact that JPMorgan highlights expected weather patterns should tell you how much temperature matters when it comes to gas storage. The early forecast calls for October and November to be average or slightly warmer than the 10-year average. The red line represents the 10-year average.

Europe has been largely "saved" by mild temperatures over the past few years. Natural gas storage levels are lower this year than in years past, so the thermometer will matter a lot when it comes to how well countries can, ahem, weather the winter. Random, but interesting.

#33. Elon Musk says he'll give a SpaceX share to every child in America next year

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said Monday that he'll give every child in the U.S. one of his shares in the company next year.

Musk currently owns about 4.8 billion SpaceX shares, according to an August SEC filing. That figure rises to 6.4 billion when taking into account unvested awards and stock options, representing a 48.4% beneficial stake in the company.

There were 72 million children under 18 in the U.S. as of July 1, 2025, according to official census data.

That would amount to the CEO giving away about $10.5 billion worth of shares, taking into account SpaceX's closing stock price of $146.03 as of Friday.

"This will be the first of many," Musk said in a post on X, without providing further details on how the share giveaway would happen.

CNBC has reached out to SpaceX and Musk's family office for further details.

Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner, founder of Invest America and Trump Accounts, praised the move and suggested in a post on X that the SpaceX shares could be distributed via Trump accounts.

"Incredible Elon!" he wrote. "This will be the largest philanthropic gift in history! 70 M accounts - every citizen under 18 & every child born forevermore now has a free, lifetime investment acct making them an owner in the upside of America & our greatest companies!"

Musk's financial giving has been in the news in recent weeks primarily for his political contributions.

The Tesla CEO has spent more than $276 million in donations to Republican groups since July, making him the biggest known donor of the 2026 midterm election.

The world's richest person poured $158 million into the Senate Leadership Fund, the Republican Party's leading Senate super PAC, in September through an affiliated Texas PAC created to support Republican Ken Paxton. Musk's two contributions of $75 million and $83 million are among the largest political donations ever.

When it comes to fulfilling his philanthropic promises, Musk has a spotty track record.

For example, the Tesla and SpaceX CEO contributed about $38 million to OpenAI, which he co-founded as a nonprofit research lab, between 2016 and 2020. But he had promised to contribute up to $1 billion, and cut off donations to the organization amid a battle with cofounders for control of the company.

In 2021, Musk said he would donate $6 billion to the United Nations World Food Program if it could show him a plan for how they'd use the money to "solve world hunger." While the WFP posted a plan, Musk did not donate.

Musk's foundation has also repeatedly fallen shy of making the minimum donations it's required to by law, and as The New York Times previously reported, its donations go to charities that closely benefit Musk and his companies directly.

Musk's post came just after Anthropic revealed plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund, with the stake potentially increasing as the company's valuation grows.

In response to an Anthropic post on X about the fund on Sunday, Musk replied, "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public," and added that's what he'd be doing.

Subject to shareholder approval, Anthropic's fund would immediately commit 5% of Anthropic's shares, with the board adding, at its discretion, an additional 2% for every 50% increase in the company's value above a set baseline that has yet to be disclosed.

The fund may be used to "explore large donations," including to traditional nonprofits or as direct distributions for specific populations, or for "bolder approaches" to study and address AI's disruption and displacement of jobs, the company said.

— CNBC's Jennifer Liu contributed to this report.

#35. CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors sour on AI debt

CoreWeave's credit stress continued to spiral on Thursday amid a broader sell-off in AI-related names.

CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure build-out. It's now facing a rebellion from stock and bond investors as concerns mount about AI overspending and debt levels.

Yields on CoreWeave debt have continued to climb, with the yield to maturity on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 reaching 15.78%. Bond yields move inversely to prices. Meanwhile, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, at one point soared above 1,140 basis points. It last stood at nearly 1,038 bps — a 16% week-over-week jump and 164% higher than a year ago.

Credit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock dropped during trading Thursday before recovering and closing 5.94% higher. The moved followed Wednesday's 15.5% nosedive.

Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure. Nebius also sank before climbing higher to close 1.29% and and Iren ultimately ended the day down less than 1%.

Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares of Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices sold off following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks. Micron closed up 1.87%, while AMD fell 1.5%.

While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power.

Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress.

Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier.

The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said.

A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

No one is questioning whether demand for CoreWeave's services is real, since the company has contracts with all the big hyperscalers, Nolan said. The question is whether the cash flows will ultimately arrive.

"It's obviously heavily negative free cash flow at the moment, and it needs that cash flow to arrive really to justify all the capex that it's spending," Nolan said.

CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves on Wednesday, according to a memo obtained by CNBC.

"When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations."

The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts including Microsoft, Meta, IBM and Caterpillar, Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity.

"The problem is this kind of concern can prove to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, and risks triggering broader issues in other AI-related names," said Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research.

Domino effects may already be happening. Oracle's five-year CDS spread also spiked this week. It was last at 282 basis points, a roughly 10% increase in one week.

"A downgrade from its BBB rating would risk pressuring IG-only investors into forced sales," Reid said.

#42. Better Emerging Markets ETF: Schwab's SCHE vs. Vanguard's VWO

The choice between the Schwab Emerging Markets Equity ETF (SCHE +0.13%) and Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF (VWO +0.19%) centers on portfolio depth, as both funds charge identical fees but differ in diversification and yield.

Investing in developing economies offers exposure to high-growth markets that often move independently of U.S. indices. Both Schwab Emerging Markets Equity ETF and Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF track FTSE indices, capturing companies across nations such as China, Taiwan, and India, while maintaining extremely low costs for long-term investors.

Beta measures price volatility relative to the S&P 500; beta is calculated from monthly returns over the available fund history (up to five years). The 1-year return represents total return over the trailing 12 months. Dividend yield is the trailing-12-month distribution yield.

Both funds are highly cost-efficient, featuring a 0.06% expense ratio. However, the Schwab fund offers a more generous payout, with a 2.7% trailing dividend yield that currently exceeds the 2.1% yield provided by the Vanguard fund.

The Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF focuses on a massive basket of approximately 5,942 stocks, emphasizing technology (32%), financial services (20%), and consumer cyclical names (10%). Its largest positions include Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co Ltd at 15.76%, Tencent Holdings Ltd (SEHK:0700) at 2.82%, and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd at 2.11%. The fund was launched in 2005, and has paid $1.22 per share over the trailing 12 months, which on its recent ~$58.79 share price works out to a 2.1% yield.

The Schwab Emerging Markets Equity ETF tracks a narrower but still expansive group of 2,238 holdings, with a sector tilt toward technology at 35%, financial services at 21%, and consumer cyclical at 9%. Top holdings include Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing at 17.59%, Tencent Holdings at 3.14%, and Alibaba Group Holding at 2.49%. The fund was launched in 2010, and has paid $0.95 per share over the trailing 12 months, which on its recent ~$36.14 share price works out to a 2.7% yield.

For more guidance on ETF investing, check out the full guide at this link.

Both the Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF (VWO) and Schwab Emerging Markets Equity ETF (SCHE) provide investors with exposure to emerging market economies, so which is the better fund to pick?

VWO and SCHE are similar in many ways, including one-year and five-year returns. Vanguard's ETF was more expensive, but it recently lowered the expense ratio, so now the two match. Where VWO has the advantage is in its far larger AUM of $164.7 billion, and substantial number of holdings. VWO is the fund for those who want maximum liquidity, a massive asset base, and a broader basket of nearly 6,000 global emerging market equities. It's also a natural choice if you are already a Vanguard customer.

SCHE wins out on dividend yield, and is a convenient choice for investors who are already Schwab customers. This fund restricts its scope strictly to larger companies, while VWO includes small-cap stocks, contributing to the significant difference in the number of holdings in each fund.

#43. NYSE becomes latest exchange to extend options hours as appetite for around-the-clock trading grows

The New York Stock Exchange becomes the second major exchange to announce extended-hours options trading for heavily-traded ETFs and single stocks, following CBOE's announcement that it will introduce extended trading for 25 single stocks and five ETFs.

Extended options trading hours for the NYSE, which is owned and operated by the Intercontinental Exchange, begin Monday, and will operate from 7:30 AM to 9:25 AM ET, while the new late trading session will operate from 4:00 PM to 4:15 PM ET.

Twenty-nine major stocks and funds are available for extended trading including Nvidia, Bank of America, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust and the iShares Russell 2000 ETF.

Beginning Dec. 6, 2026, NYSE will extend trading to 23 hours, five days a week in those same names.

"Markets have changed tremendously over the years, and that kind of progress only happens when you keep investing in your technology," said Kevin Tyrrell, chief product officer, NYSE, in a statement. "Extended trading hours for options reflects market demand for investment opportunities and reliable risk management during a longer period of time."

The fresh offering from NYSE reflects growing demand for derivatives products among traders, as well as strong appetite for 24/7 trading instruments. Crypto was the first asset class to offer continuous trading. More recently, prediction markets and perpetual futures offer a 24/7 schedule and a unique exposure across demand-heavy areas of the market.

Data from CBOE confirms the growing appetite for trading beyond the regular session. Extended hours trading just hit its highest levels on record – more than 199,000 contracts per day on average – following steady growth and an explosion of activity this year.

Volumes were very muted Monday for the first extended session for stocks. The standout volume is in options on Tesla ahead of earnings this Wednesday. A little over 3,000 contracts traded, almost all call contracts -- likely traders rolling positions -- worth a total value less than $100,000, according to SpotGamma data.

#50. Traders pile into 'bubble puts' on CoreWeave as neocloud stocks plunge

A key corner of the artificial intelligence trade is taking a beating on Wednesday and traders are betting it could get even worse.

Shares of neocloud companies – businesses that offer access to the GPUs powering artificial intelligence as a service – plunged Wednesday after debt yields for Nvidia-backed CoreWeave continued to reach new heights. (An article in The Financial Times that the company is targeting insurance companies for further debt financing apparently didn't help things either.)

Meanwhile, in a post on X, Social Capital founder Chamath Palihapitiya raised questions about a private credit bubble alongside a screengrab showing CoreWeave's bonds hitting a 15% yield. Elon Musk replied "yikes." CoreWeave stock plunged 15%. Nebius Group and Iren, popular trades connected to the data centers build-out, also fell as much as 10%.

Options volume in CoreWeave surged to more than seven times the 30-day average, Nebius almost four times, and Iren twice the normal volume. More calls traded than puts in Nebius and Iren, but in both, more calls were likely initiated by sellers than buyers, according to Cboe LiveVol data.

The most bearish action was in CoreWeave, where traders bought just shy of 200,000 puts, compared to 106,000 calls.

One standout trade happened around 10 a.m. ET when someone opened a new position of 26,000 37.5-strike puts expiring Dec. 18 that traded near the ask price, suggesting the puts were purchased, according to SpotGamma data.

"These are bubble puts," said Scott Bauer, CEO of Chicago-based Prosper Trading Academy. "These are not rip-ups that you buy thinking they'll go to zero. This is the hub, the center of the AI trade, and likely some kind of margin play for someone to hedge their exposure in highly correlated stocks or maybe even the Nasdaq."

The contracts sold for 74 cents apiece for a total of $1.9 million and need CoreWeave to erase another 42% over the next two months to pay off. Prior to this trade, there were just over 1,000 open contracts, meaning the position is a new one.

CoreWeave IPO'd in March 2025 at $40 per share.

"Maybe this is someone that was in early or in on the IPO saying this is my breakeven level," Bauer added. "Maybe they couldn't get this kind of protection in other stocks, the index, or other products."

#51. Why Palantir Technologies Stock Rallied Today

Palantir Technologies (PLTR +5.10%) stock was sharply higher Monday morning, gaining as much as 5.9%. As of 12:19 p.m. ET, the stock was still up 5.5%.

The catalyst that sent the data-mining and artificial intelligence (AI) software specialist higher was a new partnership that expands the availability of its technology.

In a press release that dropped Monday morning, Palantir announced a new partnership with Knox Systems, one of the world's largest Federal and Department of Defense (DoD) managed cloud providers. The collaboration "ensures mission-critical applications have access to the most secure infrastructure possible, while still being able to deploy their product on their schedule, at the fastest pace possible."

The partnership brings together Palantir's leading data mining and AI platform and Knox's managed federal cloud computing platform. Together, the pair will help customers accelerate their acceptance into the Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP), "getting the best technology into the hands of the warfighter and the U.S. Government," according to the release.

Palantir's AI solutions already help consolidate and process battlefield data in real time, identify and track enemy threats, and coordinate responses. FedRAMP and Impact Level 5 are two of the strictest federal certification standards. This partnership helps accelerate software deployments in these environments more quickly, getting the company's solutions to more warfighters more quickly.

Recent concerns about the future of AI adoption have weighed on Palantir, though the stock still appears pricey at 83 times next year's expected earnings. However, thanks to Palantir's triple-digit profit growth, the stock's price/earnings-to-growth (PEG) ratio comes in at 0.5, when any number less than 1 is the standard for an undervalued stock.

#53. Women may be at greater risk of AI job losses. Telephone switch operators and PCs show why

Decades before Siri or Alexa or ChatGPT, there was a real person, almost always a woman, at the center of the information world. She was so vital, most long-distance communication could not happen without her.

She was the telephone switch operator, and at one time she was part of the single largest occupation for white, U.S.-born women under age 20.

The world is struggling to figure out what the dawn of artificial intelligence means for society, culture and the economy. A lot of ordinary Americans are just wondering what it means for their jobs.

The history of technological progress — from automated telephone switches to the introduction of the washing machine and the personal computer — can offer some guidance. And that guidance suggests women are likely to be among the most affected by AI.

"AI is focused on routine tasks and numbers and finding patterns, and those types of jobs are the clerical, administrative jobs that a lot of women hold,'' said Ariane Hegewisch, a senior research fellow at the Institute for Women's Policy Research. "It's still 90% of secretaries and clerical workers who are women."

New research backs this up. The International Labour Organization in March concluded that nearly one in 10 women in high-income countries works in occupations at the highest risk from AI.

In the 1940s, nearly 95% of America's telephone operators were female. It was a relatively well-paying job for women at the time, and a complicated one: It took months of training to be able to handle the several hundred calls an hour that could come in at peak times. Operators were expected to be speedy, precise — and polite.

These women were hit hard when AT&T introduced the automated telephone switch. It was one of the largest automation investments in history — a close analog to the massive AI investment now underway — and created one of the biggest technological shocks the nation had ever seen.

In the decades after the automatic switch was popularized, an estimated 75,000 operator jobs vanished.

Economists James Feigenbaum from Boston University and Daniel P. Gross from Duke University's Fuqua School of Business studied census and paycheck data from the time and followed local employment trends along the path of AT&T's rolling investment in switches across the nation.

"The effect of this shock on incumbent operators was to dispossess many of their jobs and careers," they wrote in 2020. Many switchboard operators wound up in lower-paying jobs — or dropped out of the workforce entirely, they found.

Economist David Autor says this outcome reflects the reality that many workers are already in their highest and best-paying occupation. When the job goes away, the next step is often down.

"Most people are not changing careers very often. They make their career decisions early, and they stick with those careers," he said. "If those careers, if the value of that work … suddenly goes out of fashion, becomes technologically obsolete, they're going to, in general, do something not as good."

But Feigenbaum and Gross also discovered that the next generation of women fared better.

"Future workers found work in other fields, often taking up similar-quality jobs," they wrote, as the younger workers were "more adaptive to an evolving labor market … Anxiety over the opportunities available to future generations proved to be somewhat misplaced."

In other words: One type of job went away, but other work emerged over time that was just as good.

By the 1950s, another technological innovation would come along and have a profound effect on women: the washing machine.

Dubbed "engines of liberation" in a seminal paper on the topic by University of Pennsylvania economist Jeremy Greenwood and others, washing machines and other appliances dramatically reduced the time women spent on unpaid housework.  That meant time could be reallocated to a paycheck outside the home, even as women's responsibility for the home remained.

From 1950 to 1980, as gender norms changed, the number of employed women in the U.S. grew by more than 25 million. Their participation rate, or share of the female population in the labor force, grew to 52% from 34%. At the same time, 16 million more men found work, though the male participation rate dropped by 5 percentage points.

The relevant question for the AI boom today: How did the economy suddenly find jobs for these women? If AI creates a vast new pool of available workers, can the economy put them to work?

First, the very entry of women into the workforce meant demand for tasks once done at home moved into the paid economy, services like childcare and food preparation. Second, as the nation grew wealthier, other employment opportunities for women emerged in the service economy — in retail, restaurants, leisure and hospitality, and even some professional services. And third, as American businesses grew, they needed more people to handle the paperwork — everything from payroll to customer accounts.

Changes to the economy and businesses were partly related to the entry of women into the workforce, but it was also partly random luck that the U.S. was booming and businesses were changing to need more office workers.

"Between 1940 and 1980, there was a ton of new work created in the U.S. economy, and it was in office and clerical work that was accessible to people with a high school education,'' Autor said.

The next big revolution affecting women in the workplace was the personal computer.

Before PCs arrived on the scene, women were the backbone of office infrastructure. According to the 1980 U.S. census, nearly 4.7 million Americans worked as secretaries, stenographers and typists. More than 98% were women.

When IBM introduced the personal computer in 1981, followed by the advent of Microsoft Word just two years later, some of the middlemen, or in this case, middlewomen, became obsolete. It didn't eliminate writing, filing or editing. It simply shifted a big chunk of those tasks from dedicated clerical workers to others in the office — executives could type their own reports, book their own travel and print their own papers.

But the PC wasn't entirely bad news for women in the workforce. Studies show women were already more likely than men to be using a computer at work at the dawn of the PC era. The PC put new tools at their fingertips: spreadsheets and databases and general computing power. While many roles were eliminated, many women adapted and found new ways to use the emerging technology to make themselves indispensable to their employers.

That's a potential outcome for AI. In some cases, it will eliminate tasks but not entire jobs, enhancing the time and ability of a worker to do the remaining value-added jobs that only humans can do.

A 2022 paper by Marcus Dillender and Eliza Forsythe found that when companies adopted software to do office and administrative work, it resulted in a 1% decline in employment in the sector but a 3% increase in wages for college graduates.

Many more women have earned college and advanced degrees, and hold managerial jobs, than when other technologies ripped through the economy, offering some potential protection from automation. But maybe not for long: One of the promises of AI is that it will move up the value chain of the jobs performed by humans.

Whatever capabilities the new technology may have now, the outlook is unclear because, Hegewisch says, somewhat ominously, "AI can learn."

#60. Arista Networks Is Heading for a Big Test on Nov. 3. Here's What Could Send the Stock Soaring.

Arista Networks (ANET +4.27%) is scheduled to report third-quarter earnings on Nov. 3, but I think the most important numbers in the report won't have anything to do with the third quarter.

Instead, I'll be watching what management says about the final three months of 2026.

According to Yahoo Finance, Wall Street expects the artificial intelligence (AI) networking company to generate $3.6 billion in fourth-quarter revenue and earnings of $1.15 per share. Those are some pretty ambitious targets, but I think Arista has a good chance to exceed them.

And if management delivers guidance that beats those expectations, I think Arista stock could soar after Nov. 3.

Arista has become an important supplier of the high-speed networking equipment that connects processors and servers inside massive artificial intelligence data centers.

Companies such as Nvidia are developing increasingly powerful graphics processing units (GPUs), but those chips can't reach their full potential unless enormous amounts of information can move between them quickly.

Arista makes Ethernet switches that help eliminate networking bottlenecks, allowing thousands of processors to work together on demanding AI applications.

The company reported second-quarter revenue of $3.03 billion, a 37.7% increase from a year ago. Diluted earnings per share reached $0.95, compared with $0.70 in the year-earlier period. Management also projected third-quarter revenue of approximately $3.3 billion.

That's in line with what Wall Street projects. According to Yahoo Finance, the consensus Q3 estimates are $3.33 billion in revenue and $1.08 in earnings per share (EPS).

I'm not too worried about Q3 results -- instead, I'd rather look ahead. Investors already know that Arista is growing quickly. What they need to know now is whether demand for their networking equipment will remain strong as cloud computing companies continue to expand their AI infrastructure.

That's why fourth-quarter guidance could be more important than the third-quarter results themselves.

Arista has been introducing new networking products designed to handle increasingly demanding AI workloads.

Its 7060XE7 platform supports connections running at 1.6 terabits per second, while its recently announced Etherlink SU-144 architecture can connect up to 144 AI accelerators within a single-hop network.

Those capabilities are becoming more important as AI data centers grow larger and companies look for ways to get more performance from their expensive processors.

The opportunity is substantial, but so is the competition. Nvidia and Cisco Systems are also pursuing the AI networking market, and Arista depends heavily on spending by major cloud computing companies. Still, I think the company's recent growth gives management a reasonable opportunity to surprise Wall Street.

Arista typically provides quarterly revenue and margin guidance rather than an explicit earnings-per-share forecast. So I'll be watching whether its fourth-quarter revenue outlook exceeds $3.6 billion and whether its projected profitability supports earnings above the $1.15 consensus estimate.

A revenue forecast above expectations would suggest that demand for Arista's networking equipment remains stronger than Wall Street anticipated. Healthy margins would make that growth even more valuable to shareholders.

#61. Don't let inflation bite — how to hedge with TIPS, commodities and infrastructure funds

The Consumer Price Index hit 3.7% in September – the latest sign that inflation remains a problem that isn't going away.

It's a tough situation for investors looking for protection, but there are some good ways to hedge.

Long-term Treasury Inflation-Protected securities (TIPS) yield 2.9%, near multi-decade highs. Beyond TIPS, analysts suggest commodities, infrastructure, and other assets that can hedge against rising prices.

While inflation is down sharply from its 9.1% peak in 2022, it's still well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. Headline CPI's 3.7% rate in September topped estimates for 3.6%. Core CPI, excluding food and energy, reached 2.6%, also higher than expected. Rising energy prices drove much of the increase. But the Personal Consumption Expenditures index, the Fed's preferred gauge, also remains elevated at a core 3% rate.

Americans' inflation concerns are also rising. The New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations showed the one-year inflation outlook in September climbed to 3.9%, its highest level since May 2023.

Despite their name, TIPS haven't provided much inflation protection this year. The iShares TIPS Bond ETF, which tracks the ICE U.S. Treasury Inflation Linked Bond Index, has a total return of -1.16% year-to-date.

Like most other bonds, TIPS have been hit hard by rising rates. The 10-year Treasury note is up sharply this year and spiked Wednesday to 5.29%, near the highest levels since 2002. Bond prices and yields move inversely, and as rates climbed many TIPS funds suffered.

But higher yields have made TIPS more attractive. The 10-year TIPS' 2.9% yield is up from roughly 1.9% early in the year.

"Given where rates are, it's getting interesting," says Jason Draho, head of asset allocation Americas at UBS Global Wealth Management.

TIPS pay a fixed coupon, or interest rate, but as inflation moves higher, the principal value of the bond increases. The adjustments reflect changes in inflation, based on the non-seasonally adjusted CPI for All Urban Consumers, with a three-month lag.

The upshot is that TIPS investors earn interest on a higher principal value over time. That's the essence of the protection compared to traditional Treasuries.

TIPS' poor performance this year isn't because of a surge in inflation expectations. Almost all the increase has been due to rising real yields — the nominal yield minus expected inflation. Real yields are up because of factors like robust economic growth and a U.S. fiscal deficit around 6% of gross domestic product (requiring far more government borrowing).

If nominal rates were rising just due to inflation, then TIPS total return — a mix of yield and price — would be fine, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. But that isn't the case.

"TIPS have produced losses in total return because their income accruals have been insufficient to offset the price decline produced by the rising underlying real yields," Gallo explained.

TIPS maturing in 10 years or more are highly sensitive to duration risk, Draho notes. "You're making a big call on rates not rising any further if you buy TIPS, especially longer maturities of 10-year plus," he said.

The bull case is that inflation comes down quicker than expected. That's not the market's expectation, based on short-term Treasury yields, notes Draho. But if inflation does ease next year, which he expects, the yield curve would adjust lower.

One way to manage duration risk is to own individual TIPS rather than a fund that has to maintain duration consistent with a benchmark index. Investors could create a TIPS bond ladder with varying maturities, pegged to their income needs over the next decade, for instance.

If you hold a TIPS to maturity you may experience price volatility, but you'll get the original principal or inflation-adjusted price, whichever is greater, when the bond matures.

Short-term TIPS provide more protection against rate increases and they look attractive, said PIMCO portfolio manager Greg Sharenow.

"While as a firm, our view is that inflation will ultimately come down, that view keeps on being pushed out as real world events unfold," he said. "We've seen over and over again the last five to seven years — where we're now in our third supply shock — that you end up actually underpricing versus realized inflation," he added.

Funds focusing on short-term TIPS include Vanguard Short-Term Inflation-Protected Securities ETF, iShares 0-5 Year TIPS Bond ETF and PIMCO 1-5 Year US TIPS Index ETF.

TIPS, of course, aren't the only way to go. Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, suggests a multi-pronged strategy, including equities, commodities, and alternative assets.

"I'd start layering in more income, keep interest-rate exposure moderate, and then what a lot of people are doing is use things like alternatives to to create more balance in a portfolio," he said. "That makes a lot of sense to me."

Broad inflation-protection funds include State Street Multi-Asset Real Return ETF, Fidelity Strategic Real Return Fund and PIMCO Inflation Response Multi-Asset Fund.

The PIMCO fund's holdings include TIPS, commodities, gold and real estate investment trusts.

"The idea is to have a number of different exposures so that we can have a more balanced return and not try to be so specific in getting the exact right asset class at any one moment," said Sharenow, a manager on the fund.

He adds that he sees "significant value" in TIPS, which have the heaviest weighting in the portfolio. Commodities are the next largest holding. They have price "pass-throughs," which is how much companies can shift costs to customers through price increases. That is beneficial to investors, he noted.

Separately, the fund holds about 10% each in gold and REITs.

Draho recommends commodities, based partly on long-term asset-allocation studies that include the 1970s when inflation was far higher. "Over a long period they can help reduce risk and improve diversification," he said. "Their benefits have been most pronounced when inflation was overshooting expectations."

Rather than picking individual commodities, he suggests owning a basket that's consistently rebalanced. Gold and oil, for instance, perform well in different economic and monetary policy scenarios, and it can be tricky to get the timing right.

Commodity ETFs to consider include the Invesco Optimum Yield Diversified Commodity Strategy ETF (PDBC) and the iShares S&P GSCI Commodity-Indexed Trust (GSG).

Another asset class Draho suggests is infrastructure — operators of roads, ports, bridges, and other hard assets. Companies in the space tend to be toll takers, collecting long-term revenue under contracts that include inflation riders or built-in price adjustments.

Investors can get exposure to infrastructure through ETFs such as the iShares Global Infrastructure ETF (IGF) and ProShares DJ Brookfield Global Infrastructure ETF (TOLZ).

Draho isn't sounding alarms on inflation but says it makes sense to add protection against another move higher.

"The risk now is there will be supply side shocks that could push up inflation again," he said.

— CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.
