#62. Cornell sexual assault case has some prospective students rethinking plans, consultants say

As Cornell University faces scrutiny over its handling of sexual assault allegations, some prospective students are reconsidering whether to apply, according to college admissions consultants who spoke with CNBC.

The concerns come just weeks before Cornell's Nov. 1 early-decision deadline, when applicants must decide whether to submit an application under a binding agreement to attend the Ivy League university if admitted.

Amid public outrage over the handling of the 2024 alleged incident and the ensuing Jane Doe lawsuit, some high school seniors have decided to take the school out of consideration, according to Christopher Rim, president and CEO of college consulting firm Command Education.

"I originally had nine students applying to Cornell, four were early — now we have zero applying early," he said.

The lawsuit centers on a civil complaint filed in September by a former student identified as Jane Doe. She alleges that in October 2024 she was sexually assaulted at one of the school's fraternity houses on Cornell's campus in Ithaca, New York.

Jamie Beaton, co-founder and CEO of college consulting firm Crimson Education, also said he is "seeing some Cornell applicants reconsider applying there based on campus safety and culture concerns."

Cornell directed CNBC to Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff's Oct. 13 message. In a statement, the university said it is conducting an independent review, led by former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates, to examine long-standing policies and practices. Separately, Cornell suspended all fraternity parties and social events for the remainder of the 2026-27 academic year.

"These conversations, and campus protests, have underscored my deep conviction that we must do better: that the time for meaningful and lasting change at Cornell, and at campuses across the country, is now," Kotlikoff said in the statement.

What comes next is key, Rim said. "It's very important for Cornell to make sure they do the right thing and make actual changes to their policies," he said. "Then they are going to have to convince students and families they are serious about it."

Changing course so close to the early-decision deadline can be difficult for applicants who have spent months tailoring their applications to a specific Cornell school, a distinctive part of the university's application process, according to Beaton.

Some applicants "feel psychologically committed," he said, and are "staying the course, and are holding onto hope that the scrutiny on Cornell will force it to make serious reforms to institutional conduct and culture as a result of this."

In some cases, applying early decision can improve an applicant's odds of admission but leaves less time to work on the application or compare options. The regular-decision deadline for Cornell is Jan. 2.

Going forward, "what we expect is that things will be loud in the short term," Beaton said, referring specifically to this application cycle. But he added that there will likely be minimal long-term movement in application volumes or yield, which is the percent of students who choose to enroll after being admitted.

"Scandals at highly selective universities don't move application volumes in a lasting way, since the pull of the brand, the outcomes and the network is too strong," Beaton said.

Cornell is the largest Ivy by undergraduate enrollment. With an acceptance rate under 10%, Cornell most recently admitted 5,776 applicants to the Class of 2030, according to the university's independent student newspaper, The Cornell Daily Sun.

#74. French unrest compounds debt crisis fears. Paris-listed stocks, bonds and the euro fall

Social unrest, political instability and mounting national debt weighed on French assets on Monday, with government bonds and Paris-listed stocks under pressure.

The euro was last seen down 0.15% against the U.S. dollar, and was 0.1% lower against the British pound.

The French 10-year bond yield jumped more than 10 basis points, taking it just shy of its highest level in decades. Higher yields represent higher borrowing costs for the government in the debt market. The country's 2-year and 30-year yields were up 6 basis points and 8 basis points, respectively.

Stocks are also feeling the heat, with the CAC 40 index down 1.7% in afternoon deals on Monday. The market has significantly underperformed its European peers in recent years as political volatility has mounted — despite only around 15% of its revenues being generated domestically — with banks under particular pressure.

The French stock market is historically sensitive to any widening in the so-called "OAT-Bund spread", the extra bond yield France pays over Germany, which has hit the highest level since the European Sovereign Debt Crisis of the early 2010s. French yields now also surpass those of Italy or Greece, implying higher risk.

Widening bond spreads raise concerns about the cost for companies to raise capital and heighten fears of higher taxes and tighter regulation. The French stock market has also struggled due to the dominance of its luxury firms, which are suffering from a downturn in high-end Chinese consumer spending.

Hundreds of thousands of people marched over the weekend in protest over political paralysis, the cost of living and the state of public services, including schools and healthcare.

Mass gatherings in cities from Paris to Lyon and Marseille spilled into dramatic scenes of buildings and cars set on fire, clashes with police and more than 2,000 arrests.

"If you're an international investor thinking about whether you want to invest in French bonds, it's not helpful," Mike Bell, head of market strategy at RBC BlueBay Asset Management, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Monday.

"It looks like either the bond markets riot, or the people riot, or both," Bell said.

Overseas investors hold a growing share of French debt, rising from around 48% at the start of 2022 to nearly 60% at the start of 2026, potentially meaning higher volatility in the bond market in a risk-off environment.

"What's needed in France is to get the fiscal position in order, they need to raise the retirement age — you can't retire at 62 if the average person's living to 84 — but if this is going on even before they start talking about that, then imagine what would happen on the streets of France if you tried to raise the retirement age to... I mean here in the U.K. it's 68," Bell added.

"It doesn't make the country look that governable against a time when they need to be putting through hard choices."

France's benchmark borrowing costs are touching their highest level since 2002, with investors demanding greater returns to lend to the government.

Key concerns include uncertainty over next year's presidential election, in which far-right Marine Le Pen is topping many polls, and whether the minority government of Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu can pass the 2027 budget currently under negotiation.

Budget negotiations are increasingly fraught in France and have toppled two of Lecornu's recent predecessors in recent years.

Analysts say lenders want a credible fiscal-consolidation plan to keep France from being caught in a debt spiral: weak growth and a persistently high deficit-to-GDP ratio are pushing up bond yields, raising the government's debt-servicing bill and widening the deficit further — which could drive borrowing costs higher still.

"It will be difficult to see the budget deficit come down without painful measures," Sharon Bell, senior European equity strategist at Goldman Sachs, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Monday.

"Taxes could well go up for French businesses. I think taxes may generally go up in France, fiscal consolidation means you need to either spend less or tax more. Those things are very tricky."

"Le Pen, who is riding high in the polls at the moment, she's talked about keeping a Golden Budget [rule] during her term, but she's not really detailed how that would happen," Bell continued.

"One of the reasons that OAT-Bund spreads are not coming in is because investors are skeptical that you will see any fiscal consolidation and a decline in that budget deficit."

But Ken Egan, senior director of sovereigns at ratings agency KBRA, noted auctions last week showed there remains "still very solid underlying demand for French debt."

"It is a more risk-off morning generally, but France is clearly taking a little more of the pressure... The question markets will be asking is how easily France can actually make progress from here," Egan said by email.

Goldman Sachs' Sharon Bell added that she did not believe current conditions warranted any emergency intervention by the European Central Bank, which "doesn't want" to use tools such as its Transmission Protection Instrument.

However, she said if spreads start to disrupt market liquidity, the ECB would opt to use the mechanism.

Such a move would be politically sensitive, likely requiring France to engage in even more stringent fiscal reforms over a long period akin to those by countries such as Greece, Portugal and Ireland during the euro area crisis, she added.

"Sometimes it does take market pressure, and that's what we've seen this year."

RBC BlueBay Asset Management's Mike Bell meanwhile said France was facing a "very real risk" of its own sovereign debt crisis.

"Ultimately they need to get the fiscal house in order. If you even suggested what's actually needed for that, you wouldn't get elected, and if you tried to put it in without having put it through on a mandate for election, then you'd have riots in the street."

Before any intervention, there will be an "almighty clash between whoever wins the next election" and the ECB, Bell added. The central bank is unlikely to step in unless countries comply with its excess deficit procedure, which states that the general government budget deficit must not exceed 3% of GDP. France's current deficit is around 5%.

Banque de France Governor Emmanuel Moulin told CNBC last week that rising French yields were due to political uncertainty, but said it was "possible to get back to a 3% deficit in 2029, which is the objective of the government."

#78. Rocket Lab Delays Neutron Again. Is the Stock in Trouble?

Last week was a bad one for rocket company Rocket Lab (RKLB +3.23%). It plunged on news that it would be delaying the launch of Neutron, which is now not expected to take place until next year. There have been multiple delays, and investors are growing frustrated.

In just the past six months, the stock has declined by close to 40%, with many investors potentially pivoting instead to Space Exploration Technologies Corp, Elon Musk's rocket company that went public back in the summer.

Rocket Lab hasn't been as exciting a growth stock to own of late. But while a delay in the launch of its Neutron rocket is definitely not good news, that alone shouldn't be a reason to dump the stock. Here's why this may potentially be a good time to buy Rocket Lab on this weakness.

Rocket Lab has not only generated strong growth in recent quarters, but its future remains highly promising. In its most recent quarter, which ended on June 30, the company's revenue rose by 62% year over year to $234 million. Its backlog was even more impressive, rising by 137% to a little less than $2.4 billion.

The company is also in the midst of acquiring satellite company Iridium Communications, which has a global mobile satellite network, and which would open more opportunities relating to communications.

The launch of Rocket Lab's Neutron rocket, however, is arguably the most anticipated event for growth investors, as it's capable of handling significantly larger payloads than Electron, and could help the business attain profitability in the future. A successful launch would mark a new wave of opportunities for the business. While a delay is disappointing, it's only a delay. When it comes to rockets, safety has to be the top priority.

There's a ton of growth potential for Rocket Lab, and while the market may have reacted negatively to news of Neutron being delayed yet again, that doesn't mean the business is in trouble. At a lower valuation, the stock may be a much more appealing investment option to consider.

There's still risk here as the business isn't profitable, and it could be a long time before that changes, but for long-term investors who are willing to be patient, there are many reasons to remain optimistic about Rocket Lab's future.

#82. UnitedHealth shares are doing something unusual ahead of earnings

The only thing more expensive than health insurance is perhaps the costs of insuring shares of health insurers. Case in point: UnitedHealth Group, which reports earnings Tuesday.

Implied volatility is running at twice realized volatility ahead of the October 13 quarterly earnings release. In other words, options prices - the cost of insuring the underlying stock - are expensive, which sets up well for short premium strategies.

In the case of UnitedHealth shares, traders can sell November premium to cut the cost of a longer-dated January call by more than half. UnitedHealth heads into Tuesday's report with much of the damage from its prior missteps already priced in. While rising healthcare costs always remain a headwind, management's 13% to 16% EPS growth target looks achievable. The stock has basically been flat over the last five years.

By the way, according to the company, 90% of United's 52 million customers worldwide are in the U.S. By its own statistics, the company covers about 12% to 13.5% of the U.S. population.

Growing enrollment is critical to EPS growth, but so too is underwriting margin. In the managed care and health insurance business, underwriting margin represents the core operational profitability generated directly from managing healthcare risk. It measures the financial return an insurer achieves strictly from collecting premiums and managing medical care. On the enrollment side, ACA marketplace-driven enrollment appears poised to decline, a headwind for revenue in a segment that had been a growth driver. Fortunately, it's a smaller piece of the enterprise than Medicare and Commercial. Commercial fee-based enrollment grew ~2.9% YoY between 2024 and 2025, while total Medicare enrollment grew 4.5%. The commercial segment growth may not look impressive as a headline number, but given the U.S. workforce grew ~1.4% over the same period, United appears to be gaining market share.

At 17 times forward earnings, and with free cash flow at 5.7% of enterprise value and 6.5% of market cap, the stock isn't priced for any recovery. On the options side, the market is implying 40% volatility for a stock that's been realizing 20%. Granted. The 40% number captures this week's earnings, and it's likely elevated because the stock has had a couple of eye-watering earnings moves in the past 8 reported quarters. In January, the stock fell almost 20% following earnings, and April 2025 saw a similar sharp decline.

As it stands, UNH is about 12-13% below the midpoint of the two-year high and low. The stock has traded lower in five of the last 8 earnings. Current options prices imply a 6.5% earnings move, according to Cboe LiveVol data. That's the second highest implied move in almost two years.

Sell the November 340/420 strangle to help finance the purchase of the January 2027 400 call. Buying the Jan 400 call costs $18.20. Selling the Nov 420 call at $5.80 and the Nov 340 put at $4.80 brings in $10.60, for a net debit of about $7.60, cutting the call's cost by roughly 58%. If UNH finishes November between 340 and 420, both short legs expire worthless and the January call is held for $7.60, with a breakeven of $407.60 at January expiration. A rally through 420 is covered by the long 400 call. The real risk is below: a close under 340 means buying shares there, for an effective basis near $347.60 including the debit.

#84. In pictures: More than 500,000 took to the streets as France protests erupted into violence

Protests in France against rising living costs and declining public services turned violent over the weekend, with more than 500,000 people taking to the streets.

Hundreds of thousands of people marched through various cities and protested peacefully but others set fire to the city hall in Limoges, gutting the 19th-century building.

Lyon's city tourist office was also set ablaze, supermarkets were looted and there were attacks on police officers and vehicles and luxury boutiques, in what was described as the country's worst unrest in years.

Officers used tear gas to restrain the crowds. One protester died of a heart attack, and another lost a hand.

"Those who looted will have to pay back for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable," French President Emmanuel Macron said in a televised address to the nation on Sunday.

He blamed "unrestrained violence" on "insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals."

The demonstrations began last month as high school students across Paris lamented poor school conditions, including teacher shortages and unsatisfactory facilities. The demonstrations evolved into a nationwide protest.

#87. Federal Reserve Board finalizes changes to enhance the transparency and public accountability of its stress test and reduce volatility in its stress test-related capital requirements

An official website of the United States Government

Official websites use .govA .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPSA lock (LockLocked padlock icon) or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Federal Reserve, the central bank of the United States, provides the nation with a safe, flexible, and stable monetary and financial system.

Review of Monetary Policy Strategy, Tools, and Communications

Mergers, Acquisitions, and Other Applications

Financial Stability Coordination & Actions

Financial Market Utilities & Infrastructures

For release at 9:00 a.m. EDT Share

The Federal Reserve Board on Wednesday finalized changes to enhance the transparency and public accountability of its stress test and reduce volatility in its stress test-related capital requirements. The two final rules are largely similar to the proposed rules from 2025. The Board also requested comment on a proposal to better capture differences in banks' business models to generate fee income.

The Board conducts stress tests to ensure that large banks are sufficiently capitalized and able to lend to households and businesses even in a severe recession. In December 2024, the Board announced it would modify the test to improve its resilience.

"The stress test is an essential component of our regulatory capital framework," said Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman. "Today's changes preserve its resilience by ensuring that it is transparent, granular, and risk-sensitive. The public will now have greater assurance that the risks banks take will be reflected appropriately in their stress test losses and their capital requirements."

The first final rule requires the Board to invite public input annually on the stress test scenarios and any material model changes. It also updates the framework that guides the design of the hypothetical scenarios and adopts the models that will be used for the 2027 stress test. In addition, the final rule makes several adjustments to the stress test calendar. The final rule also updates the global market shock component, which is a set of shocks to specific market components applied to banks with large trading books. These banks will now be tested against two global market shock components each year, and the Board will use the shock that produces the largest losses for each firm to calculate the firm's stress test results.

The second final rule requires the Board, when calculating stress capital buffer requirements, to average the results from the two most recent annual supervisory stress tests for firms subject to the stress test in both years. The Board will begin averaging stress capital buffer requirements in 2028 to ensure that only models incorporating public input are used in the calculation.

The proposal would request public comment on a revision to the Board's noninterest income model that would improve the stress test's ability to capture business model diversity across firms. If adopted, these adjustments would replace the current noninterest income model that projects each bank's fee income under stress. Comments are due 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

Together, the changes are likely to reduce year-over-year volatility in capital requirements by approximately 50 percent and are not expected to materially affect aggregate capital requirements.

#90. 1 eVTOL Stock That Could Turn $5,000 Into $50,000 -- and the 1 Risk That Could Wipe It Out

Electric vertical take-off and landing (eVTOL) aircraft could eventually replace helicopters for short-range flights because they're quieter, greener, and easier to land in crowded urban areas. According to Fortune Business Insights, the nascent eVTOL market could grow at a 36.8% CAGR from 2026 to 2034, making it a great time to invest in early movers.

One of the leading early movers is Joby Aviation (JOBY -0.97%). Joby's S4 eVTOL carries a single pilot and four passengers, travels up to 150 miles on a single charge, and reaches a maximum speed of 200 miles per hour. It can travel faster and stay airborne longer than many other eVTOLs -- including Archer Aviation's (ACHR +0.12%) Midnight -- because it uses single tilt-rotor propellers for lifting and cruising rather than using separate, heavier propellers.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) hasn't approved Joby's first commercial flights in the U.S. yet, but it's closer to completing the FAA's multi-stage certification process than Archer. If Joby achieves that certification and becomes a vertically integrated "transportation as a service" provider that manufactures, owns, and operates its own air taxi fleet, analysts expect its revenue to soar from $53 million in 2025 to $432 million in 2028.

Therefore, Joby could turn a $5,000 investment into $50,000 over the next decade if it successfully scales its business. However, one major risk could also wipe it out.

When interest rates were low, it was easy for Joby to take on more debt to expand its business. But as interest rates rise, it will become harder for Joby to take out loans at favorable rates. Over the past year, Joby has burned about $100-$200 million in cash per quarter. Its liquidity rose, but only because it raised cash through two stock offerings and a convertible debt offering.

Data source: Joby Aviation. FCF = free cash flow.

That strategy caused its share count to rise 13% over the past 12 months. Its total liabilities increased 156% year over year to $985 million at the end of the second quarter. Therefore, a recession could severely throttle its cash flow and reduce its liquidity. It could also easily cut Joby's stock in half, since it's already valued at ten times its 2028 sales.

Moreover, a recession could drive Joby's major partners -- including Toyota for manufacturing, Delta for airport-to-home flights, and Uber for broader air-taxi flights -- to rein in their spending. Reduced consumer discretionary and corporate spending would also impact the initial demand for pricey air taxi flights. Simply put, this isn't a stock you want to hold when the market crashes.

#96. Robot factories and hypersonic missiles: JPMorgan Chase's first $5 billion of defense investments

JPMorgan Chase has made $5 billion in startup investments in the first year of its U.S. security and resiliency initiative, the company said Monday, a faster-than-expected pace that indicates the bank is finding plentiful opportunities in emerging defense, manufacturing and supply chain firms.

The bank, which last year said it would deploy $10 billion into startups over a decade, may expand the program beyond that initial dollar amount, JPMorgan co-President Doug Petno told CNBC in an interview.

Todd Combs, the former Berkshire Hathaway executive who leads the JPMorgan group in charge of making startup investments, has "hit the ground running," Petno said. "He's done a great job and put us in some really interesting companies," he added.

Most of those investments have yet to be disclosed, but two known stakes seem emblematic of the project's mission to bolster companies that are needed for a more dangerous and chaotic era of geopolitics. JPMorgan, the biggest U.S. bank by assets, has taken direct stakes in defense-related startups Hadrian and Castelion.

Wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, as well as trade disputes with China, have threatened the flow of energy and key components needed for U.S. industries and defense, which spurred JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon into creating the initiative a year ago.

He put Petno, widely seen as one of two key possible successors, in charge of the overall investment project. Combs, a former board member of the bank, reports directly to Dimon.

The scope of the project extends beyond supply chain, defense and manufacturing to include frontier technologies and the pharmaceutical and health-tech industries.

"There's a lot of really interesting companies that have been working to solve some of these problems," Petno said.

These "early venture-stage, advanced manufacturing companies have found ways to build these capabilities in the U.S." rather than relying on overseas trading partners, he said.

In August, the bank helped lead a $1.4 billion funding round for Hadrian, which builds automated factories that make parts for the defense, aerospace and maritime sectors. A California factory run by Hadrian has 10 robots for every human employee, according to the startup's founder.

That month, JPMorgan was also involved in a $1 billion funding round for Castelion, whose flagship product is a relatively low-cost hypersonic missile called Blackbeard. Castelion was founded in late 2022 by a group of former SpaceX engineers.

"Our approach is to find generational companies and partner with them for the long term," Combs said in a statement Monday.

"Putting more than $5 billion to work in our first year shows how many exceptional businesses are building in industries that strengthen critical supply chains," Combs said.

JPMorgan making billions of dollars of direct investments in nascent companies is a departure from its usual role as a lender and advisor.

Before the defense initiative, the bank had moved away from taking startup stakes, which can be relatively risky bets on unproven technologies. JPMorgan spun off its private equity business, One Equity Partners, more than a decade ago.

In its more traditional role, JPMorgan has also financed and facilitated more than $230 billion for industries that support American national interests, according to the bank.

That part of its security and resiliency project, meant to hit $1.5 trillion over 10 years, is led by Jay Horine, a former co-head of investment banking.

JPMorgan built a team for the project of about three dozen bankers, who are aided by hundreds more across the firm, as it expanded the initiative to Europe and Canada.

Its bankers are mapping distribution lines for key products, from submarines and missiles to aircraft, to identify suppliers that may lack the capital or capacity to meet rising demand, according to Petno.

JPMorgan is also in regular communication with the U.S. Department of Defense and Department of Commerce about the government's needs, he said.

#101. Micron Technology Stock: Is It a No-Brainer Buy at Less Than $900?

Has the bubble burst for Micron Technology (MU +3.81%)? That's what many investors may be asking right now, as the tech company, which has been experiencing significant demand for its memory and storage products over the past year, has suddenly fallen out of favor with investors. It's been falling sharply in recent days, and last week, it fell below $900.

It's now trading at levels it hasn't been at since August, and the concern is that this may be the beginning of an even greater decline ahead, particularly as the market has been growing concerned about an artificial intelligence (AI) bubble.

But with Micron trading at a low valuation with respect to profits, and demand remaining robust, is the market overreacting, and could Micron actually be a no-brainer buy while it trades below $900?

There's no denying Micron's results have been stellar in the past year. Not only has revenue been through the roof, but so too have earnings. The growth has been exceptional, making it little wonder why the stock has surged over 1,000% in the past five years. The big concern is whether the company can keep on generating such impressive growth in the long run.

MU Net Income (Quarterly) data by YCharts

The answer is not necessarily clear. While demand appears insatiable and prices for its products keep going up, there have been flags raised that a bubble may burst soon, with famed investor Michael Burry being one of the more prominent critics, believing that "the bubble in AI may burst sooner than later." Many investors, thus, may be heading for the exits and cashing out profits before that happens.

Micron looks incredibly cheap, as it's trading at just seven times its estimated future earnings (based on analyst expectations). But expectations can change, and if the outlook worsens for Micron due to more supply becoming available sooner rather than later, that would adversely impact its share price and could send it into a deeper tailspin.

It's difficult at this stage to know how long the strong growth will last for Micron. It could very well prove to be a good buy right now due to the incredibly strong demand for memory and storage products, but this is not a slam-dunk buy or a stock I'd simply buy and forget about, given that so much depends on expectations.

For growth investors who are considering buying Micron's stock today, it'll be important to keep a close eye on market conditions, as things could change quickly.

#107. Boomers are buying into the promise of monthly income from options ETFs, but there's a tax catch

Covered call ETFs have gained a following for their ability to generate monthly cash flow. But a tax surprise could be lurking for many investors.

These actively managed funds have different underlying assets and strategies. But the premise is generally the same. Covered call funds hold equities and sell call options or use related derivatives to generate income. Investors receive attractive income yields in exchange for limited capital upside. The tax piece is more complicated, however.

A fund that realizes option premiums, short-term gains or other income still has taxable amounts to distribute. The tax hit can be easy — and costly — for investors to miss, especially since ETFs are typically understood to be tax-efficient investment vehicles, and especially since most investors aren't looking at the tax implications until they receive a 1099-DIV at tax time, the IRS tax document issued by financial services companies to report dividends and related distributions paid to investors during a tax year.

Even if a fund has good returns and a favorable 30-day SEC yield — which measures the net investment income of bond funds or equity funds and is annualized to reflect the yield an investor would expect to earn over the course of a full year — investors need to look under the hood and understand the tax implications of covered call ETFs. "The after-tax net total return might fall below your expectations," said Matthew Smart, chief investment officer at WWM Investments in Chicago.

Here's what investors need to know about covered call ETFs and taxes:

Distributions from covered call funds come in several forms: dividends, capital gain distributions, or non-dividend distributions. The distribution mix can vary by fund and change year to year. Non-dividend distributions are commonly known as return of capital — payment or distribution from a portion of an investor's original principal rather than an economic profit, capital gain, or dividend earnings. And this is where it can get confusing for investors because ROC distributions aren't treated as current income. Instead, they reduce the investment's cost basis by the distribution amount, so they are tax-deferred until shares are sold.

Covered call ETFs take different approaches to distributions. "Some covered call strategies make distributions characterized only as ordinary dividends. Other strategies make distributions that may include all three types. And since investors' individual tax rates vary significantly, there can be a large difference between what investors receive in fund distributions on a pre-tax basis, and what they keep after paying taxes," ProShares wrote in a blog on covered call strategy and tax efficiency.

Some covered call ETF investors are surprised at tax time by the magnitude of the qualified dividends and ordinary income, said Edwin Retter, senior wealth advisor in the Melbourne, Florida, office of Mission Wealth.

They are also confused by the ROC concept. While it seems favorable from a distribution standpoint in the short term, it's investors' own money coming back to them, which reduces the cost basis. Having a lower cost basis generally increases the investor's capital gains tax liability at the time of sale.

"You're not avoiding the taxes; you're just delaying it until you sell," said Aaron Brachman, wealth manager at the Washington Wealth Group of Steward Partners in Washington, D.C.

Investors who decide to purchase a covered call ETF should ideally do so within a tax-deferred account such as a traditional IRA, Retter said. "I don't know how many investors give so much thought to that. They just find out at tax time that they've put it in a less tax-desirable account."

By investing in a covered call ETF through a traditional IRA, investors don't have to worry about taxes until they pull money out of the account. "You can really save a lot of time and taxes by putting it in the right account structure," Retter said.

Investors who want to better understand how taxes come into play in a covered call ETF can use a measurement known as the tax-cost ratio. The Morningstar Tax Cost Ratio measures how much a fund's annualized return is reduced by the taxes investors pay on distributions. Investors can type in the ticker of the fund they are researching on Morningstar.com, click on the price tab, and scroll down to see the tax-cost ratio.

"It is a flexible tool that can help investors easily compare different time periods, different funds, and different categories. Investors pay taxes when they receive a taxable distribution and these costs are just as relevant as the expense ratio in reducing an investor's take-home return," Morningstar wrote in a paper explaining the methodology for the calculation.

For instance, the JPMorgan Equity Premium Income ETF (JEPI) has a three-year tax cost ratio of 3.11, according to Morningstar. That means after-tax returns are reduced by about 3.11 percentage points annually for investors in the highest tax brackets.

Another example is the JPMorgan Nasdaq Equity Premium Income ETF (JEPQ). The fund's three-year tax cost ratio is 4.30. By contrast, the Neos S&P 500(R) High Income ETF (SPYI) has a three-year tax cost ratio of 0.48.

The tax picture can be very ETF-specific because it depends on how the fund is structured, said Brent Sullivan, an independent tax analyst at Tax Alpha Insider. SPYI has a higher return of capital than some of its peers, lowering the more immediate tax consequences, but there's still a cost-basis and fund growth issue for investors to consider, he added.

It's not just taxes investors have to consider with these funds. "It's good to look at the portfolio returns, and it's good to look at tax consequences, but NAV has to grow faster than the distribution rate," Sullivan said. "The fund's NAV must keep going up to sustain those distributions. It's not magic. The money has to come from somewhere, and it can't just come from new investors," he said.

Investors should also look at a fund's 30-day SEC yield to get a sense of what the company is generating in terms of income. JEPI has a 30-day SEC yield of 7.45%, compared with JEPQ's 11.56%, and SPYI's 0.45%.

Several financial advisors said they aren't fans of covered call ETFs for tax, complexity and other reasons.

With the 10-year U.S. Treasury continuing to hover around 5%, there are more opportunities for investors to find attractive income in bonds, from ultra-short bond funds to corporate bonds.

"I'd rather have a person in a portfolio that's predominantly fixed income and hedge the interest rate risk with 20% to 40% of the portfolio in high-quality growth stocks," said Andrew Urbanski, founder and chief investment officer at N10 Assets in Greenwich, Connecticut. "If the income isn't enough, draw on the principal from the bond or stock portion of the portfolio in a way that's more risk and cost-efficient," he said.

Covered call ETFs do cap an investor's upside. In a taxable account, an investor might instead buy an S&P 500 ETF — or a total market ETF to get more small and mid-cap exposure — collect the dividends, and make systematic withdrawals through small periodic share sales after a year for tax-efficiency reasons, Retter said.

Index-based ETFs generally have lower expense ratios than their actively managed counterparts. The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO) has an expense ratio of 0.03%. The Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF (VTI) also has an expense ratio of 0.03%.

By contrast, JEPI and JEPQ each have an annual expense ratio of 0.35%. SPYI has an expense ratio of 0.68%.

Meanwhile, many of the covered call ETF funds include the large tech stocks such as Nvidia, Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta that have been driving the market's growth, so it is important for investors to know whether these stocks are already well represented in their portfolio.

#111. 2 "Magnificent Seven" Stocks to Buy and Hold for the Rest of the Decade

If I were going to buy two "Magnificent Seven" stocks and hold them for the rest of the decade, my choice would be easy. I'm buying Alphabet (GOOGL +1.46%) (GOOG +1.31%) and Amazon (AMZN +5.12%). The two companies actually have a lot in common, as they are two of the world's largest cloud computing providers. Over the next several years, I think these are the type of AI stocks to own.

The pick-and-shovel providers of AI infrastructure, like Nvidia, have clearly dominated the early phase of AI. Right now, there is a rush to build out AI data centers, which has driven huge demand for chips, networking, and other components. However, as the market starts to mature, the large cloud providers, such as Alphabet and Amazon, will be the best positioned.

The reason is simple: The big cloud computing stocks can win in both a high-spending environment and a slow-spending one. Right now, both Amazon and Alphabet are getting strong returns on their AI infrastructure spending. Amazon has said it is signing five-year or longer contracts and getting a payback within two to three years, with chips having about a six-year useful life.

Meanwhile, Alphabet is getting a payback in around two years, and in half that time when it uses its own tensor processing units (TPUs). With these types of returns getting locked in, it makes sense to invest as much as possible into building out AI infrastructure.

However, the companies also win when demand starts to slow. In that scenario, Amazon and Alphabet can cut back on their AI infrastructure capex, which in turn will lead to huge free cash flow generation. They will then be able to quickly pay off any debt associated with their AI investments or start buying back stock. In essence, they are in a win-win scenario.

Amazon and Alphabet are also in a strong position due to their custom chip businesses. Over the long term, they should be able to achieve much better returns than providers that rely on Nvidia GPUs, like neoclouds or SpaceX. Alphabet is already starting to see this, and Amazon should see better returns as its custom chips become a bigger part of its business.

In addition to their fast-growing cloud computing segments, both Alphabet and Amazon have strong core businesses that generate substantial cash flow to fund their AI infrastructure build-outs.

Alphabet, of course, is the world's search leader with Google Search. As search and AI chatbots blend together, Alphabet is in an enviable position because it controls the distribution. By owning the world's leading browser and smartphone operating system, together with a revenue-sharing deal with Apple to be the default search engine on its devices, Alphabet is the de facto gateway to the internet.

Meanwhile, it has incorporated its top-tier Gemini AI model into its search solution with features like AI Overviews and AI Mode, which bring AI to consumers without them having to change their normal routines or open a separate app.

By having its own chips, Alphabet is also able to train its AI models more cheaply than competitors. At the same time, its vast ad network allows it to monetize consumer AI better than newer start-ups, giving it a significant overall advantage in the space.

Amazon, meanwhile, remains the world's largest e-commerce provider. The business continues to see strong sales, and Amazon is also pushing into new areas to drive growth. Meanwhile, the company's investments in robots, where it is the world's largest manufacturer, and AI have created tremendous efficiencies, which have led to strong operating leverage in its e-commerce operations.

Both Alphabet and Amazon have multiple avenues to be AI winners, making them my top Magnificent Seven stocks to own for the long term.

Geoffrey Seiler has positions in Alphabet and Amazon. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, and Nvidia. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

The Federal Reserve Board on Thursday requested public comment on two proposals related to establishing a regulatory framework for Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers under the GENIUS Act.

The first proposal would require that Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets, such as short-term Treasury bills and certain other high-quality, liquid assets. The proposal would also establish standardized capital requirements to address certain credit and operational risks of payment stablecoin activities, as well as risk management standards, in accordance with the law. Separately, the proposal would introduce rules for Board-supervised firms that safekeep the assets backing payment stablecoins. It would also clarify the permissibility of stablecoin and related activities for Board-supervised banks.

The second proposal would establish a tailored application process for Board-supervised banks applying to issue payment stablecoins. These applicants would be required to submit a business plan and financial information, among other documents. The proposal would also create a process governing appeals, hearings, and final determinations for applications.

The comment period will close 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

For media inquiries, please email [email protected] or call (202) 452-2955.

#118. The Internet Is About To Expand Again—Here’s What Business Leaders Should Know

​Tony Kirsch is the commercial director and cofounder of the Brand Safety Alliance (a GoDaddy Registry Initiative).

Domain names have long been the internet’s version of real estate. ​

There are high-value web addresses with short, recognizable terms, and there are longer, more obscure addresses that carry smaller price tags. There are well-known neighborhoods that have been around since the beginning, such as .com and .org, or country-specific domains, such as .uk or .de. There are also newer options based on interest, community, city or industry, such as .shop, .bank or .nyc.​

The number of web extensions available to consumers is set to expand again—and here’s why this matters for businesses.

The most important term to understand is the top-level domain (TLD), the word or letters to the right of the dot at the end of the domain. In Forbes.com, for example, the TLD is .com. TLDs that don’t represent a country or territory are also sometimes called generic TLDs, or gTLDs.​

For many years, the web operated on a limited number of TLDs. Then in 2012, the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN), the global organization responsible for coordinating the domain name system, opened applications for new gTLDs—and received almost 2,000.

​Ultimately, more than 1,200 new gTLDs were added to the DNS root zone database, including .shop, .online, .club and .xyz. Some brands also secured extensions for their own exclusive use, including .google, .bmw, .barclays and .canon.​

The key takeaway is that the domain landscape businesses operate in is not fixed. We saw a monumental shift 14 years ago, and we’re poised for another soon.

In April 2026, ICANN opened a second new gTLD application round that resulted in over 1,600 applications. On October 7, ICANN published the applications on “Reveal Day,” giving business leaders their first official look at who has proposed extensions and where multiple applicants are competing for the same extension.​

This doesn’t mean 1,600 new extensions will suddenly appear online. Applications still need to progress through evaluation and, in some cases, objection or contention processes. ICANN will confirm the final list of applied-for strings on November 17. It may be years before we see the full impact of this round, but it’s possible that some new extensions may be available before the end of 2027. ​

So why should business leaders pay attention now?​

New extensions create new opportunities for branding, identity and representation online. ICANN was explicit in its goals for the gTLD program in 2012: “to enhance innovation, competition and consumer choice.” And from that perspective, it has been highly successful, with more than 48 million domains registered in an extension beyond the traditional .com. ​

But innovation changes the risk landscape, too. Every change to the domain ecosystem changes the environment businesses are trying to protect. More namespaces means more territory for security and brand teams to monitor—and more places where consumers must decide whether something is legitimate.​

One lesson from the previous round is that new gTLDs aren’t inherently risky. However, the internet landscape is going to become more complex, and businesses need visibility into what affects them.

Reveal Day gave us a snapshot of what applicants want in the next expansion of the domain namespace. ​

At a high level, 1,614 applications are proceeding for a total of 986 unique “strings,” or domain extensions. This means some gTLDs received more than one application, and a public auction process will determine who gets to proceed. A few interesting trends are already emerging:​

• New online real estate is attracting big buyers. From technology and commerce to lifestyle and professional services, applicants are staking their claims across a wide range of industries. More than a quarter of proposed extensions attracted competing applicants. Brands can expect new opportunities and potentially new territory to protect.​

• AI is shaping the next generation of domain names. The most-contested string was .agent, with 13 applicants, while agi, .api and .robot also attracted considerable interest. As AI reshapes how businesses and consumers interact online, leaders should pay attention to the new naming conventions and digital identities emerging around it.​

• Brands are investing in their own online identities. Around one in five applications was for a brand-specific extension. Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft and others are seeking extensions associated with their products and services, from .gemini and .pixel to .instagram and .alexa. These applications show how major businesses are exploring greater control over their digital identities and the ways customers interact with them.​

• Some extensions could change how consumers judge what’s legitimate. Applications for .official, .brand and Chinese-language terms meaning “official website” raise interesting questions about trust and authenticity online. These extensions aren’t inherently risky, and we’ve seen similar examples with .llc and .company, but brands should consider how they might be used, and potentially misused, to create an impression of authority.​

Taken together, the applications point to a more diverse and commercially competitive domain landscape, with emerging technologies, brand identity and online trust all playing a role in shaping what comes next.

You don’t need to have applied for a gTLD to get value from Reveal Day data. You can use the published applications to start identifying which parts of the proposed expansion actually matter to your business. ​

• Understand what’s been applied for, particularly gTLDs relevant to your brand, sector, products, geography or customers.​

• Consider how the changing domain landscape affects your existing exposure and where customers could reasonably encounter confusion or impersonation.​

• Ask whether your current domain monitoring and brand/security strategy gives you sufficient visibility and coverage as new namespaces come online.​

• Think about shifting to more proactive protection, such as domain blocking, to reduce your reliance on monitoring and enforcement.​

• Keep watching as the program develops and successful applications are finalized.​

Reveal Day gives leaders a rare opportunity to witness the evolution of the internet in real time.​

You don’t need to become a domain name expert or overhaul your domain portfolio overnight. ​Not every proposed extension will require a response or pose a threat. But understanding which extensions intersect with your brand, industry and customers will help you prioritize your brand’s protection efforts as the next generation of the internet takes shape.​​

#119. Why hedge funds could be making a bond market shock more likely

Hedge funds' increased presence in global bond markets makes the likelihood of a broader market shock "greater than what it was," Bank of England deputy governor Sarah Breeden told CNBC Thursday.

Breeden — the central bank's deputy governor for financial stability, and a member of its rates-setting Monetary Policy Committee — said the changing mix of bond market investors, and their increased use of leverage, raises the risk of localized market turbulence turning into broader financial stress.

"One of the things that has become increasingly apparent over the last several years is that the investors in our core government bond markets globally have changed," Breeden told CNBC's Sri Jegarajah in an interview Thursday.

"It's not the real money investors, the insurance companies and pension funds, in the way it used to be. It's increasingly hedge funds, and those hedge funds are price-sensitive, leveraged, international. That, of course, means that the likelihood of a shock in one market transmitting to another is greater than what it was."

Breeden was speaking on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand.

With gross assets now standing at about $13 trillion, hedge funds have become an increasingly important part of the global investor landscape, the IMF said on Tuesday.

In its latest Global Financial Stability Report, published Tuesday, the IMF acknowledged hedge funds' role in supporting market liquidity and efficiency.

But it also warned that the hedge fund industry's use of leverage to boost returns, and its tendency to pursue crowded trades, could turbo-charge market stress in times of turmoil.

That, in turn, could spill over into broader financial markets, and areas such as banks' prime brokerage businesses, according to the IMF.

"The source of the shocks are bond markets, and the likelihood of a spillover is higher than it was," Breeden said.

Hedge funds' presence in the global government bond market — particularly their use of so-called "basis trades" — has come under sharper scrutiny this year, following the sharp sell-off in sovereign debt.

Hedge funds held a record 7% of the $30 trillion Treasury market at the end of 2025, according to U.S. Office of Financial Research data published on Aug. 19.

Basis trades are an arbitrage bet in which hedge funds are positioned long in cash Treasurys while shorting their corresponding futures contracts, with the aim of profiting from the price gap. While the price differential between the two is relatively small, hedge funds often employ large amounts of leverage to further inflate returns.

Earlier this month, 10-year and 30-year Treasury yields hit their highest levels since 2002. Across the Atlantic, yields on 10-year U.K. government bonds, known as gilts, also touched multi-decade highs.

Yields on France's government bonds, known as OATs, have moved sharply higher in recent weeks amid rising concerns about the country's fiscal outlook — fueling fears of a fresh sovereign debt crisis impacting the euro zone.

#124. Junk bonds are 'flashing yellow.' Watch these warning signs

Cracks are forming in the junk bond market as investors demand higher payouts for owning the market's riskiest debt. It isn't time to ditch high-yield bonds, but investors should pay attention to the warning signs.

High-yield bonds now yield 8.1%, up from 7.22% a month ago. The increase reflects a jump in yields across the curve as investors bake in more inflation from high energy prices and other pressures, including concern about the deficit — hitting nearly $2 trillion in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30.

The high-yield market is also showing stress on the credit side with spreads recently widening to levels not seen since April, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Credit spreads are the difference in yield between the bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. Wider spreads mean investors are demanding higher yields for holding corporate debt, viewing it as riskier.

Spreads are at 315 basis points in the overall high-yield market, higher than a year ago but still below levels in March when they reached 346 bps. One basis point equals one one-hundredth of a percent, or 0.01%.

The high-yield market consists of bonds rated BB+ by S&P and Fitch and Ba1 and under by Moody's. The lowest-rated cohort, CCC and below, has seen the most movement with spreads climbing dramatically over the past year to roughly 1,250 bps.

Right now, the high-yield market is "flashing yellow" but is "far from red," said Michael Arone, chief investment strategist at State Street Investment Management.

It makes sense that investors are demanding more compensation for taking on additional credit risk as borrowing costs rise, he said.

Yields are elevated across the board with the 10-year Treasury reaching its highest level since 2002 earlier in the week.

"The bigger question is whether this is simply a repricing of interest rate risk, or the beginning of a more fundamental reassessment of credit quality," Arone said.

He's in a wait-and-see mode since earnings are still growing, interest-coverage ratios remain good, and while default rates have ticked up some, he believes it is not concerning.

That said, the starting point in spreads is likely weighing on investors' psyche, since they are still low by historical standards.

"There's a small margin of error here, which I also think raises the anxiety level," Arone explained. "The compensation that investors are receiving for taking on this credit risk isn't overwhelming relative to history, and therefore subtle changes in credit spreads can be concerning."

While there may be concerns about part of the lower-rated market, the overall high-yield market is in good fundamental shape.

In fact, credit quality is at a record high, with BB bonds making up over 60% of the market compared with 38% prior to the global financial crisis, said Kelley Gerrity, a fixed income strategist at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

"We've had higher-quality companies coming in, and with higher rates now, you also have more discipline from companies that are more indebted ... just because of the higher cost of capital, so that actually is creating a bit of a healthier picture as well," she said.

The lowest tier of high yield has always been more speculative, since the bonds have a higher default risk. Therefore, it's no surprise that they are the ones seeing the most widening in spreads, said Collin Martin, head of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research.

The overall move in high-yield spreads have been "orderly," he said. "Are there cracks forming? I think the cracks are logical cracks with the lowest-rated bonds and it's too early to say that it's spreading to the broad credit market."

In addition, fluctuations within the CCC-rated and lower spreads have been idiosyncratic, Gerrity added. Morgan Stanley recently broke down the spreads in the lowest cohort into two buckets: performing assets and non-performing assets, which are defined as spreads above 1,000 bps.

The non-performing spread to worst is 2,818 bps, while the performing bucket — the biggest piece of the CCC market — is 461 bps, she said.

"It is isolated," she said. "I'm not necessarily sure that that will go away anytime soon, but it doesn't tell the story of overall concern and flashing caution for credit markets right now."

For now, investors should remain selective within higher yield, Gerrity advised.

"We're looking for the best relative value opportunities, and we think that exists within that single-B cohort, and so we're leaning into that," she said.

Investors should be concerned if there is a steep widening in the broader high-yield market.

But there's scant evidence of stress in the BB cohort. Spreads in that group are at 194 bps, up from 179 bps a year ago — although the move hasn't been in a straight line.

"We're going to be focusing our attention on what are considered some stronger businesses," Martin said. "If we start to see the markets demand higher spreads there also, that's what we'll be looking at to see if risks are really rising."

It's also important to understand that the Federal Reserve is raising rates in a strong economic environment, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. The central bank is concerned about an inflation problem amid high fossil fuel prices due to the Iran war, while growth has been stronger than expected, he noted.

"With growth being good as the reason that the Fed is hiking, then you wouldn't expect high yield to blow out because growth means revenues stay up, means cash flow and profitability stays up," he explained.

High yield becomes a disaster when the economy is heading into a sharp economic downturn, Gallo said.

"That's when spreads really widen out," he said. "But a recession is not the odds-on bet. Now, talk to me in six months if the Fed keeps hiking over and over, if oil prices stay high for longer, well, then maybe we will start to wonder."

#130. Anthropic commits 5% of shares to new public benefit fund that could address AI job disruption

Anthropic said Sunday it plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund, with the stake potentially increasing as the company's valuation grows.

Subject to shareholder approval, the fund would immediately commit 5% of Anthropic's shares, with the board adding, at its discretion, an additional 2% for every 50% increase in the company's value above a set baseline that has yet to be disclosed.

Anthropic said that while it has already committed $200 million to study the AI's effects, "given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed."

The fund may be used to "explore large donations" — including to traditional nonprofits or as direct distributions for specific populations — or for "bolder approaches" to study and address AI's disruption and displacement of jobs, the company said.

An August Pew Research Center report found that 71% of adults think AI will lead to fewer jobs in the U.S. over the next two years.

The fund will be established as a wholly owned limited liability company rather than a 501(c)(3) tax-exempt nonprofit or other format to adjust between different forms of giving, the release said. Equity held by the LLC will not be used for lobbying or political giving in the U.S. or internationally, Anthropic said.

Anthropic told investors its third-quarter revenue stands at $16.8 billion ahead of its planned initial public offering reportedly slated for November, CNBC reported.

The timing of Anthropic's public fund announcement is both mandatory to prepare for an initial public offering, and "beneficial from an image perspective," especially as AI reshapes the jobs market, Lise Buyer, partner at IPO advisory firm Class V Group, told CNBC.

Buyer said Anthropic's move could be seen favorably if the funds support retraining or help workers find alternative employment when the technology disrupts their jobs.

"Of course, it is also to burnish their reputation at a time when AI is coming under significant scrutiny," she added.

Anthropic said it will share more about the fund structure and governance in the coming months, including valuation milestones that may increase the stake. It said it will also share progress on the fund in an upcoming public benefit report.

In response to Anthropic's announcement, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on X that he "recommend[s] giving the shares directly to the public."

#135. Living with Mom and trading on margin. The regular investor gets in on Wall Street's record stock borrowing binge

HOUSTON — During a late night at home in May 2021, Hy Luu, a 29-year-old engineering consultant, was researching how to obtain more capital to invest in shares of Tesla.

That's when he discovered margin investing: the act of borrowing money from a broker to buy securities such as stocks, while using existing investments as collateral. Borrowing would give him more buying power, and he could pay it back as the stock appreciated. The main risk would be a margin call, or having to deposit more money into the account, if its value fell.

It was all too good to be true, Luu thought.

Luu — who lives with his mother, Kim Nguyen, in a three-bedroom, two-bathroom house in Houston — decided to get her opinion on the topic, given that she used to work as an accountant and just so happened to still be awake that evening. The 66-year-old retiree found it interesting.

That was the reassurance he needed, and it wasn't long before he started using margin to invest in Tesla for the first time. A year or so later, he had amassed more than $100,000 of margin debt.

"I went really crazy," he told CNBC in an interview. "The stock was going up, and so I was like, 'There's no way I could lose.'"

After five years of margin investing — including a period in 2022 where he worried that further declines in Tesla could trigger a margin call — Luu is working to pay down his largest margin balance ever. In June, he exercised $165,000 on five Tesla call options and bought 500 shares at $330 per share. After accounting for the cash in his account, this drove his borrowing to more than $156,000.

Tesla swung from below $370 a share to more than $430 during that month.

Between his Tesla investments, his company stock and 401(k) — while subtracting his margin debt as well as other debt he's accumulated, such as his car loan and student loans — Luu's net worth has skyrocketed to more than $800,000 from negative territory seven years ago.

"I'm very close to becoming a millionaire," the investor said. He did stress, "What I'm doing is risky. I don't recommend anyone do it."

Yet, Luu has found himself part of a growing trend taking hold in the market.

Retail investors like Luu are borrowing more and more money to invest. Robinhood's margin book grew to a record $21.6 billion in the second quarter, up 127% year over year and a 332% increase from the $5 billion seen in Q2 2024. To margin invest on the platform, eligible users must have a portfolio value of at least $2,000.

"Robinhood has made a really concerted effort to go after customers that are actively using margin because they're the most active traders," said Devin Ryan, head of financial technology research at Citizens.

Brokerage firms can benefit from margin investing by collecting interest on margin loans, while highly active customers can also generate additional trading-related revenue.

"If you look at the offers that Robinhood has had in the market over the past couple of years, it's been targeting those customers with obviously transfer bonuses, but also very low margin rates, very high yields on their cash," Ryan said.

To be sure, other parts of Robinhood's business are also growing, including retirement assets — which have nearly quadrupled in the last two years.

Another factor fueling the rise in margin investing is easier access through smartphones, according to Ryan.

"Having very little friction in investing and having everything at your fingertips, and then having a really seamless mobile experience where it's not clunky, I think, plays a big part of that," he said.

A Robinhood spokesperson told CNBC its products are designed to appeal to a number of customers, saying that "we don't believe it's accurate to characterize" its transfer promotions as specifically targeting "active traders who are trading on margin or may trade on margin." The company said it tries to "meet users where they are," and they "reject any implication" that the company is "encouraging risky trading."

Robinhood's margin debt isn't the only one reaching records. Total margin debt hit an all-time high of around $1.5 trillion in June, per the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, which incorporates data on both institutional investors such as hedge funds and retail investors.

Not all of that debt is driven by fresh borrowing due to new borrowing decisions. For example, as equities rise in value, an investor may need to cover a short position that's been marked to market, or valued at its current price.

Nonetheless, Sam Huszczo, chief investment officer at SGH Wealth Management, thinks the market's bull run — which has seen multiple record highs this year alone — is feeding a shift in investor psychology, and margin debt is one sign.

"That's greed," the founder said, adding that it's "not everywhere" in the market, but it's "certainly creeping into pockets."

"Margin, that's only the tip of the iceberg of what we can see," he continued. "Fear of missing out is just the emotion of jealousy with a brokerage account."

Huszczo considers the market to actually be "way healthier" than people think. Though he recognizes that increasing margin debt and the rise of risky assets such as leveraged ETFs inject more fragility in the system.

"People need to differentiate between what's a legitimate momentum growth investment and what's reckless chasing," Huszczo also said.

Huszczo shares the commonly held belief among financial advisors that investors' portfolios shouldn't be overly concentrated in one stock or even one sector.

Yet Luu has been zeroed in on Tesla ever since he bought his first share in late 2019. Earlier that year, he had started his current job — a time when he knew nothing about investing, he said. It wasn't until a co-worker told him to download Robinhood months later that he began looking into stocks and other assets.

"I started making money, and I quickly learned, 'Now I'm making money, what do I do with it?'" he said. "I started investing in index funds and even in crypto, and then I did the math. I looked at the returns, and I was like, 'This is very slow returns. I'm never gonna reach retirement, financial independence until like 65.'"

Little did he know that a decision he had made that summer would become his guiding light.

"I was choosing between a Honda Civic and a Tesla Model 3, and my friend, he scheduled a test drive for me to drive the Model 3," Luu said. "My plan was only to go into it just to test drive it. I wasn't going to buy anything. I wasn't going to put in any reservation. Long story short, after the test drive, I put in my reservation the same day, and I got the car like two weeks later."

Seeing the value the car provides in his life, Luu said he can envision a future where electric and autonomous vehicles are commonplace. Because of how much he believes in that future, he considers Tesla the "easiest" investment he's made, and over the course of seven years of investing in the company, he has generally held his shares.

However, things got a bit more difficult with his strategy when Tesla shares began falling in 2022, putting him in the vulnerable position of potentially receiving a margin call. 2022 was Tesla's worst year on record, with the stock finishing off the year at $123.18 after a roughly 65% decline.

In search of more capital, Luu made a serious financial decision with his mother's approval.

"I refinanced the house to get access to an extra $30,000 of capital, and I used that to pay down my margin debt," he said.

Luu understands the level of risk that accompanies trading with margin. Because he's been using margin for most of the nearly seven years he's been investing in Tesla, he has deemed his investing strategy "gambling with an asterisk."

For now, it has paid off. In the last five years, Tesla shares have risen more than 43% to $375. However, the volatile stock is about 25% off of its all-time high near $499.

"It's very easy to see it as gambling, because obviously all your money is in one stock, and that's inherently risky," he said. "But the reason why I say there's nuance to it is because it's a matter of investing temperament, financial discipline and time horizon."

With a time horizon of "many decades," a temperament he labels as "very calm and collected" and a "very high" conviction in Tesla, Luu believes he's "at no risk of panic selling," even when the market tanks.

Still, the situation points out another danger: Missing an opportunity to make an investment when an equity is undervalued. When Luu was scrambling to raise funds to meet his margin obligation, it reduced his flexibility to purchase more Tesla shares at the lower price.

Margin levels this high have been followed by risk-off periods in equities.

Whenever monthly margin debt has grown above 45% year over year since 1960, there were declines in the stock market five out of six times, data from Fundstrat Global Advisors shows. June's margin debt record came in at 49%, but the S&P 500 has still added more than 13% in 2026. A swing into the red by year-end in accordance with this historic pattern would be a dramatic move — one that would be considered highly unusual for the stock market.

The firm also found that the median performance for S&P 500 forward returns following a breakout of 40% year-over-year margin debt growth has been worse off 12 months later as opposed to one month after it. To be exact, the S&P 500's median 12-month forward return is a 4.2% decline, while the median one-month return is a drop of 2.2%.

In essence, the more rapidly margin debt rises, the worse it is for S&P 500 returns over 12 months.

While margin debt doesn't necessarily cause S&P 500 declines, it can exacerbate existing moves to the downside if there's a significant amount of leverage in the market, said Hardika Singh, economic strategist at Fundstrat.

"The premise of gains beget gains, it turns into losses beget losses, and that's what's troublesome," Singh said. "You have these losses, they keep piling up, and then the stock gets sold, and everyone's starting to close out their position, and it becomes this huge train wreck that's very hard to stop, and it adds a lot of volatility to the market."

Then again, Singh sees why investors like Luu are leaning into such a risky strategy. "No one ever got rich by diversifying," she said.

Luu, who said he's been a "hobbyist" from an early age, has folded in investing as one of his many hobbies, which include activities like climbing and playing guitar. It's become such a hobby that he's created his own social media account detailing his investing journey.

Even if Luu reaches his financial goals, he "wouldn't ever stop investing," he said. Instead, he said he "would probably start investing in SpaceX."

It's not just Luu who views trading as a hobby.

Fundstrat's Singh explained that American traders, particularly younger ones, feel they have to take bigger risks to get ahead. She said it's part of a broader trend dubbed financial nihilism, in which young investors grappling with a tough job market and high inflation turn to less-stable investing tools.

"It makes a lot of sense why individuals, specifically retail investors, keep gravitating towards this margin debt," the economic strategist added. "This is like a drug, and I think people just can't get enough of it in this economy."

Kevin Davis, a 59-year-old retail investor who made a living as a rapper in the 1980s and '90s before becoming a stock broker, believes the risks with leveraged trading outweigh the rewards.

"It's gambling. You're borrowing money you don't have, and so if it goes the other way, now you have a clock on your money, and it's ticking," said Davis, who owns an investing technology platform. "The market's not going to save you. It never does."

"Don't play the margin game," the Florida resident warned.

Luu became an engineering consultant because his father, who died of lung cancer in 2012, exposed him to computing. His mother said that between her two sons, Luu most resembles his father not only in terms of his features but also his character.

Reflecting on what her late husband might have thought about Luu's investing pursuits, Nguyen paused for a moment, holding a slight smile.

She then said, "He would've said he's proud of him."

— CNBC's Charlotte Morabito and Deena Zaidi contributed to this report.

#140. Roth conversions: When the ‘juice isn't really worth the squeeze,’ according to a top-ranked advisor

Roth individual retirement account conversions can potentially reduce lifetime taxes. But the strategy isn't right for everyone, and the choice is now more complex amid updates from President Donald Trump's "big beautiful bill" and other changes.

Roth conversions transfer pretax or nondeductible IRA funds into a Roth IRA, which kick-starts tax-free growth. The trade-off is that they can trigger more income in the year of the conversion.

The move can be attractive if you have large pretax retirement balances and you expect higher tax rates when it's time to withdraw the funds, experts say.

At year-end 2025, IRA-owning households in the U.S. had $15.9 trillion in assets in traditional IRAs, compared with $2.4 trillion in after-tax Roth IRAs, according to a 2026 report from the Investment Company Institute, an investing trade organization.

Read coverage of CNBC's 2026 Financial Advisor 100 list, including stories featuring ranked firms and their advisors:

Weighing Roth conversions, or partial Roth conversions, is "a strategy that continues to be very popular year-over-year," said Charissa Anderson, a certified financial planner who is an executive vice president at Ferguson Wellman Capital Management in Portland, Oregon. Her firm ranked No. 52 on CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 list for 2026.

As of March 31, Roth conversions were up 41% this year compared with the same period in 2025, according to the latest Fidelity data, based on an analysis of 19.6 million IRA accounts.

But experts say the strategy isn't right for everyone.

"There are just so many variables" when analyzing a possible Roth conversion, said Tommy Lucas, a CFP at Moisand Fitzgerald Tamayo in Orlando, Florida. His firm is ranked No. 44 on CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 list for 2026.

These could include when you claim Social Security, your life expectancy and legacy goals, among other factors, he said.

Depending on your tax bracket, "sometimes the juice isn't really worth the squeeze," said Lucas. "And we're going to have to squeeze every single year" because multiple factors can change the analysis.

If you're eyeing a Roth conversion before year-end, here are some key things to consider.

When deciding on a Roth conversion, projections should include the current year's taxes, along with an analysis of future years, financial advisors say.

"The [tax] bracket you see isn't always the rate you pay," because more income could phase out, or reduce, other tax benefits, according to CFP Tommy Blackburn, senior financial planner and partner at Mason and Associates in Newport News, Virginia. He is also a certified public accountant.

As an example, Blackburn pointed to a client in the 22% tax bracket with a child in college. Income from a conversion could trigger taxes above 30% because the client would lose an education tax credit, which is subtracted from their taxes owed, he said.

By comparison, a client in the 10% tax bracket could convert a limited amount under their standard deduction without owing additional taxes for the current year, he said.

More income could also impact temporary tax deductions enacted via Trump's "big beautiful bill," which have varying income phaseouts.

These could include the bigger federal deduction limit for state and local taxes, known as SALT, worth up to $40,400 for 2026, or the $6,000 senior "bonus" deduction, among others.

Retirees should also consider income-related monthly adjustment amounts, or IRMAAs, which increase Medicare Part B and Part D premiums once income exceeds a certain level. The surcharge is based on modified adjusted gross income from two years prior.

Boosting your AGI with Roth conversions can also reduce the premium tax credit, which makes Affordable Care Act marketplace health insurance less expensive.

Earning even $1 more than a certain income limit can threaten eligibility for the credit — known as the "ACA cliff" — and enrollees could owe full premiums for health coverage.

The cliff affects ACA enrollees when household income exceeds 400% of the federal poverty line, which varies by family size. For 2026, those limits are about $63,000 for a single person or $129,000 for a family of four.

That's why marketplace health insurance enrollees should "proceed with caution" before completing a Roth conversion, said CFP Bill Shafransky, a senior wealth advisor with Moneco Advisors in New Canaan, Connecticut.

"This is one of those financial strategies where you really want to dot your i's and cross your t's before acting," he said.
