#144. 1 Green Flag and 1 Red Flag for Bloom Energy Investors

While many fuel cell investors are still waiting for their investments to flourish, Bloom Energy (BE +3.58%) shareholders have enjoyed an impressive performance of late. Since the start of 2026, Bloom Energy shares have soared more than 166%.

But it's foolish to assume that simply because Bloom Energy shares have rocketed higher, the stock is a screaming buy. Let's take a closer look at both the good and the bad ahead of the company's reporting of its third-quarter 2026 financial results on Oct. 22.

When evaluating the fundamentals of companies, investors can sometimes struggle to find any semblance of financial well-being. But that's hardly the case with Bloom Energy.

From growing both revenue and earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) to maintaining a strong balance sheet (Bloom's net debt-to-EBITDA ratio was a conservative 0.35 at the end of Q2 2026), there are numerous indications of the company's impressive financial health. It's what's found on the cash-flow statement, however, that stands out as a bright, green flag.

Generating $175 million in free cash flow for Q2 2026, Bloom Energy has repeatedly produced free cash flow on a trailing-12-month basis for more than a year, proving that its ability to generate organic cash is more than a flash in the pan.

Plus, Bloom Energy's consistent free-cash-flow generation is uncommon among hydrogen-focused companies like Plug Power and FuelCell Energy, which have resorted to raising capital through substantial equity and debt issuances to keep the lights on.

In stellar financial health and with a significant market opportunity (Fortune Business Insights projects the fuel cell industry will grow from $16.8 billion in 2026 to $139 billion in 2034), Bloom Energy is certainly an alluring growth stock. The strong fundamentals, however, come at a cost.

Bloom Energy shares are currently changing hands at 347 times trailing earnings. As if its price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio wasn't steep enough, consider the steep cash-flow multiple: Bloom shares are priced at 109 times operating cash flow.

Because Bloom hasn't consistently generated earnings and positive operating cash flow for several years, it's impossible to compare the stock's current valuation to historical earnings-and cash-flow-based valuations. With respect to sales, though, investors can gain some insight. Trading at a notable premium to its five-year average sales multiple of 3.3, Bloom Energy's stock is changing hands today at 24.3 times trailing sales.

While the stock's valuation will surely deter value investors, those who don't typically prioritize bargain-bin stocks may also find the fuel cell stock's price tag prohibitive.

Since its initial public offering (IPO) in 2018, Bloom Energy has ascended into rarified air for hydrogen stocks, demonstrating both robust revenue and earnings growth, though the company's free-cash-flow production that is one of the most alluring qualities right now.

Although Bloom stock is pricey, it's not so pricey that those with multi-year investing horizons should look elsewhere to scratch their itch for quality growth stocks.

#145. Unsure how long this AI bull has? Bonds now offer a cushion at the best values in years

"It gets late early out there," was Yogi Berra's illogically brilliant take on the late-summer left-field shadows at the old Yankee Stadium.

Also works pretty well as an assessment of today's markets, where constant assurances that the AI theme is "still early" and widespread belief in unceasing economic momentum coexist with some late-cycle characteristics.

S&P 500 operating-earnings growth in the second quarter exceeded 30% and is projected to hit that threshold again in the third, yet the index itself is merely 2% above its June peak from before those stellar results were reported.

The S&P forward P/E has compressed from 23 a year ago to 19 today, which can be read as a signal both that investors are reluctant to pay up for current record profit margins and next year's decelerating growth — and that rising government-bond yields are relevant to the aggregate cost of capital for companies.

Consumer spending has held up fine, because unemployment is low and Americans spend what they make, though real incomes have begun to lag inflation, requiring some dissaving to support consumption.

Corporate-debt spreads have begun to rise in recent weeks from historically tight readings, as technology bond issuance and Treasury volatility combine to test investor risk appetites.

And, of course, the Federal Reserve has transitioned from last year's "insurance" rate cuts to a rate hike, with market expectations of a couple more, which while digestible in a strong economy at least raises the prospect of restraint on an expansion that's carried on for more than half a decade.

Every one of those items can be spun as mid-cycle adjustments, of course, and they may well be. In dynamic markets not governed by a clock, "getting later" is not the same as "almost over." It's tough for an economy to veer quickly into a ditch when the government is running deficits of 6% of GDP while the private sector is investing in new productive assets in multi-trillion-dollar bursts once reserved for emergency government stimulus measures.

And if the valuation compression in the AI-buildout bellwethers is a signal that investors are mindful of an eventual growth plateau, it is also the best argument against the criticism that AI equities are in a bubble. Micron still trading 15% below its June peak and Nvidia sitting at such a steep discount to the market P/E and that of defensive, capex-light Apple, suggest a level of sobriety that – all else equal – could mean that some risk has been drained away.

The extraordinary dissonance in market behavior has made it tough to infer clear macro signals. For weeks, historically anomalous statistics have piled up: Never before have so many new 52-week lows registered with the S&P 500 either up on a given day or so close to a record high.

Treasury yields making new highs has exacerbated the arrhythmic action, as pressure on cyclical parts of the market propels money into the rate-insensitive AI-levered tech giants, which produces all those new lows as the S&P 500 carries higher. In this market moment, very few index rally days are emphatic, no selloffs are fully bereft.

After a June 2 all-time high of 7620, the S&P 500 went sideways in a narrow range for two months and two days until breaking higher to a fresh, if marginal, new record on Aug. 4. Today is two months and two days since that breakout, and the index has merely gone sideways in a narrow range but enters the day about half a percent from another new high.

Yet since the Aug. 4 pop above 7700 for the first time, the median S&P 500 stock, the Russell 2000, the KBW Bank Index and the equal-weighted consumer-discretionary sector are down between 4% and 11%.

There have been times when this kind of unsettled action generates more stress than the broad indexes can absorb, such as in late 2018, when tightening financial conditions and internal market weakness in a mid-term election year caused the S&P 500 to drop nearly 20% into year-end, even with earnings growing 20% and no recession in sight.

That, granted, was a brief if treacherous gut check, giving way to a re-expansion of valuations and a march to new highs through 2019 right up until Covid struck.

Dean Curnutt, founder and CEO of Macro Risk Advisors, articulates the challenge facing risk-aware investors: "The US Treasury market, long referred to as the 'risk-free' asset, is more likely a sponsor of risk than a stabilizing asset in a portfolio…As stock/bond correlation pushes portfolio volatility higher, the correlation among stocks drags it lower. Much lower. The realized correlation among stocks in the SPX over the last 6 months is 4%. This inconceivably low level of correlation is Ozempic for volatility at the index level."

Of course, many people tolerate Ozempic well and are healthier for it. The current market structure has been remarkably generous toward undiscriminating passive index investors. The S&P 500 – by growing more leveraged over time to the strongest secular-growth theme while sidelining disrupted or cyclically vulnerable ones – has protected its owners from deeper drawdowns.

At some point, presumably, the AI-tech dominance of the index will carry too far and the S&P 500's great structural sheltering mechanism will leave it exposed to a bust cycle and a wave of capital destruction. Against that daunting but impossible-to-time prospect, the bond market is now offering a cushion at the best values in years.

This indicator from John Kolovos of Macro Risk Advisors uses several data points to reflect both what investors are saying and what they are doing.

Kolovos on the latest reading: "Bullish sentiment abated last week on the heels of tightening financial conditions and the rise in cross-asset implied volatility.  Cyclicals are washed out, and the number of stocks hitting 52 week lows and four week lows, along with the percentage of stocks reaching oversold RSI readings, looks much more like something we would normally see after an 8-10% decline. Yet the S&P 500 has only fallen roughly 3% peak to trough. Historically, that oversold combination has been a good one for forward returns."

-David Snyder, founder of Journey 1 Advisors and the source long known as my Mystery Broker before we identified him late last year, has few qualms about calling this a late-cycle market environment. He has believed since last year that the secular bull market was in its final phase, usually involving a tech-driven momentum blowoff.

In a piece last week, he cited the extraordinary and persistent outperformance of "high-beta" stocks, a phenomenon counter to a generation of finance theory, as something that will eventually face a devastating reversion to the mean.

-As a CNBC journalist, I'm not permitted to invest in individual stocks. And as a late adopter by temperament and disposition, I have interacted very little with AI tools.

So, it was up to a friend who's deeply involved in AI and investing to instruct AI to generate a hypothetical long-short portfolio reflective of my every utterance on TV and each word published under my byline.

The result was quite a bit more conservative than I might have guessed, though the quality and anti-hype attributes make some sense: Long Microsoft, Chevron and Coca-Cola, short Super Micro Computer, Micron and Robinhood. Hope the imaginary AI risk manager had some tight stops on those shorts.

-Reputationally and with plenty of justification, Generation X is not known for its placid acceptance of the "next big thing" that washes over society. Yet in a recent LinkedIn survey, GenX professionals stood out as being most enthusiastic about AI's impact, while their much younger GenZ counterparts are skeptical.

Perhaps it's that GenXers are already established in their careers and not searching for a foothold in a workplace with fewer entry-level jobs. Or maybe this is read by my peers between their late-40s and early-60s as simply another technology transition. In the words of one respondent: "We've lived through every major workplace reinvention of the last three decades…It's just the next chapter." One can hope.

Entering this time of year as a bear has meant fighting uphill, typically.

Below is this year's Dow Jones Industrial Average path set against Ned Davis Research's Cycle Composite chart for 2026. This combines the annual seasonal pattern, the four-year election cycle and the decadal tendencies (years that end in 6).

Right around now is when the tailwinds would start to kick in if historical statistics were all that mattered.

The disclaimers are crucial, though. For one, note the differing scales on the Y-axes – this is mostly about the shape of a year rather than magnitude of moves.

And more to the point, see the profound divergence early this year, when the Iran war and oil surge struck what was supposed to be a first-quarter levitation. It's nice to be aware of the seasonal winds, but as I like to say, such historical patterns are climate, not weather.

#154. CoreWeave Dropped 20% Last Week. Is It Time to Panic or Buy?

It was nothing short of a brutal week for CoreWeave (CRWV +1.29%). The AI cloud computing company's stock was crushed, falling more than 20% as of Oct. 16. The cause of the precipitous fall is mainly twofold: debt and spending worries. Is it time for CoreWeave's shareholders to panic, or is this an opportunity?

First, investor concerns regarding CoreWeave's debt load are real. The company has approximately $35 billion in total debt, compared to just $5.5 billion in cash. Net interest payments are racking up and hit $640 million in just the second quarter. The yields on CoreWeave's unsecured bonds are approaching 15%. S&P rates the company a B+, which is essentially junk bond territory.

The company's extraordinarily high capital expenditures this year are also cause for concern. CoreWeave spent just over $16 billion in the first half of 2026 and expects to spend up to $39 billion total this year. That's triple its revenue guidance of $12.4 billion to $13.2 billion.

Lastly, there's growing public resistance to data centers. States are considering imposing restrictions and moratoria to curb development.

So, with all this bad news, are there still reasons to invest? Yes, and it has to do with demand and CoreWeave's backlog. In the second quarter alone, revenue grew 112% year over year, and the backlog exceeded $104 billion. Even Nvidia's (NVDA +1.87%) CEO Jensen Huang came to CoreWeave's defense, saying that he's optimistic about the stock even after this plunge.

Aa long-term investor, I have reservations about CoreWeave right now, as many others do. I think this price drop presents an opportunity, but only for the most risk-tolerant. If buying CoreWeave now, I'd likely build a position slowly over time. The company needs to prove it can convert its backlog efficiently and manage its debt load effectively.

#159. Nvidia's $6 trillion milestone looms. Here's when options traders see it happening

There's a simple reason the Nasdaq-100 Index closed at new records Friday: The world's biggest company notched its first record since May.

Nvidia, which accounts for 13% of the Nasdaq and 8% of the S&P 500 Index,  added 1.3% Friday, ending seven weeks of sideways trading surrounding a high-stakes meeting between President Donald Trump and corporate executives leading what Trump calls "super intelligence."

The rally puts the value of Jensen Huang's semiconductor business at just under $5.7 trillion, and based on the price of options trading at Nvidia, it will likely cross the $6 trillion threshold by the end of this month. It should be a comforting notion for equity bulls. Currently, there is about a 50% chance Nvidia will reach a $6 trillion valuation between now and the end of this month, and a 13% chance it happens this week, according to market-maker pricing of deltas on Nvidia options expiring this week and Oct. 30, which measure the sensitivity of options pricing relative to moves in the stock. The odds it happens between now and Dec. 18 is about 67%.

They're also implying about a 1-in-16 chance Nvidia could hit $7 trillion by Nov. 20. Based on the current share count, Nvidia would need to touch $248 to cross the milestone.

"Nvidia's buyback announcement was a bright spot," Ben Emons, managing director at Highline Asset Management, wrote in a note to clients last week. "The buyback is not just a payout but a capital-allocation event that asserts confidence in long-run AI demand."

It's important to note when using deltas to gauge a range of possibilities that the same size move in the opposite direction is also just as likely. While that's largely the case for Nvidia, some of the stock's call options are currently trading with a higher implied volatility than the equivalent puts, Barchart data shows. Such "call skew" is a sign that traders have a bias toward hedging for a rally.

#162. Always on, always listening: New AI devices are pushing legal limits and could put users in jeopardy

Thomas, 43, wears a pair of Meta's camera-equipped glasses, a Fieldy note-taking pendant around his neck and a wristband from Amazon's Bee, all of which record his daily life. A Pittsburgh-based business owner and a livestreamer, Thomas relies on the devices to help him stay organized, pay bills on time and set reminders.

"I'm forgetful AF," Thomas said in an interview. "My life is so crazy that not having to remember to remember is fantastic."

Not everyone is on board with his lifestyle. Earlier this week, a bystander at a local bar noticed his Meta Glasses.

"He was like, 'I don't feel comfortable,'" Thomas said. "I don't turn it off, I take it off completely because people don't really believe it's off."

It's the type of interaction users are increasingly navigating as more tech companies introduce AI-powered, always-listening devices and features, which have been marketed as useful tools to transcribe meetings, keep track of conversations, set reminders and offer personalized recommendations.

The latest example of these gadgets arrived Thursday with Amazon's Bee Frontier wearable and Bee Eclipse, a card-shaped device that attaches to a smartphone. Both devices are designed to record, transcribe and analyze a user's day.

Apple's latest Apple Watch Series 12, unveiled in September, will have Siri Recap, which "ambiently" takes notes throughout the day and generates summaries of conversations. Another feature called Live Rewind can recap 15 seconds of a conversation via a text transcription.

Meta's popular smart glasses can take photos, capture video and record voice notes or reminders. Startups including Plaud and Pocket also developed card-sized note-taking devices, while Friend offers an AI necklace.

The devices have fueled concerns that they could erode privacy, by enabling covert recording without obtaining bystanders' consent and collecting sensitive data that's potentially accessible to others.

Amazon, Google and other makers of voice-activated smart speakers faced similar privacy concerns when their devices first hit the market, in some cases leading to lawsuits and regulatory fines.

But this new generation of AI devices is also testing the limits of privacy law.

Unlike earlier smart speakers that were activated via a so-called "wake word" and sometimes stored recordings or sent audio to the cloud, some of these products can continuously listen, interpret speech, and extract its meaning without retaining the underlying audio. This capability has raised a largely untested question about whether that processing itself can amount to an unlawful interception.

"With new technology like this, my statement is always to embrace with caution," Karen Panetta, dean of graduate education at Tufts' School of Engineering and a fellow at the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, said.

She added, "If I'm giving permission for myself to be recorded, or for everything I look at to be recorded, that doesn't mean everybody else around you has given that consent."

Apple and Amazon appear to have sidestepped some of the privacy concerns that dogged earlier voice assistants.

Apple says the feature does not store audio, send recordings to its servers, or involve human review. Amazon has said it doesn't store audio from Bee devices, and conversations are processed in a secure environment "where no one, including Amazon, can access your data."

But that may not resolve the legal question.

Many state wiretap and eavesdropping laws are written around whether a private communication was intercepted or its contents were acquired — not simply whether a conventional audio recording was created.

Colin Zick, a privacy and data security attorney at Foley Hoag, said Apple appears to have learned from the first wave of litigation over voice assistants. But the new technology raises questions those earlier cases never had to answer: Can a system that is continuously listening, interpreting speech and turning it into a summary still amount to an interception if it never saves the underlying audio?

Some state laws define interception broadly. Massachusetts, for example, defines an intercepting device to include equipment capable of "transmitting, receiving, amplifying, or recording" a communication, while the "contents" of a communication can include its substance and meaning.

In Zick's view, a device that continuously receives speech and produces a written summary could potentially fall within that language even without retaining an audio file.

And in some states, the bigger legal risk may fall not on Apple, Amazon or other AI gadget makers but on the person wearing the device.

"A non-wearer did not buy the watch, agree to Apple's terms, or choose to have their conversation summarized in the app," Zick said.

Daniel Pi, an associate professor at the University of New Hampshire Franklin Pierce School of Law, said New Hampshire's statute is broad enough that he believes the Watch's new audio-intelligence features would qualify as an interception. The law covers not only recordings, but the "aural or other acquisition" of the contents of a communication.

That could create an unusual situation in which an ordinary consumer turns on a feature built into a mainstream device and, at least technically, runs afoul of state law by using it during a private conversation without everyone's consent.

Pi said a user in New Hampshire could potentially face civil or criminal liability for doing so, though he stressed that the practical risk of prosecution is far lower. It could be difficult to know whether someone had the feature enabled in the first place, and he said he would be surprised to see prosecutors pursue cases involving a bare statutory violation where no one was harmed.

The legal questions are also different from those raised by earlier smart speakers and voice assistants. Those cases often centered on devices mistakenly activating or capturing speech that was not intended as a command. Here, the feature is designed to acquire and interpret the substance of a conversation — and the user has deliberately opted in.

That changes the analysis, Pi said, and could also shift responsibility toward the wearer rather than the technology company itself.

The broader privacy concern extends beyond who is legally responsible.

Michael Stokes, a former CIA officer and senior vice president of emerging technologies at Veilant, said the bigger shift is that people can be swept into AI-powered surveillance without owning or knowingly interacting with the device doing the collecting.

"I think the bystander problem is really the concern I have — that you can be surveilled without owning the technology," Stokes said.

He pointed to the growing number of cameras, microphones, and sensors embedded in consumer devices, from smart glasses to watches and AI recorders. The difference now, he said, is that AI can rapidly interpret what those devices collect and draw meaning from far larger volumes of information than earlier generations of consumer technology.

For Stokes, that makes the Apple Watch part of a much larger change in the privacy landscape. During his time at the CIA, he helped develop the concept of ubiquitous technical surveillance, describing a world in which everyday devices continuously generate information that can reveal identities, locations, and associations.

The concern is not simply that more data can be collected, he said, but that the cost of making sense of it has fallen dramatically.

In the past, Stokes said, intelligence collection could require thousands of hours of work to gather, sort and analyze information about a person. AI increasingly automates that process, making it cheaper and easier to extract useful information from data that may have been gathered incidentally.

That creates a new kind of exposure for people who never opted into the technology in the first place — whether it is a private conversation picked up by a nearby wearable or information collected by a device they do not own.

"We no longer have these pockets of small privacy that we thought we did in the past," Stokes said.

Aida Baradari, founder of the startup Deveillance, is trying to give some control back to people worried about being recorded without their consent.

The company created a hockey puck-shaped gadget, called the Spectre I, that uses AI to scan for nearby devices and sends out "adversarial signals" that scramble a person's speech before microphones can process it.

Baradari said she watched as more AI wearables hit the market and felt users should have a greater say in how they interact with them.

"We need to be able to use technology while not giving up our core values or rights," she said.

#165. Why Sandisk Stock Shot Higher Today

Shares of Sandisk (SNDK +6.60%) charged sharply higher on Monday, jumping as much as 8.3%. As of 11:24 a.m. ET, the stock was still up 7.9%.

While a rebound in technology issues certainly helped, the semiconductor specialist rallied on positive news in the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) space.

Earlier this year, Nvidia (NVDA +1.87%) announced the development of NVHBM, the company's custom HBM architecture. NVHBM is a custom HBM die that delivers 15% lower power consumption and 30% higher bandwidth, all on a smaller die than HBM4e. To be clear, this isn't a replacement for traditional HBM, but rather connective technology between Nvidia's NVLink and HBM chips.

A report emerged over the weekend that Nvidia has asked Samsung Electronics to adopt Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing's 3-nanometer chipmaking process to produce the NVHBM dies, according to a story that first appeared in the Seoul Economic Daily. This will mark the first such collaboration between TSMC and Samsung, according to the report.

Moreover, Nvidia has approached the industry's biggest memory producers, including Micron Technology and SK Hynix, to use this process, which would standardize it across multiple memory suppliers. This, in turn, would free up valuable real estate on the compute die, resulting in up to 30% additional compute.

Investors have been concerned that demand for artificial intelligence (AI) could falter, thereby reducing demand for the AI chips. This move by Nvidia suggests that -- despite fears to the contrary -- the adoption of AI still has room to run. This suggests that the same is true for memory chip suppliers.

Even in the face of unprecedented demand for memory chips, Sandisk stock is selling for just 19 times earnings and 6 times forward earnings. This gives investors the opportunity to pick up shares at a discount.

Markets remained on edge with higher oil prices and Treasury yields weighing on investor sentiment and triggering fears of additional interest rate hikes.

In this climate, investors with a long-term horizon can track recommendations from top Wall Street analysts to find stocks with solid growth prospects.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

CRWV stock performance has been underwhelming as investors worry about high capital spending, the analyst noted. Chatterjee noted the 25% price hike in July across CoreWeave's product offerings and frequent price increases by rivals like Nebius (NBIS), adding that some peers are charging nearly three times more for short-term compute contracts than what CoreWeave charges on longer-term deals.

After a review of Palo Alto's product-level growth catalysts, Powell sees clear upside to both revenue and next-generation security (NGS) annual recurring revenue (ARR) in fiscal 2027. #175. A SpaceX-Tesla Merger Could Happen Before the End of 2026. Here's What That Could Mean for the Stocks

Elon Musk runs both Tesla (TSLA +4.07%) and Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (SPCX +1.95%), better known as just SpaceX. Both businesses work on overlapping projects at times, and there's considerable incentive for them to merge, as doing so could unlock synergies and make it easier for them to raise money. Plus, combined, their growth potential would be even more massive, potentially attracting more growth investors along the way.

Many growth investors and analysts have concluded that it's a matter of when, not if, a merger will take place. There have even been rumblings that a deal could materialize before the year comes to a close. But that doesn't mean either stock would be likely to surge if that were to happen.

An analyst at Barclays, Dan Levy, suggested that due to favorable conditions under the Trump administration, there may be an incentive to get a deal done sooner rather than later. While the U.S. president and Musk have at times had a volatile relationship, Musk has reportedly donated $276 million to support Republican campaign efforts in the upcoming midterm elections, which the president would likely view favorably.

That doesn't, of course, mean that a deal is likely or that it would obtain easy approval, but it does suggest that the relationship may not be strained at all. Meanwhile, Levy points to Tesla's annual general meeting, which must take place by Dec. 6, as a key date to watch, as it could be when a vote on a potential deal takes place. There isn't an awful lot of time before then, but there is certainly a case as to why a merger may at least be announced in the near future.

SpaceX and Tesla are both highly valued and expensive stocks. The reality is that while a merger would certainly unlock more growth opportunities, investors have likely already priced that into their respective valuations. Thus, even if an announcement does take place, it may not lead to a huge surge for either stock.

It's also not necessarily a guarantee that a large premium would be paid for the company being acquired, which can sometimes send shares of the business much higher.

SpaceX isn't profitable, and while Tesla is, its stock trades at a hefty price-to-earnings multiple of more than 300. Both stocks have plenty of long-term growth and bullishness priced into their valuations; investors shouldn't expect them to take off, even if a merger is announced. And with high valuations, they still have plenty of downside risk.

David Jagielski, CPA has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Tesla. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#176. Software’s new consolidator gets big vote of confidence from Berkshire

At the time of its Nasdaq debut in July, Bending Spoons was a little-known holding company out of Italy that owned older internet names like AOL, Vimeo, Eventbrite and Evernote.

Less than four months later, the Milan-based firm has emerged as a surprising home for former high-flying software startups that have been thrust aside by the artificial intelligence boom. Its M&A plan got a major boost this week from the most famous holding company on the planet: Berkshire Hathaway.

Berkshire, which Bending Spoons describes as a "longstanding inspiration" for its strategy, has now invested over $900 million in the company, including a $330 million stake disclosed on Wednesday. Wall Street loved the deal, sending Bending Spoons' stock up 41%, though some of those gains were lost later in the week, leaving the company with a market cap of about $30 billion.

"Berkshire's decision to add to its position just a few months after the IPO and at these levels provides another vote of confidence in the Bending Spoons model from one of the world's most respected long-term investors," wrote analysts at Mizuho, in a report after the announcement.

The other big news out of Bending Spoons this week underscores the flipside of the business: job cuts. In August, Bending Spoons announced it was buying workflow software provider Airtable for about $1.3 billion, or almost 90% below the company's peak valuation from late 2021. Bending Spoons said Monday that a "large portion of the pre-acquisition team" from Airtable would be leaving with "substantial separation packages." Layoffs were previously implemented at Evernote, Vimeo, WeTransfer and others in the portfolio.

For the technology industry, Bending Spoons' moves represent the latest example of how quickly fortunes are turning in the AI era, as new agents powered by large language models displace software developers and the products they built. With Anthropic and OpenAI marching toward trillion-dollar valuations, businesses are putting more valuable work in their hands at the expense of a host of software-as-a-service names, creating a phenomenon that's become known as the "SaaSpocalypse."

Shares of Intuit, HubSpot and Adobe are all down at least 30% this year, and a long list of private SaaS companies that were once venture darlings are now struggling to find capital, with the public market showing no appetite for IPOs. Last month, Bending Spoons agreed to buy collaboration software vendor Miro, once valued at $17.5 billion, for $1.36 billion.

"You're either like a hot thing or you're nothing," said Ethan Kurzweil, founder and managing partner at Chemistry VC and a veteran software investor. Kurzweil said he uses Airtable, and said there are plenty of good SaaS products on the market led by solid teams, "but they're not on the frontier anymore."

Bending Spoons was launched in 2013 by friends Luca Ferrari, the CEO, Matteo Danieli and Francesco Patarnello. A mobile app they'd created called Evertale failed to take off, and they used the $40,000 they had left to build an operating company instead of "products nobody wanted," according to the IPO prospectus.

Bending Spoons has announced all of its biggest deals in the last few years, beginning with Evernote in 2022, followed by Brightcove in 2024, and Vimeo, AOL and Eventbrite in 2025.

The company held its IPO on June 30, raising about $1.7 billion at $29 a share, and hit the Nasdaq the next day. The stock closed Friday at $47.07.

Prior to Bending Spoons' recent jump into enterprise software, some of the leading acquirers in the space over the past decade were private equity behemoths Thoma Bravo and Vista Equity Partners. Those firms were aiming to buy what they viewed as undervalued SaaS companies and, through a combination of cost cuts, efficiency improvements and rollups, turn them into assets that could be sold or taken public at a higher price.

Bending Spoons is using a different playbook. The company isn't looking for eventual exits but rather wants to generate profits from the businesses it buys, similar to the Warren Buffett model. But unlike Berkshire, Bending Spoons' focus is technology, and it's taking a hands-on approach with its own software, operations and personnel decisions.

Nick Mehta, former CEO of cloud software vendor Gainsight, said private equity firms are limited now because "they got their nose bloodied."

"They paid much higher prices and have so many troubled companies that it's difficult for them to take swings now," said Mehta, who sold Gainsight to Vista in 2020.

Thoma Bravo and Vista didn't respond to requests for interviews. Bending Spoons told CNBC in a statement that it hadn't been outbid for a target in "several years."

As the company started jumping into SaaS, Mehta said "Bending Spooned" became a verb in Silicon Valley, referring to companies getting scooped up for pennies on the dollar.

"Unfortunately, a lot of my friends in that game are stuck," Mehta said. "Investors want out but there are no buyers. Anything pre-ChatGPT is legacy now."

Lloyd Walmsley, an analyst at Mizuho, said Bending Spoons' model is distinct from the older buyout approach.

"I think there aren't a lot of people that do what these guys do in terms of the depth of operations and the willingness to make substantial product changes," Walmsley said in an interview. "It's not typical of traditional private equity firms to make anywhere near this level of change."

For customers of the companies that Bending Spoons buys, sudden price hikes can follow.

In April 2023, months after the Evernote acquisition, Bending Spoons lifted the annual personal subscription price to $130 from $70. Later, the company changed its offerings, charging $100 for its so-called starter plan and $250 for "Evernote Advanced," compared to the $170 it had been charging for the pro plan.

"My first reaction was like, Oh man, I guess I have to switch to OneNote," said Walmsley, referring to Microsoft's notetaking app. But he said he stuck with Evernote.

"They're really savvy at finding these things that they provide a lot of value, and the switching costs are really high," Walmsley said. "The price isn't that high relative to the switching cost."

Bending Spoons uses the profits from its portfolio companies for future growth, the "overwhelming majority" of which comes from doing more deals, Ferrari told CNBC in an interview on Thursday.

"There are certain opportunities for improvement we can unlock over the first few years, and then the business will have whatever organic growth is intrinsic in that market," Ferrari said.

For Berkshire and its fellow Bending Spoons investors, the bet is still unproven.

The products have to remain desirable enough that customers are willing to pay up at a time when AI is squeezing margins across much of the software sector. In its first earnings report as a public company in August, Bending Spoons said revenue more than doubled from a year earlier to over $700 million, with growth almost entirely driven by acquisitions, while net income climbed 171% to $177 million.

That was before the Airtable deal had closed and Miro had yet to be announced. In the coming quarters and years, Wall Street will get a clear picture of whether the firm's structure can revive software.

On the earnings call in August, an analyst asked whether Airtable represents a long-term shift in the M&A strategy towards enterprise.

Ferrari said that about half of Bending Spoons' revenue already comes from professional businesses, largely through Brightcove and Vimeo, which has an enterprise component. The focus on software of late, he said, has more to do with where he's finding value after a hefty selloff.

"Most enterprise SaaS businesses were valued at irrationally high levels until somewhat recently," Ferrari said. "We never saw those prices making any sense."

— CNBC's Ari Levy contributed to this report.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

TL;DR: Falling Treasury yields are taking mortgage rates down with them.

Mortgage rates are starting off this week with a nice drop, though the likely reason for the fall could be a little anxiety-inducing.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.20% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 15 basis points lower than Friday and 12 basis points lower than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.

Rates started this slide last week, as investors' previously sky-high confidence in AI came a little closer to earth. Tech stocks lost a bit of their luster, and bonds looked more appealing. Greater demand for bonds pushed up bond prices, dropping bond yields (they move inversely). And mortgage rates are often indexed to the yield on the 10-year Treasury so, huzzah, lower mortgage rates.

On one hand, yay! But on the other hand … uh, what was that about stocks? For way more detail, keep reading below the chart.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Like I mentioned above, mortgage rates started edging lower last week as Treasury yields came down. Mortgage rates are generally benchmarked to the yield on 10-year Treasury notes, so where the yield goes, rates go, too.

The yield is basically the return investors get on a bond. A bond is a little piece of government or corporate debt; when an investor buys a bond, they're making a tiny loan to the issuer. The issuer agrees to pay them back a set amount over the bond's lifespan (that's the yield), and when the bond matures, the investor gets the bond's original price back. That's why unlike anything-could-happen stocks, bonds are generally considered relatively low risk.

A bond investor who buys a bond at issuance knows immediately: Here's my cost, here's what I'll earn and here's when my initial investment will be returned. When investors sell bonds to each other, things get more interesting, because the market now determines the price, and that shifts the relative value of the yield.

Here's how that works. If you bought a $100 bond with $5 annual yield payments, that yield is 5%. But say you want to sell that bond but can’t find a full-price buyer; the best price you can get for it is $80. The annual yield payments are still $5, but since they're relative to that lower price, the yield is now 6.25%.

For much of the summer and early fall, we saw lots of Treasury bond selling, which drove prices down and yields up. That kept pushing mortgage rates higher. Additionally, tech companies issuing loads of corporate bonds to help fund AI buildout meant that bond investors had a sexier option than Plain Jane Treasuries.

Last week, that dynamic reversed as doubts crept in about the potential profits from AI. September's Consumer Price Index, which came out last Wednesday, and Producer Price Index, from Thursday, showed that inflation's still running hot. If prices are climbing, the costs of building data structures and other AI infrastructure will increase, right? So to get solid returns on these investments, tech companies are going to have to make some serious profits. That right there is where some investors are having misgivings.

It sort of played out like a teen movie. Investors realized that the hot, popular girl (tech stocks) might not actually be all that, and their eyes turned to the reliable girl-next-door who'd been there for them all along (Treasuries).

Just so we're clear: No one is saying the AI bubble is bursting, or really that there even is an AI bubble. But yes, prices for Treasuries went up and yields fell, so mortgage rates ebbed, too. Whether this downward trend will last depends on a lot of factors, including whether tech companies can convince investors that they're on track for strong profits and whether anything can improve fuel prices, since that's a massive factor in inflation.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you could start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.70% or higher — but there just aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

#180. Lula or Bolsonaro: Wall Street braces for two wildly different results in Brazil election

With the first round of Brazil's presidential election taking place Sunday, Wall Street is gearing up with starkly different market predictions depending on the outcome of the neck-and-neck race.

"The Brazil trade is: Does Lula win or does Bolsonaro win?" said Fernando Marengo, chief economist at Black Toro Global Investments.

Those names should sound familiar. Lula is 80-year-old leftist Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who is running for a fourth term against 45-year-old right-winger Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. If neither candidate gets more than 50% of the vote, a runoff will take place Oct. 25.

In short, if Bolsonaro wins, Wall Street expects a rally in the country's bonds, currency and stocks.

As Bolsonaro has come from behind in the last few months, Brazilian stocks have moved higher along with his poll numbers. In a recent note to clients, JPMorgan noted that the MSCI Brazil "rose by 0.25% on average each day that Flavio gained in the polls."

Kalshi markets now show Bolsonaro favored to win 60% to Lula's 39%. Prediction markets are prohibited in Brazil, so they may not reflect local sentiment. In a note to clients, Aurora Macro Strategies senior advisor Richard Lapper said, "the balance has shifted toward Flavio over the past month, but not nearly as far as the prediction markets are pricing."

Bolsonaro is the favored candidate of the markets because he's promising more fiscal discipline, something many economists say Brazil desperately needs. Debt-to-GDP stands at 81.9%, up 10% since Lula took office.

"We need a 3-3.5% fiscal adjustment to stabilize the public debt in relation to GDP," said Leonardo Porto, Brazil head economist for Citi. And it can't just come from one-offs like privatization of state assets, he said. "Brazil needs a permanent fiscal adjustment."

That means cutting spending or raising taxes — either of which will be difficult. Roughly 90% of Brazil's budget is mandatory, some of it required by the constitution. At 32%, Brazil's tax burden is already the highest in Latin America, according to the OECD, and its prospects for growth are low.

But there's a lot to be gained if Bolsonaro wins and manages to implement a "robust reform agenda," said JPMorgan.

The firm looks to what happened under his father Jair when he was in power from 2016 to 2020. Bolsonaro Sr. managed to pass pension reform, which saved hundreds of billions of dollars. It imposed a minimum retirement age of 65 for men and 60 for women. Previously, men could retire at any age after working for 35 years, and women could retire at any age after working for 30 years. On average, the male retirement age was 56, and 53 for women.

During that period of reform, JPMorgan said Brazil's 2-year yields fell almost to 4.7%, and the equity market gained 130%.

If Brazil enters another period of reform, JPMorgan analysts say interest rates could decline to their neutral level, 6% in real terms, 10% in nominal terms, and "we would be thinking about the MSCI Brazil upside potential between 21% and 41%." They believe the forward P/E could move from a current level of 8.6 to as high as 13.3, last seen in 2020.

The currency outcome is "bimodal," said JPMorgan, with USD/BRL moving to 5.50 if Lula wins and 4.90 if Bolsonaro wins.

The entire lower house, and one third of the upper house are also being decided in this election. The composition of the legislature will be a key factor regarding the ability to achieve reforms.

Black Toro's Marengo points out that other recent victories by pro-business candidates in Latin America have led to big upside moves in the countries' stocks, bonds and currencies. He notes Colombia's risk premium compression "was about 200 points, and it was one of the stock markets that rose the most — something similar to what happened in Peru." Marengo cautions some of the move is already priced in in Brazil.

As with all emerging markets, a key risk is rising global interest rates, and for Latin America in particular, the El Niño weather phenomenon which could lead to crop damage for agricultural exporters.

#186. Investors are buying up vast tracts of timberland across U.S. in one of market's longest-term bets

When the economy and the market look shaky, gold and government bonds are the traditional places to park money. Lately, some investors have also been looking at something more rooted: timber.

The pitch is easy to like: a back-to-basics, natural asset that grows on its own, matures into a harvest and can be cashed in all while you use it to hunt, pitch a tent, or forage.

Institutions have been buying timberland at a rate of one million acres per year, according to Bank of America, and some financial advisors say individual investors, including younger Americans priced out of the housing market, are also taking a look at the asset class. But it is far from a rush, and investors who already own timberland caution that it may not be very profitable in the short term.

"Timber is a very low return investment. I have curtailed my investments," said Pat Dorn, founder of Anchor Investment Management, a fee-only advisory firm in Columbia, South Carolina, and a former chairman of the South Carolina Forestry Association. Dorn owns 2,500 acres of timberland in South Carolina's booming upstate region. Dorn said the problem is that right now more timber is being grown than is needed in a sluggish housing economy.

"Supply beats demand, and that causes flat prices. Timber is not an investment I would make currently," Dorn said.

Nationally, the Bureau of Labor Statistics' producer price index for logs, bolts, timber, pulpwood and wood chips ticked up in September, but prices have been mostly on the decline since summer 2022. This measures prices received by producers for those products, rather than timberland values or investment returns. Over the very long-term, prices have climbed substantially.

Financial institutions point to the asset class as one of interest specifically for the long-term investor.

Ken Shepard, head of specialty asset management at Bank of America Private Bank said that timberland is not a tactical asset class that can be easily entered or exited in response to short-term market conditions. "We view it as a strategic, long-term investment supported by several favorable secular trends, including the continued expansion of the timber industry in the U.S. South and growing demand for wood products beyond traditional construction uses," Shepard said.

For example, he said, demand for wood pellets used in bioenergy, while controversial, has increased significantly. In addition, timberland values are benefiting from strong demand from recreational and lifestyle buyers, providing support for land prices beyond the income generated from timber harvesting.

The National Council of Real Estate Investment Fiduciaries' Timberland Property Index, which tracks privately held U.S. timber properties owned at least partly on behalf of institutional investors, posted a total return of 0.95% in the second quarter of 2026, comprising 0.34% income and 0.61% appreciation.

Bank of America's 2026 outlook reported that the one-million-acre annual pace of buying is a three-year streak of dealmaking it expects to continue.

According to Bank of America, timber managers acquired 55% of all acres that changed hands in 2025 against just 15% sold. Institutions are playing the long game. Large timberland managers buy for pension funds and endowments that can wait decades, and that can make bets on a longer-term recovery in a currently slumping U.S. housing market that will be good for lumber pricing. But a private owner living through today's market sees things differently.

Dorn pointed out that timber companies buy less mature trees for pulpwood, which goes into paper towels or notebook paper, and those trees can take 12-14 years to mature. The chip-and-saw variety of trees take a little bit longer, while the big prize, timber cut for houses, can take 25 years. "That is where the top value is," he said.

According to Dorn, what landowners are paid for standing timber varies depending on what the trees are used for. Pine pulpwood consists of trees ground into paper and packaging, while pine sawtimber is made up of larger trees cut into lumber for homebuilding. Meanwhile, hardwood sawtimber, consists of oak and other big trees used in flooring, furniture and pallets. Each product feeds a different set of buyers, so one can climb while others fall.

South Carolina Forestry Commission data show statewide average pine pulpwood stumpage prices, what buyers pay landowners for standing timber, fell from $5.67 a ton in the third quarter of 2025 to $3.79 in the third quarter of 2026, a decline of about 33%. Pine sawtimber prices fell about 6% over the same period, from $22.78 to $21.47 a ton, while hardwood sawtimber prices rose about 40%, from $16.04 to $22.52.

Historically, pulpwood has been as high as $12 to $18 a ton, according to Dorn, and twenty years ago, soft timber was in the $35-$40 range. He said those prices could make a comeback if the housing market ever recovers, because pine sawtimber is cut into lumber for new homes, so its price tends to follow home building.

Strategically placed, timber may not be a bad investment, according to Dorn, though that would be because of the land itself more than the timber. "The return is in the land, not the timber," Dorn said.

He advises anyone thinking of investing in timberland to scout for prime parcels of land located outside growing metro areas that may be poised to pop as the local population keeps spreading. "If one hopes to buy land near growing metro areas and holds on to it, timber is a reasonable way to keep it earning something — a very low return — while you hold that land," he said.

Michael Martin, a timber owner in western New York and vice president of market strategy at brokerage firm TradingBlock, says timberland can be a good long-term investment but the reality of being an owner belies the romantic image of acres of untouched timberland. It is not as passive an investment class as it may seem to be.

Direct ownership is highly illiquid and comes with management costs, property taxes, harvesting expenses, exposure to local timber markets, and risks including wildfire, pests, disease and trespassers hunting or cutting trees.

And when it is time to harvest timber, you need to make sure you are getting the best deal. "If you simply go with a small local outfit without getting competing bids, you don't always know if you're getting the best price," Martin said.

He also said timber prices are very local and can impact whether it's a solid investment.

"I am constantly checking stumpage reports because timber prices are extremely local. An oak tree in western New York may have a completely different value from one in the Adirondacks," Martin said.

In addition, partial timbering every ten years or so has barely covered the property taxes. "At the end of the day, I barely break even," he added.

Some in local real estate and investing markets say younger buyers are curious, though firsthand evidence is hard to find.

"As a millennial and a realtor, I understand the appeal. I've thought about buying timberland myself," said Jake Kennedy, a Nashville-based realtor, noting that his generation has lived through the dot-com crash, the Great Recession, a pandemic, huge swings in housing and now inflation. "One lesson from all of that we have learned is that scarcity matters when it comes to places to park your money," Kennedy said, adding as examples that more IPOs can be announced or new crypto created.

"But you can't manufacture another 500 acres of land," Kennedy said. "Timber itself is a resource that takes decades to grow. And there is something reassuring about owning an asset that is tangible," he added. But he also cautioned that timber's durability doesn't mean profitability. Trees can be temperamental and subject to many variables.

The people Kennedy has spoken with see timberland as a relatively safe place to park money, he said, because demand for timber products isn't going away. "In the meantime, yes, hunting is a common activity while owners are waiting for the investment to grow and mature, literally," he said.

"I don't think my generation is suddenly giving up on houses and becoming timber barons. However, I do think we are a lot more interested in alternative places to store wealth than previous generations might have been," he added.

For many millennials, homeownership has become increasingly difficult due to elevated home prices, higher mortgage rates, and limited inventory in many markets. "As a result, some investors are looking for alternative ways to participate in real assets and potentially build equity without purchasing a home directly," said Nadeem Kassam, chief investment strategist at Marnoa Private Wealth Counsel.

Outside direct or institutional fund ownership, there are timber ETFs and timber-focused funds that provide exposure to a theme that is closely tied to long-term housing demand and construction activity, though they remain highly niche investments in an ETF market now valued in the trillions of dollars.

Kassam pointed to the iShares Global Timber & Forestry ETF (WOOD), with roughly $260 million in assets, and the Invesco MSCI Global Timber ETF (CUT), which has roughly $30 million in assets.

"The investment case is supported by persistent housing shortages across many parts of the U.S. and growing bipartisan support for policies aimed at increasing housing supply and improving affordability. If these efforts lead to increased homebuilding over time, demand for lumber and wood products could benefit," Kassam said.

But he noted that investors should understand that timber ETFs are not a direct investment in timberland. Neither ETF owns trees.

"Most own publicly traded companies involved in timber, forest products, wood manufacturing, and other parts of the housing value chain," Kassam said, explaining the advantage is liquidity and accessibility, but returns will be driven by more than just timber prices.

WOOD's largest holdings include Weyerhaeuser, a major timberland owner, alongside Brazilian pulp maker Suzano, Nine Dragons Paper and West Fraser Timber. CUT is weighted toward paper, packaging and materials makers such as Svenska Cellulosa, UPM, Stora Enso and Avery Dennison. WOOD has drawn about $73 million in net inflows over the past year, according to ETF Database.

"For investors who are priced out of the housing market, timber ETFs may offer a way to participate in the long-term housing and construction story through a diversified, liquid investment vehicle. The key is recognizing that you're buying exposure to businesses that benefit from housing-related demand, not a direct ownership stake in land or residential real estate," Kassam said.

Junyi Liu, professor of economics at Soka University of America, who studies international and development economics, said he is not seeing evidence of a boom, but that timberland does have some unusual characteristics as an alternative asset.

"Returns can come from biological growth, timber prices, and land appreciation, and owners sometimes have the option to delay harvesting when timber prices are unfavorable," Liu said. But for retail investors, Liu added, it is quite different from "the simple 'trees grow while you wait' investment story."

#187. Why Intel Stock Popped on Monday

Intel (INTC +4.18%) stock jumped 4.6% through 10:55 a.m. ET Monday.

You can thank the friendly analysts at JP Morgan for that -- because they no longer say Intel's a sell.

JP Morgan analyst Harlan Sur removed his sell rating on Intel stock this morning, upgrading the semiconductor company from "underweight" to "neutral" -- essentially a shift from sell to hold. And why?

Intel stock is down 36% from its June peak and nearly 22% since the start of October. As Intel drifts ever closer to Sur's $85 target price, more and more risk gets squeezed out of the stock.

There's good reason for that, says Sur in a note covered today on StreetInsider.com: Intel's server CPU market share has dropped from 77% to 53%, and its PC CPU share has dropped from 81% to 68% -- and both those numbers are still falling. The company's foundry business isn't doing so hot, either, with only $1 billion in annualized sales to companies other than Intel -- not even a rounding error next to the $150 billion in annualized sales at archrival TSMC!

That's the bad news. The good news is that Sur sees at least some progress being made in foundries. He also thinks new CEO Lip Bu Tan is improving yields, manufacturability, and advanced packaging performance in CPUs destined for AI data centers.

As Intel's turnaround progresses, and as it enjoys a tailwind from demand for artificial intelligence chips, the risk-reward ratio on Intel stock improves. At the same time, many analysts predict Intel will finally turn profitable again next year -- giving the stock a positive P/E ratio that will make Intel stock appear more investable.

I personally think the risk here is still too high, but it's undeniable: The upgrade is giving Intel stock a lift today.

Rich Smith has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Intel and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#189. Dividend Stocks vs. Bonds: Which Makes Sense Right Now?

I came of age during the Great Recession, when the Federal Reserve slashed interest rates to zero and kept them there for almost a decade. (The Fed cautiously started to raise rates a tiny bit in the late 2010s, only to slash them back to zero during the pandemic[1]FRED. Overnight Bank Funding Rate (OBFR). Accessed Oct 15, 2026. View all sources .)

So for most of my adult life, Treasury bonds paid basically nothing in yield. If you were looking to earn passive income as an investor, dividend stocks were pretty much the only game in town. If you’re under the age of ~40, this is probably true for you, too.

But we’re in a different world now. Benchmark rates (and bond yields) have generally gone up over the last five years, and if recent economic data is any indication, they could go even higher in the months ahead. (You can get caught up on the latest inflation reading in our write-up here[2]Bureau of Labor Statistics. Consumer Price Index Summary. Accessed Oct 14, 2026. View all sources .)

As I write this, the 3-month T-bill yield is around 4.07% and the 5-year note is getting close to 5%. You can see the yields for other Treasurys and savings rates in the table below:

That’s a lot higher than we’re used to seeing bond yields. It’s also a lot higher than quite a few dividend yields. In fact, it’s higher than the vast majority of yields in the Dividend Aristocrats index (a group of S&P 500 companies that have raised their dividend payouts annually for at least 25 years).

So if you’re looking for a dividend yield that’s higher than current bond yields, you’re probably looking at a risky dividend that could be cut. This raises an interesting question: Is dividend investing worth it in this age of high bond yields?

There isn’t a simple answer. Both dividend stocks and bonds have some unique advantages over each other. We’re breaking it down below.

Potentially higher yields. Treasury bonds now pay higher yields than the vast majority of the Dividend Aristocrats, but not all of them.

As noted on our page here that shows the top seven Dividend Aristocrats by yield, you can see yields range from 4.5% to 5.92% as of Oct. 16.

If you look at the broader universe of dividend stocks and dividend ETFs, there are even higher yields available.

More capital gains. Income isn’t everything. Both bonds and dividend stocks are also assets that have market prices. When it comes to price gains, dividend stocks still have a big advantage over bonds (in part because rising bond prices mean falling bond yields[3]Investor.gov. Investor Bulletin: Fixed Income Investments — When Interest Rates Go Up, Prices of Fixed-Rate Bonds Fall. Accessed Oct 14, 2026. View all sources ).

If you look at a chart of the ProShares S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats ETF (NOBL) compared to the iShares U.S. Treasury Bond ETF (GOVT), this becomes clear:

More frequent payments (sometimes). Treasury bonds and notes pay interest semiannually, while short-term bills are sold at a discount to their face value, meaning that you realize their yield when you cash them in at maturity for the face value[4]Treasury Direct. Understanding Pricing and Interest Rates. Accessed Oct 14, 2026. View all sources . That means that if you’re investing in individual Treasury securities, you’re going to wait at least three months (the shortest commonly marketed Treasury duration) between payments.

Many large-cap dividend stocks also pay out dividends quarterly, semiannually or annually, but there are some monthly dividend stocks. (We have a page that tracks the highest-yielding monthly dividend stocks.)

One caveat here: If you’re more of an ETF investor, you should note that there are ETFs that pay out monthly dividends that contain both dividend stocks and bonds. In fact, our page on the highest-yielding monthly dividend ETFs shows a mix of both.

» If these things appeal to you, check out our roundup of the best brokers for dividend investing.

Virtually no default risk. Treasurys are widely regarded as the benchmark for a risk-free investment worldwide. The risk of a default isn’t exactly zero (that’s technically not true of any investment), but Treasurys are backed by the full faith and credit of the United States government, which oversees the largest national economy in the world.

A U.S. Treasury default is extremely unlikely, and it’s sort of a “giant asteroid” scenario — if it were to happen, it would precipitate an unprecedented global financial and political crisis, and “darn, I should have bought dividend stocks instead” would probably be the least of your worries.

State & local tax exemption. Income from Treasurys is taxable at the federal level, but not at the state and local levels[5]Investor.gov. Treasury Securities. Accessed Oct 14, 2026. View all sources , while dividend income is taxable at all three levels. That means that if you live in a high-tax jurisdiction, like I do (New York City greatest city in da world baybee), the after-tax yields of Treasurys compare even more favorably to those of dividend stocks.

Predictability. If you buy Treasurys and hold them to maturity, you are guaranteed by the U.S. government to earn the yield at the time of purchase. That dependability can make planning a lot easier, especially if you’re using short-term or mid-term Treasurys as more of a savings vehicle than an investment.

By contrast, dividend stocks are much less predictable. Stocks are more volatile than Treasurys. That gives them the potential for greater capital gains, as shown above, but it also gives them the potential for greater losses when the market gets turbulent.

Plus, dividend cuts do happen; they’re a much more substantial risk than the doomsday scenario of a Treasury default. Even Dividend Aristocrats, which are generally the most reliable dividend stocks, occasionally stop being Dividend Aristocrats and cut their dividends, as Walgreens Boots Alliance (WBA) did last year[6]Associated Press. Walgreens suspends dividend, breaking 90-plus year streak of shareholder payouts. Accessed Oct 15, 2026. View all sources .

» If these securities are more your speed, check out our roundup of the best brokers for Treasurys.

#193. Berkshire buys more Lennar shares, but pace of purchases slows

(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)

Berkshire Hathaway added to its bet on Lennar this week, raising its stake in the homebuilder to 11.2%, although the pace of its buying appears to be slowing.

In an SEC filing late Wednesday, Berkshire disclosed it bought a total of $53.6 million of Lennar's Class A shares and another $329,000 of the super-voting B shares on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday.

That puts the position at a total of 26.6 million shares valued at $2.1 billion based on Friday's closing prices.

At the end of the second quarter, Berkshire owned a 5.4% stake of 13.4 million shares valued at $1.2 billion. That was an increase of almost 30% from the 10.3 million shares it owned at the end of the first quarter, which was, in turn, an increase of 43% from 7.2 million shares at the end of last year.

As the stock continued to falter in the third quarter, Berkshire continued to buy in secret until its stake hit 10% in mid-September, triggering an SEC rule requiring it to disclose additional moves within two business days.

That prompted two filings last week revealing Berkshire bought almost $349 million of Lennar shares on six out of the seven trading days between Sept. 17 and Sept. 25.

That's an average of $58 million per calendar day.

This week the average is just under $18 million through Wednesday.

Since Berkshire has not made a new filing as of publication of the newsletter Friday night, it appears Berkshire didn't do any buying on Thursday.

That would put the 4-day average at $13.5 million.

We won't know if there was activity Friday until after Monday's filing deadline.

While Berkshire is making a bet that Lennar will benefit from a long-term recovery in the nation's troubled housing market, Morgan Stanley is pessimistic about the stock's more immediate future.

It started coverage Thursday with an "underweight" rating and a price target of $65 per share. That's a drop of almost 19% from today's close of $79.81, a 2.8% decline for the day.

The nation's housing market is struggling. Six straight weeks of increases have brought the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage to 7.30%, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association. That's the highest it's been since late 2023.

CNBC's Diana Olick reports the high rates have deterred potential homebuyers, who are also seeing higher house prices compared to last year.

Warren Buffett has reclaimed the No. 10 slot on the Forbes ranking of the world's richest billionaires.

The publication reports Buffett moved ahead of Amancio Ortega Thursday afternoon after a month-long decline of almost 8% for the shares of Inditex, the fast fashion group the Spaniard founded that is best known for its Zara chain of stores.

As of 5:15 PM ET Friday, Forbes estimates Buffett's net worth is $143 billion, $3 billion more than Ortega's $140 billion.

Buffett is the only non-tech name among the ten richest people in the world.

Warren Buffett explains why he put a slot machine on the third floor of his house when his now-adult children were growing up.

WARREN BUFFETT: The human propensity to gamble is huge.

Now, when it was legalized only in — pretty much in Nevada — you had to go to some distance, or break some laws, to do any serious gambling.

But as the states learned to — you know, what a great source of revenue it was, they gradually made it easier and easier and easier for people to gamble.

And, believe me, the easier it's made, the more people will gamble.

I mean, when I was — my children are here, and 40 years ago, I bought a slot machine and I put it up on our third floor.

And I could give me kids any allowance they wanted as long as it was in dimes. I mean, I had it all back by nightfall. (Laughter)

I thought — I thought it would be a good lesson for them.

Now they weren't going to Las Vegas to do it, but believe me when it was on the third floor, they could find it, you know.

And my payout ratio was terrible, too, but that's the kind of father I was. (Laughter)

The — but gambling, you know, people are always going to want to do it.

And for that reason, I particularly think that access — you know, in terms of friendly gambling or anything like that, I'm not a prude about it.

But I do think that to quite an extent, gambling is a tax on ignorance.

I mean, if you want to tax the ignorant, people who will do things with the odds against them, you know, you just put it in and guys like me don't have to pay taxes.

I really don't — I find that — I find it kind of socially revolting when a government preys on the weaknesses of its citizenry rather than acts to serve them. And, believe me, when a government — (Applause)

When a government makes it easy for people to take their Social Security checks and start pulling handles or participating in lotteries or whatever it may be, it's a pretty cynical act.
