#194. The Era Of AI Choice: Why Winning Companies Make Fewer Bets, Not More

Patrick Pugh is PwC‘s US and Global Alliance & Ecosystems Leader, helping organizations accelerate AI-driven business transformation.

​Enterprise leaders are overwhelmed with AI choices and options. New models, agents, platforms and ecosystem partners are emerging at a dizzying pace, each promising to change how businesses operate.

Optionality and choice are typically a good thing, but when I speak with leaders, I see another side of it. They are being asked to move faster on AI while making decisions in a market that is changing underneath them. Which technologies deserve investment? Which partners will matter two years from now? Where should they commit, and where should they keep their options open? Where can they get an expected return?

When nobody knows exactly which technologies will win, the natural response is to hedge. Launch another pilot. Add another tool. Test another provider. Keep as many options open as possible.

The companies that pull ahead in this next phase of AI won’t necessarily be the ones making the most bets. They’ll be the ones with the discipline to make fewer, clearer bets and create the space for what works to scale.​

Experimentation has been essential to the progress we’ve made with AI. Organizations needed room to learn what the technology could do, where it could create value and how people would use it.

But experimentation is a means, not an outcome.

There’s a difference between experimentation that helps an organization decide and experimentation that delays progress. When every promising technology becomes another pilot, organizations can spread their people, capital and attention across so many initiatives that few have what they need to become meaningful at scale.

That can take a toll on people, too. Employees are already navigating a constant public narrative about how AI will change their jobs, while being asked to adopt new tools and rethink how work gets done. When organizations layer one experiment on another without clear direction, that uncertainty can turn into caution. Instead of feeling empowered to use AI to rethink work, experiment and find new avenues for growth, people can become hesitant to commit to any one path.

The next phase of enterprise AI will require as much discipline as curiosity. Leaders still need to encourage teams to test and learn, but they need mechanisms to decide what moves forward, what gets investment and what stops.

Stopping matters. Every initiative an organization funds is a choice not to concentrate those resources elsewhere.​

The market may look very different a year from now. That uncertainty can create paralysis, with leaders preserving optionality rather than committing to the wrong model, platform or provider.

The goal isn’t to perfectly predict which technology will win. It’s to get clear on the outcomes you want to achieve and confidently match the technology to those needs, rather than reacting to what’s generating the most attention in the market.

That starts by changing the question. Instead of asking, “Which technology should we bet on?” leaders should ask, “Which business outcomes matter enough for us to commit investment behind them?”

Technologies will continue to change. A clear business problem gives an organization something more durable around which to make decisions.​

Strategic restraint can sound like an argument for moving too cautiously. It isn’t.

Organizations should move quickly when they have conviction. What they should avoid is confusing activity with progress. Making fewer bets means concentrating resources behind the opportunities where AI can create meaningful business value, while preserving flexibility as capabilities evolve. Leaders need to know where commitment matters and where flexibility matters.

That’s also why the ecosystem surrounding an AI investment is increasingly important. Organizations aren’t just choosing technologies; they’re choosing ecosystems. Every AI investment connects to a broader network of cloud providers, software platforms, implementation partners and data environments. Leaders should consider how technologies work with their data, workflows, existing platforms and partners, and whether that environment gives them room to evolve.​

As the AI market gets more crowded, organizations need a repeatable way to separate an interesting possibility from an investment worth scaling.

• Does this solve a business problem that matters? A compelling technology demonstration isn’t enough. Leaders should connect an investment to an outcome the organization values.

• Can we meet this need by expanding technology that’s already in our environment? Sometimes the better choice isn’t adding something new, but getting more value from what the organization already has.

• Are we prepared to scale it if it works? Before launching another pilot, ask whether the organization has the data, ownership, resources and willingness to change how work gets done if the experiment succeeds.

• What would cause us to double down, change course or stop? Define those conditions before momentum and sunk costs make the decision harder.

These questions won’t eliminate uncertainty. They’re not supposed to. They create discipline around making decisions despite it.​

AI leaders have spent the past few years learning how to experiment. The next challenge is learning how to choose.

The market will continue producing new models, new agents and new capabilities. There will always be another promising technology around the corner. Organizations can’t wait for that market to settle before deciding where they want to create value.

The leaders who succeed will give their teams permission to explore, but they’ll also know when exploration has produced enough information to make a choice. They’ll concentrate behind the opportunities that matter, stop investing in the ones that don’t and leave enough flexibility to adjust as the technology evolves.

In an era of nearly unlimited technological choice, knowing what not to chase may become just as important as knowing what to pursue.

#195. PepsiCo Was Just Dealt Another Blow by Coca-Cola

PepsiCo (PEP +0.78%) has been having a difficult year, with sluggish sales of soft drinks and snack foods as well as decreasing margins. And now, it just got some more bad news.

On Oct. 15, fried chicken chain KFC announced it will switch from serving Pepsi products to serving Coke products in its 4,000 U.S. locations. That's a big win for Coca-Cola (KO -0.46%). Though the loss in overall sales from the switch is fairly modest relative to PepsiCo's overall beverage sales, it's more significant symbolically.

In terms of revenue, the KFC-Coca-Cola deal is expected to cost PepsiCo some $50 million. The company's North American Beverages unit had sales of $7.7 billion in the third quarter.

Keep in mind, however, that PepsiCo once owned KFC, as well as Pizza Hut and Taco Bell, but spun the three off in 1997 to create a company that later became Yum! Brands. So the company had a long and special relationship with the chicken chain known for its founder and brand ambassador, Colonel Sanders. The KFC decision ends a 40-year friendship that began when PepsiCo acquired the chain back in 1986.

It's not PepsiCo's first loss to Coca-Cola this year. In July, Marriott International announced a deal with Coca-Cola to switch from Pepsi products, and Costco Wholesale recently did the same.

Interestingly -- and perhaps tellingly -- KFC made the switch in an attempt to help its own flagging fortunes. The chain is trying to win back customers it lost in recent years to rivals Popeyes and Chick-fil-A, and it believes switching to Coke products will help that effort.

PepsiCo reported third-quarter earnings earlier this month, and they were slightly better than expected. Revenue of $25.3 billion was 5.6% higher than a year ago, and earnings per share were $2.34, compared to $2.29 a year ago. Both were slightly higher than Wall Street forecasts. Management, however, lowered its full-year 2026 guidance for both organic revenue and earnings growth.

PepsiCo's major snack brands are also highly exposed to people cutting back on processed snacks due to changing consumer habits and the rapid adoption of appetite-suppressing GLP-1 drugs. Lay's, a major brand of the company, is considered one of the products most exposed to the shift in calorie intake due to GLP-1s.

Coca-Cola has held up better against these trends. While studies show that people using GLP-1 drugs consume less full-sugar soda, some 68% of the company's portfolio consists of low- or no-calorie options. Perhaps that's why PepsiCo's stock is down 8.7% this year, while Coca-Cola shares have climbed 34%.

It seems PepsiCo still has a lot of work to do to turn things around.

Matthew Benjamin has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Costco Wholesale. The Motley Fool recommends Marriott International and Yum! Brands. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#196. Trump's student loan overhaul could lead to more bankruptcy filings, former judge says

In Judge Sarah Sharer Curley's nearly three decades presiding over bankruptcy cases, some were especially painful to witness, she said — such as the 73-year-old woman who stood before her in 2012 with a student loan balance of more than $584,000.

The debt dated back to the 1970s and had grown throughout the woman's public sector career, Curley writes in her new book, "The Price of Forgiveness: Debt, Bankruptcy, and the Future of Fairness in America." She had "never made a lot of money," Curley said, and by the time she sought debt relief, the woman was living in poverty, with Social Security as her only income. Even so, strict bankruptcy laws can make it nearly impossible to discharge student loans.

Curley, the first woman appointed to the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the District of Arizona, said it was a familiar story.

"We allow the financial markets to take innumerable risks, yet we refuse to allow an individual to be forgiven for choosing to pursue an advanced degree," Curley wrote.

Curley retired in 2014. CNBC spoke with her this month about her new book, in which she describes a legal system that often fails to give indebted Americans the second chance it promises. In 2025, more than half a million personal bankruptcy cases were filed — an almost 50% rise from three years prior, according to the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts.

The interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Annie Nova: What do people get most wrong about those who file for bankruptcy?

Sarah Sharer Curley: People assume that individuals who file for bankruptcy are committing fraud, trying to hide assets and cheating creditors. Nothing could be further from the truth.

AN: And so why did people end up in your court?

SSC: People are subject to many unexpected events. People can't always plan adequately for the next earthquake, hurricane or natural disaster. But usually, it's someone losing a job. It could also be an illness that becomes chronic with medical costs that increase dramatically over a short period.

Student loans is another area of concern. Universities are charging more for basic degrees, as well as graduate programs. The cost of medical school over four years can be more than $400,000.

AN: You write that many people who file for bankruptcy are not unemployed; they're just living paycheck to paycheck. What does this tell us about our economy and labor market?

SSC: Despite the increase in wages that most economists tout, many people are working as independent contractors. They receive few benefits and have few rights. The company is not responsible to them.

Other individuals may be working for a company but find the wages or benefits are insufficient. Many people are forced to work for several employers to meet their needs on a weekly basis.

Although unemployment may be low, the quality of the employment is also low.

AN: The story in your book about the woman in her 70s with the six-figure federal student loan balance really stood out to me. What happened in her case?

SSC: The federal government would not agree to any settlement. I was the one who would have to decide whether her debt would be discharged or not. But the case law I had to follow was not in favor of discharging student loan debts. So, I didn't have a lot of flexibility in granting her relief.

However, I gave her credit for seven years of public service helping out troubled teens in San Diego County, since people who are in certain types of public service only have a 10-year repayment period. That meant that she'd need to repay the debt for just three more years.

AN: Wow. Why wouldn't the federal government agree to any settlement with her?

SSC: The federal government retains law firms to represent it in bankruptcy court, allowing the law firms to have a certain amount of discretion as to how to proceed. As a result, some law firms are aggressive in the positions that they take.

In the case of the woman in her 70s, the law firm attorneys didn't believe her when she said she had no assets and was on Social Security. But the law firm did not do an adequate investigation. I found her credible.

AN: Under President Joe Biden's administration, it reportedly became easier for federal student loan holders to get their debt discharged in bankruptcy. What's the current situation like?

SSC: There were attempts by the U.S. Department of Education to work out repayment plans for student loan borrowers who could not repay their debts. There was also the possibility that the Education Department would agree to forgive at least a portion of the student loans.

However, once the Education Department was gutted in 2025, there were few, if any, employees who could approve the debt modifications through one of the offered programs. As a result, it has become harder to reach a settlement with the Department of Education.

AN: In your book, you describe President Donald Trump's "big beautiful bill," which passed in July 2025, as an "attack" on student loan borrowers. How so? Do you expect the new law to drive up bankruptcy filings?

SSC: The bill created unrealistic federal loan caps for students. As a result, if a student takes out a loan from a private financial institution that's not federally guaranteed, that loan will often be provided at a higher interest rate.

Let's say the student needs a $300,000 loan to go to medical school. If the individual has a lower credit score, their interest rate may jump to 16%, leading to a payment of $5,017 per month over 10 years, or $302,040 in interest.

These expenses are not sustainable for most individuals. The rate of bankruptcy filings will most likely increase.

AN: You write that medical debt is another major reason people need to file for bankruptcy. Can you say a little more about this?

SSC: There were many individuals who appeared before me who had chronic illnesses. Chronic diseases are a problem because the person can only discharge the debt they owe at the beginning of the bankruptcy case. As with any chronic illness, the debt continues to mount day by day for years to come.

AN: You write that the bankruptcy process is "tortuous" for most individuals. How so?

SSC: Dramatic changes were made to the bankruptcy law in 2005. People are required to jump through many hoops to get relief now.

There was no evidence to support certain beliefs that individuals were engaged in fraud or filing bankruptcy cases every few months. But the creditor lobby pushed to make the bankruptcy law more pro-creditor. The many forms that need to be filled out and the hearings that need to be attended usually keep the individual in a perpetual state of stress.

AN: How does filing for bankruptcy affect people emotionally?

SSC: Many individuals are traumatized when they file a bankruptcy case. They had believed if they just work harder, they could solve their debt problems. However, when they're about to lose their homes, their cars or their businesses, they turn to bankruptcy.

Many see their inability to solve their financial problems as a moral failure. They feel they have failed.

AN: What was it like for you, day after day, seeing people under the pressure of insurmountable debt?

SSC: At times, at the end of the hearing, after I had rendered my decision, I would let the individual know that under the current law, I couldn't provide them with what they really needed. I told them that the law needed to be changed. We give a break to large financial institutions and corporations, and it's time that we do so for individuals, too.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates went up a little today.

Mortgage interest rates are up today, but only by a little.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage rose to 7.35% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is three basis points higher than yesterday but six basis points lower than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.

In the coming days, the direction of mortgage rates will depend a lot on whether markets think the Fed will raise borrowing rates again later this month. For more on this, read our analysis below.

One more thing: While the economy never sleeps, markets are closed on the weekends. The rates you see Friday are unlikely to change much (if at all) until Monday.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

If you were hoping for rates to fall, we have bad news: One major entity in the housing market thinks that even higher rates are coming.

Fannie Mae releases a housing forecast each month that includes projections for the quarterly average 30-year mortgage rate. October’s report dropped earlier this week, with a predicted average rate of 7.4% for the fourth quarter of 2026 (which we’re currently in) and 7.5% for 2027.

Why would markets think rates will go up? One important factor is inflation. The Bureau of Labor Statistics released the September Consumer Price Index, a major inflation report on Wednesday. It showed that inflation rose 3.7% last month, largely driven by rising fuel costs.

Raising the federal funds rate, which is the short-term borrowing rate the bankers set, is the Fed's main tool for fighting inflation. Even though the Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, changes to the funds rate ripple out through the entire economy. So a rate hike from the Federal Reserve  — or even markets having relatively certainty that a hike is coming — can put upward pressure on mortgage rates.

In the hours following the report drop, futures traders initially revised their projections in favor of another rate hike on Oct. 28. Today, expectations are cooler, with traders now expecting that central bankers will probably vote to hold rates steady for now before hiking in December.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has previously expressed his wish that investors would interpret data themselves, instead of dissecting central bankers’ public statements for Easter eggs about how they’ll vote.

For now, markets are still pretty much hanging on their every word. Any time a voting member of the Federal Open Market Committee publicly voices an opinion about inflation, it has the potential to shift mortgage rates.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.85% or higher — but there just aren't too many people for whom that's true.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

#202. CME vs. Coinbase Global: Which Financial Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?

The battle for financial infrastructure is heating up as traditional exchanges and crypto platforms collide. Investors must choose between the steady stability of CME Group (CME -0.05%) and the high-growth volatility of Coinbase Global (COIN -1.37%).

CME Group operates the world's largest derivatives marketplace, providing essential risk management tools for global institutions. Coinbase Global serves as the primary gateway for retail and institutional crypto trading. While both companies benefit from market volume, they operate in distinct regulatory environments, offering different profiles for growth and risk.

CME Group operates as a central hub for global derivatives trading, selling contracts that allow clients to manage price risks. Its marketplace covers major asset classes including interest rates, energy, and agricultural products. The company maintains exclusive license agreements with S&P Global (SPGI -0.72%) and Nasdaq (NDAQ -0.41%) for popular index products.

Strategic partnerships also drive its expansion into new technology and retail spaces. The exchange maintains a 10-year technology migration agreement with Alphabet (GOOGL +1.39%) (GOOG +1.31%) for its cloud infrastructure. Additionally, a joint venture with Flutter Entertainment (FLUT +0.06%) subsidiary FanDuel provides prediction markets for retail customers.

In its latest annual report, filed for fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $6.5 billion, up 6.4%. Net income was close to $4 billion, which resulted in a net margin of 62%. This high level of profitability demonstrates the scaling power of a global exchange platform as volumes increase.

As of CME's December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.1. This ratio compares total debt to shareholder equity, indicating the company uses very little borrowed money. The current ratio is approximately 1.0, meaning it has enough short-term assets to cover its immediate obligations.

Free cash flow, which is cash from operations minus capital expenditures, was approximately $4.2 billion. Because stock-based compensation accounted for only 2.2% of operating cash flow, CME does not rely heavily on non-cash compensation. This strong cash generation supports its ability to pay dividends and reinvest in market technology.

Coinbase Global provides a comprehensive platform for individuals and institutions to trade Bitcoin (BTC +1.19%) and other digital assets. The company generates revenue through transaction fees, subscription services, and its partnership with Circle (CRCL -0.05%) for stablecoin management. It also serves roughly 245,000 ecosystem partners across more than 100 countries.

The company is expanding beyond simple trading by developing infrastructure like the Base blockchain network. These services aim to make the company a foundational layer for the decentralized economy. By offering custody and prime brokerage, it attracts large institutional clients who require high security for their digital holdings.

In Coinbase's latest annual report, filed for fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $7.2 billion, a 9.4% increase from the previous year. Net income was roughly $1.3 billion, yielding a net margin of nearly 17.6%. While revenue grew, this net margin was lower than in 2024 as the company invested in new business lines.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio is approximately 2.3. This figure measures the ability to cover short-term debt with current assets; a value over 1 indicates a healthy cushion. The company maintains a debt-to-equity ratio of about 0.5, showing a moderate level of leverage.

Free cash flow for the year reached nearly $2.4 billion, providing significant capital for expansion. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 34.6% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement. This high level of stock-based pay is common among growing tech-heavy companies.

CME Group faces intense competition from other major exchange operators including Intercontinental Exchange (ICE -1.63%) and Cboe Global Markets (CBOE -2.10%). The company must also navigate complex global regulations that could change capital requirements or transaction taxes. Operational risks include reliance on third-party data providers and the constant threat of cybersecurity breaches.

Coinbase Global operates in a highly uncertain regulatory environment where authorities may classify certain assets as securities. Revenue is heavily concentrated in Bitcoin and Ethereum (ETH +1.59%), making the business sensitive to price swings in those assets. The company also competes with decentralized trading platforms and traditional financial giants entering the crypto space.

CME Group trades at a lower multiple of future earnings estimates, while Coinbase Global trades at a lower price relative to its sales over the past 12 months.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

Coinbase Global doesn't appeal to me because crypto doesn't appeal to me. Investing in crypto only makes sense if you ascribe to the "greater fool" theory, because crypto doesn't produce earnings or cash flow, and it has no real-world utility (you can't buy anything with crypto because it's so volatile). Buying crypto is entirely a bet that someone will later buy it from you at a higher price; it has no inherent value.

And Coinbase's fortunes are inextricably linked to crypto, as seen in this chart:

I don't think crypto is a legitimate investment asset, and I don't think you can forever count on greater fools jumping in to buy your tokens. So Coinbase's crypto ties make it an unattractive investment to me.

Furthermore, CME's net margin dwarfs Coinbase's. CME also has a much more reasonable forward P/E ratio and pays a modest dividend. I'd much sooner buy shares of CME.

#203. The Two Worst Words In Enterprise AI

Daniel Fallmann is founder and CEO of Mindbreeze, a leader in enterprise search, applied artificial intelligence and knowledge management.

​Two words are starting to dominate enterprise AI usage: with review.

The agent will open the service ticket with review. Update the record, issue the credit, adjust the order, with review. Those two words are why the risk committee signed off. They are also, in most cases, why the project will not produce the promised return.

Here is the uncomfortable arithmetic. Automation only creates value when checking the work costs meaningfully less than doing it. If a person must open the system, reconstruct the context and confirm each action the agent took, you have not removed labor. You have converted it from execution into verification and moved it to a different desk. Verification is expensive not because humans are cautious but because they are uncertain.

A study published in June examined what happens when agent guardrails escalate decisions to a human. Oversight capacity is finite and depletes. By the 300th approval of a benign action, a reviewer is fatigued and primed to keep clicking approve, so a dangerous action buried in that stream gets waved through. A guard who escalates only five times a day gets a reviewer who reads carefully. The system with more oversight produced the worst outcome because its trivia escalations drew from the same finite pool of attention the serious matter needed.

Attention is not a policy setting; it is a consumable. Every low-stakes approval spends down a budget you will need later, for the one decision that actually mattered.

A paper in AI and Ethics argues that current approaches fail in one of two ways: They strip agents of the autonomy that made them worth building, or they reduce the human to a rubber stamp who signs off on plausible outputs without interrogating the reasoning underneath. The authors separate two kinds of agency: 1) the system holds operative agency and executes, or 2) the human holds evaluative agency—the capacity to verify, steer and override.

Most enterprises have deployed the first and assumed the second, and field research on how people actually oversee software agents suggests the assumption is doing a lot of unearned work. A human who can understand what the system did in time to act on it is a control; a human merely sitting near it is not. Only one is on your org chart.

The law has reached the same conclusion. Article 14 of the AI Act requires high-risk systems to be designed so a person can effectively oversee them in use, not merely in principle. It obliges providers to keep the overseer aware of the tendency to over-rely on the output, naming automation bias explicitly as a design consideration. European law now holds that a human rubber-stamping an AI recommendation is not oversight and that the burden of preventing that failure sits with those who built and deployed the system.

I would resist filing this under “later.” In June, the Council of the European Union gave final approval to the Digital Omnibus on AI, moving the high-risk obligations from this August to December 2, 2027, for stand-alone systems. The relief was audible, and misread. Sixteen months is two budget cycles, and effective oversight is an architectural property decided at design time, not retrofitted in 2027 onto systems being specified this quarter. Only the deadline moved, not the requirement. And the “with review” line in your business case is about to become a legal claim you may have to substantiate.

The organizations getting real returns aren’t the ones with the most autonomous agents or the most review gates. They stopped treating oversight as a uniform policy and started treating it as an allocation problem. Four principles do most of the work.

Tier by consequence, not convenience. A blanket review policy fails both ways: It throttles harmless work and exhausts the reviewer before consequential work arrives. The teams that recover from an overwhelmed queue all did the same thing: They mapped actions to consequence tiers before automating.​

Reduce uncertainty before reducing oversight. Organizations often try to minimize review by improving models. The larger gains usually come from improving the quality, governance and accessibility of the enterprise knowledge those systems rely on. Better context produces better decisions, which reduces the need for verification. We watched teams buy more capable models to reclaim reviewer time and gain nothing because the hesitation was never about fluency.

Design actions to be verifiable, not merely reviewable. There is a large difference between an agent that produces a paragraph a human must read and second-guess and one that produces a structured, reversible action a human can confirm at a glance. The first consumes attention; the second barely touches it. Reducing the cost of verification is the highest-leverage design decision available, and it is almost always treated as an afterthought. What convinced me was seeing which outputs reviewers actually trusted: always the bounded, reversible ones, never the free-text paragraph.​

Instrument the reviewer, not just the model: escalation rate, override rate, time per approval. If override rate collapses toward zero over a quarter, that is not the agent getting better. That is oversight quietly turning into theater, the leading indicator of the incident you have not had yet. The signal that reshaped my thinking was override rate falling to zero, which every time meant the reviewer had quietly disengaged.

The prevailing question in enterprise AI is how much a system can do on its own. It is the wrong measure. The return is not how much work an agent performs; it is how much of that work a human does not have to check. Capability without verifiability only moves labor around.

The defining challenge is becoming less about model capability than about enterprise knowledge. Spend that budget deliberately, or the system will spend it for you.

#206. Europe’s winter energy crunch may already be underway. Two U.S. stocks that may benefit

Oil flows through Hormuz are rising, more ships are safely getting through the Strait, and oil prices seem to be coming down — at least for now. Goldman Sachs wrote Wednesday that Persian Gulf exports have "recovered to their 2025 average after doubling in September." The firm expects Brent crude prices to "moderate" to $85 per barrel by year's end. That's good news on oil, and maybe good news for both the United States and China.

My take → I know the term "reopen the Strait of Hormuz" is popular, but I just can't bring myself to say it. Hormuz is an international waterway, and no one country can "close" it. Yes, Iran — or the Houthis in Yemen — can threaten ships in Hormuz or near the Red Sea, making it more dangerous to pass through. But no country has the power to "open" or "close" a public, international waterway. I get that I'm the outlier in saying that — and I wouldn't have it any other way.

The not-so-good news involves natural gas and Europe. Despite the improvement around Iran and oil, it could still be a long, expensive winter for our friends in Germany and much of Europe.

For five years, I've been highlighting a few of the continent's major energy challenges: how more and more U.K. families have had to choose between heating and eating — aka "energy poverty"; how rising electricity costs are hurting industrial companies; and how American liquefied natural gas has become a type of "Marshall Plan for energy," helping make sure the lights can stay on across Europe.

One big worry I highlighted in my reporting was that parts of Europe might face critical natural-gas shortfalls at times during the year. Thankfully, those worries proved wrong. The worst-case scenarios did not happen, largely due to the weather. Much of Europe has enjoyed a multi-year run of fairly benign weather: not too hot, not too cold. That enabled countries to preserve precious natural-gas storage.

This summer, Western Europe broke the 2003 record for its hottest summer on record. And while much of the continent does not use air conditioning at the same levels as the U.S. or some other countries, cooling does exist — and it's getting more and more common. So when temperatures climb, companies and consumers want to crank it. A/C is great, but it's a huge power drain. As power demand rose, natural-gas inventories were drawn down.

The Swiss Federal Office of Energy tracks natural-gas storage levels against the five-year average (for more, click here). The chart below highlights that the European Union's storage level is at its lowest point in those five years.

As you can see HERE, Germany is in slightly worse shape. France, not shown, is as well.

Despite lower storage levels and higher prices, European leaders remain seemingly unbothered. A group representing the coalition writes that, despite "lower storage levels compared to historical levels, the Commission and EU countries reconfirmed that EU gas supply remains stable."

One: Natural-gas storage remains "stable" only because of American exports. U.S. companies are saving Europe from an even more dire energy scenario. This is not hyperbole. The natural gas liquefied and loaded onto ships in Texas, Louisiana, and other ports is the difference between Europe having "stable" supplies and Europe struggling to meet demand. The sabotage of Qatari gas has made Europe even more reliant on LNG from the U.S. and — wait for it — Russia.

It's hard to believe, but Europe is still buying billions of dollars' worth of natural gas from Russia, albeit via ships and not the ill-fated Nord Stream pipeline. My producer Harriet Taylor and I stood incredulously and watched cargoes of Putin's gas steam into the Port of Rotterdam. Many believe because Nord Stream was blown up that Moscow isn't making any money off Europe's energy needs. Think again.

European leaders still argue they will cut out Russian LNG by January 1 and end all contracts to buy Russian gas by late next year. Color me skeptical. Given that people tend to get angry when they don't have electricity or heat, I would venture to say that Russia will be selling plenty of gas into Europe well beyond these feel-good headlines. Time will tell.

Two: It's not just about supply; it's also about price. On the ICE exchange, prices for October futures on European-traded natural gas are more than double those for February. While many power companies have already locked in purchase costs, anyone needing to buy gas on the open market is going to face the double shock of higher gas prices and higher shipping costs to get the LNG. For spot cargoes, Europe has to compete with buyers in Asia, with both sides ready to pay whatever they have to in order to keep the lights and heat on this winter.

If you're looking for a silver lining, it's that prices have come down in recent days, buoyed by hopes of a real, longer-lasting peace deal that allows for risk-free shipping through Hormuz. Peace in the Middle East would be the best outcome on many levels.

Beyond that, it would also be hugely helpful if Europe had another relatively mild winter, reducing demand for heat and natural gas. This would keep storage levels sufficient and allow power companies and countries to get a better head start on refilling natural-gas storage for next year.

Much of that LNG supply is going to come from the United States. We have more natural gas than we can export. If you're looking to invest around this theme, two obvious names are exporters Cheniere Energy (LNG) and Venture Global (VG). Less obvious: the biggest holders of U.S. LNG capacity are based in France and the U.K. They are TotalEnergies (TTE) and Shell (SHEL).

TotalEnergies CEO Patrick Pouyanné — arguably the most important CEO in global oil and gas — spoke with us this week about Europe's energy challenges, prices, and more in a Power Insider interview.

Speaking of TotalEnergies, it's time to buy that stock — and BP, too. So says the team at HSBC.

HSBC is upgrading both BP (BP) and TotalEnergies to buy. Higher natural gas prices play a part in the call. The firm raised its TTM European natural gas price forecast — what we showed you above — by 34% for the rest of this year and 40% for next year, while also slightly raising its 2028 outlook. Analyst Kim Fustier also sees "substantial upgrades" across both firms' oil and refining-margin outlooks, as well as huge cash generation and stock buybacks.

BP and TotalEnergies are not the only energy stocks the firm loves. It maintains its buy ratings on Shell (SHEL), Spain's Repsol (REP-DE), and Chevron (CVX). Fustier sees about 20% upside for her Buy-rated stocks.

I think it's a fascinating call, in part because Fustier acknowledges that the situation around Hormuz may not improve rapidly anytime soon. HSBC's base case is that the situation is prone to "repeated breakdowns" and "continued uncertainty," though it does see shipping volumes continuing to improve.

HSBC isn't the only firm getting hotter on BP these days.

JPMorgan also just upgraded BP to overweight. In a note titled "Road to Redemption," the firm says a return to the "value of simplification" and "renewed long-term growth" look good for BP investors. While the firm notes that BP's recent history has been beset by operational and strategic issues, it sees the company getting things right under new-ish CEO Meg O'Neill.

Insider → Also, get to know some new geography. JPMorgan highlights how BP's discovery in Bumerangue may be a big deal. Bumerangue is a big Brazilian offshore oil block. It's BP's largest discovery in 25 years, according to Wood Mackenzie. I had never heard of it before reading this note.

I agree that BP is a company to watch closely over the next 12-24 months.  The company made a hard pivot away from its core competency - oil and gas.  The company once known as British Petroleum even went so far as to make an ill-fated rebranding effort to be known as "beyond petroleum."   That didn't last long.  While the company remains a player in solar and battery technologies and has a joint venture in wind power, it is refocusing back on what originally made it one of the world's biggest companies.

BP investors are also desperate for some consistency in leadership, and should have found that in new-ish CEO Meg O'Neill. O'Neill is a super smart veteran of the industry.  She came to BP from Woodside Petroleum and before that was the CFO of ExxonMobil.  She knows the industry and how to compete on a global scale.  The big question any BP investor should be asking is: is it too late to really effect the kind of change investors are looking for?   My take is that it is not, but BP will have to act fast.  Oil itself may take eons to create, but the industry never stops. O'Neill needs her foot on the gas pedal.

This week's Take A Look is a conversation with energy executive David Crane. He's currently the CEO of Generate Capital, and previously served as CEO of NRG and as an energy official in the Biden White House. It was great to sit down with David for a longer conversation about power, energy, nuclear, and why he believes the stock market is making a mistake with some energy-related names.

This week's Inside Line is with TerraFlow Energy CEO Jon Parrella. TerraFlow is building out battery and storage technologies and just signed an agreement around data centers.

You know things are getting hot when the world of energy partners up with NBA basketball! That's exactly what just happened as Bloom Energy strikes a multiyear deal to place its name on the Philadelphia 76ers' jersey. With the arrival of superstar LeBron James to Philly this year, we'll see if this deal is a… slam dunk.

#207. 'Everyone laughed' when he started a pumpkin farm—now it brings in $2 million a year

Three decades ago, when Kelly Schultz announced his intention to start a pumpkin farm, "everybody laughed at me," he says. Schultz, a second-generation antique seller, had no prior experience with farming when he bought a small farm in Clarence, New York, in 1993.

Schultz, 74, is the owner and operator of The Great Pumpkin Farm, a seasonal attraction about 15 miles northeast of Buffalo that draws over 100,000 visitors each fall.

The Great Pumpkin Farm brought in $2 million in annual revenue in 2025, according to documents reviewed by CNBC Make It — and it's open just seven weeks a year.

This year, the farm is open to visitors between Sept. 19 and Oct. 31, and they're not just coming to buy pumpkins. With a $20 weekend admission ticket, fall enthusiasts can ride the farm's pumpkin-themed train, explore its giant corn maze and compete in pie-eating contests, among other attractions.

Halloween is big business for Schultz and other seasonal business owners. Halloween-related spending is expected to reach $13.5 billion in the U.S. in 2026, according to a consumer survey by the National Retail Federation published in September. Among the 74% of Americans celebrating the holiday this year, 42% said they plan to carve a pumpkin.

At The Great Pumpkin Farm, "attendance is increasing just about every year," according to Schultz.

During the fall, "there are people that come here almost every weekend," he says. "They love it so much, they just keep coming back."

Schultz, who runs an antique store and an antique auction business year-round, says he was inspired to start his farm after visiting a pumpkin patch in upstate New York in the early 1990s. That farm had "muddy parking lots and not a whole lot of restrooms," he recalls, but there were "a zillion people" walking around and buying pumpkins.

"I looked around and I said, 'I could do this, better than this,'" Schultz says. So when the old cow farm next to his antique store went up for sale, he bought the 85-acre property for approximately $650,000, he says.

With the help of other local farmers, Schultz learned how to grow his own gourds, and The Great Pumpkin Farm officially opened in 1996. But Schultz had even bigger plans for his farm. That same year, he asked Ray Waterman, founder of the World Pumpkin Confederation, an organization dedicated to growing giant pumpkins and squash, to host his annual World Pumpkin Weigh-Off at The Great Pumpkin Farm.

Schultz bought prize indemnity insurance, which covers the cost of contest and promotion prizes, and offered $50,000 to anyone who brought in a pumpkin that weighed 1,000 pounds or more. He took out ads in papers "across the country" to promote the weigh-off. The winning pumpkin, grown by a couple from Lowville, New York, broke the world record at the time at a whopping 1,061 pounds.

"We were in magazines and newspapers all over the world," Schultz recalls. "That put us on the map right off the bat."

The Great Pumpkin Farm still hosts a weigh-off event every October, and this year's heaviest pumpkin weighed a whopping 1,908.5 pounds, almost double the weight of the 1996 winner.

These days, Schultz focuses less on growing gourds — to keep up with demand, he purchases most of the farm's pumpkins from nearby farms. But The Great Pumpkin Farm's 50-foot pumpkin pyramid, which is visible from the road, is still the first thing that incoming visitors see. According to Schultz, the farm stocks over 25,000 pumpkins each year.

Weekend visitors pay $20 per ticket, which covers admission for both days. They can access a vast range of activities including hayrides, pie-eating contests, magic shows, a giant slide, live music, train rides, a kid-friendly "boo barn" and pumpkin pedal kart rides, just to name a few.

For an extra fee, visitors can try the farm's amusement rides, pumpkin cannons, zombie paintball train, carnival games and Buffalo Bills-themed corn maze. Alongside the farm's bar and bakery, Schultz hosts festival food vendors whose offerings range from barbecue to specialty grilled cheese sandwiches.

"You can come out here and spend the day and still not have done everything," he says.

Weekdays require no admission charge, and are more low-key. Visitors can purchase pumpkins, visit the Halloween store, bar and bakery, and enjoy the outdoor playground, petting zoo and hay maze.

Creating this fall festival requires a huge amount of labor, according to Schultz. He employs over 100 seasonal workers during the seven weeks the farm is open each year, and their job duties range from driving tractors for hay rides to serving pumpkin donuts.

Rising gas costs are another major expense, Schultz says: It takes "lots and lots of gallons of fuel" to maintain the grounds and operate tractors for the hay rides. Since Schultz tries to avoid raising admission costs, he predicts that the business will "make a little bit less" in 2026.

"The business has been profitable, but we generally take most of the money and try and put it back into it," Schultz says.

Because Schultz owns the land surrounding the farm — approximately 300 acres in total — there's always room to expand, he says. Each year, he aims to add "something new, something fun, or upgrade what we already have."

The farm has grown into a family operation: Schultz's son Ben has helped him run it, and his antique businesses, for the last 25 years.

"I just like hanging out with my dad, so that's how I got involved in all this," says Ben Schultz, 45. "I'm very proud of what he created here, and I'm just happy to be a part of it."

Their shared goal for The Great Pumpkin Farm, according to Ben Schultz, is to "continue the momentum." From the farm's simple beginnings, "it's hard to imagine that it's gotten as big as it has," he says.

Kelly Schultz's grandchildren have also started to help out around the farm, he says.

"They love coming here," he says. "They all want to be here all the time, every day."

"I'm sure that the pumpkin farm will be a generational business," he continues. "It's definitely a family event."

Throughout October, the farm is buzzing with activity, but after Halloween, everything shuts down, according to Schultz. The petting zoo animals go back to their original farms; the amusement park rides are packed up and removed, and pig farmers pick up the remaining pumpkins to use for feed. Putting everything away and cleaning up the property takes approximately a month, Schultz says.

For the rest of the year, around 20 full-time staff help maintain the Great Pumpkin Farm's old barn buildings and keep the grass mowed.

Otherwise, it's back to selling antiques for Schultz and his family — at least until next fall.

#210. KLM Unveils New Delft House And Starlink Wi-Fi

The Delft house is modeled after a Dutch winery with a little aviation connection.

Editor/Content Strategist & Smart Travel Podcast Host

The Netherlands-based KLM Royal Dutch Airlines celebrated its 107th anniversary with an old tradition and new upgrades: a new Delft miniature house and free Starlink Wi-Fi coming in 2027.

This year’s Oct. 7 anniversary kicked off with the unveiling a new Delft miniature house. KLM passengers have received these houses when they fly business class on long-haul flights since the 1950s, and it’s one of the most recognizable business class collectibles in aviation.

The airline also announced other upgrades for long-haul passengers, including free Starlink Wi-Fi and a redesigned business class meal service.

Here’s what I learned about the new additions from KLM’s Oct. 7 celebration in the Netherlands.

World Business Class passengers on KLM’s long-haul flights receive a collectible house, designed to look like iconic buildings around the Netherlands. The houses are passed around on a tray by the flight crew before landing.

Like many collectibles, each house is numbered on the back to help you identify it. This year’s is no. 107 (representing each year the airline has been in business) and the house itself is modeled after a winery in Dreischor, Zeeland. Wijnhoeve De Kleine Schorre produces a variety of white and rosé wines that are served onboard KLM flights in World Business Class seasonally.

Each Delft house is filled with alcohol, specifically Bols Genever, a malted, grain-based spirit produced in the Netherlands. For flights to “dry” destinations where alcohol is not allowed, the houses are hollow.

If business class airfare is out of reach, all hope is not lost. Flying Blue regularly puts World Business Class mileage redemptions on sale as part of its monthly Promo Rewards. If you don’t have Flying Blue miles, you can transfer them from several credit card programs.

You might not have to cough up thousands of dollars or miles for a business class flight to snag a collectible Delft house. You can find them in antique stores as well as online on sites like eBay. The prices will vary based on how rare the house is, and there are some really hard-to-find ones, as well as limited-edition specialty houses not available on any KLM flight. They include models of the Royal Palace or the New York Historical. These are typically reserved for VIPs or given as a special gift by company executives.

Many customers, including Flying Blue elite members, shared that they go out of their way to make sure their long-haul flights are on KLM aircraft so they can build their collection.

It’s an honor for a location to be selected as the model for one of the KLM Delft houses. These houses get displayed in hotels, restaurants, shops and of course, homes. Nearly a million houses a year get produced and given to passengers on board. In fact, there are reports that once a house becomes part of the collection, its real estate value jumps significantly.

The selection process involves winnowing down the nominations for houses or buildings, usually of some historic or noteworthy significance, around the Netherlands and the Dutch Caribbean. The decision for each year’s house is a closely guarded secret and based on a variety of internal criteria. The final decision comes down to just two people, including the airline’s CEO.

Then, on Oct. 7 each year, invited guests gather for speeches and a big party at the actual location of the house for the big reveal.

For this year’s Delft house, KLM President and CEO Marjan Rintel told NerdWallet the arrival approach by airplane to Amsterdam often passes over the province of Zeeland, where the winery is located. Wijnhoeve De Kleine Schorre is significant because its region may be the first glimpse of the Netherlands for some passengers.

“I think there is something wonderfully unexpected this year about choosing a Dutch wine estate for KLM House #107,” said Mark Zegeling, author of “Little Kingdom by the Sea,” a book that outlines the history and significance of each house in the collection.

“Who would expect to find a vineyard in a country better known for windmills, water and beer?” adds Zegeling. “Today, this corner of the province produces wine that travels the world, carrying a taste of its unique terroir with it.”

Another reason becoming a Delft house is so significant? It introduces travelers to new parts of the Netherlands and the Dutch Caribbean.

Zegeling’s book, “Little Kingdom by the Sea,” serves as a guide book around the Netherlands for travelers interested in visiting the houses themselves.

You can also download an app called “KLM Houses” that lists each of the houses, has information on their location and history, and even includes a notes section so you can record when or where you added it to your collection.

If you want to explore more of these houses, but don’t have time to travel to different parts of the Netherlands, you can visit Madurodam, a park in The Hague, to see several replicas of the most well-known houses in one afternoon. Models of the Anne Frank House, Rijksmuseum and Station Valkenburg are all on display. The park is a walkable miniature city, complete with a mini Amsterdam Airport Schiphol.

KLM is making significant changes to its onboard experience in the next few years. The biggest one is Starlink Wi-Fi. By the middle of 2027, the airline expects to roll out free Starlink Wi-Fi on intercontinental flights for all passengers. This is in addition to the free connectivity already available on many of its intra-European flights.

By mid-2028, it expects all long-haul flights to offer the free Wi-Fi option, joining a long list of other airlines adding Starlink to their aircraft. Currently, Flying Blue members can access free messaging on long-haul flights.

Earlier this month, the airline took delivery of its first Airbus A350 aircraft, a much more fuel-efficient aircraft that will help replace its older A330 planes. The airline will begin retiring the A330s in the coming years as more A350s come online. By next year, KLM expects to have six of the type within the next three years.

Starting in early 2027, KLM will offer a new business class amenity kit to passengers. They come in two colors (light and navy blue) and include products from Marie-Stella-Maris, a Dutch brand.

In World Business Class, KLM will roll out an entirely new meal service delivery concept. On long-haul flights, the airline will ditch the use of trays for the meal in favor of laying a table cloth in front of each passenger and serving each plate and glass individually, much like you might see in a restaurant. The second, pre-landing meal service on long flights will continue to use a tray. KLM confirmed to NerdWallet it will not offer dine-on-demand business class meal service any longer, in favor of this new service pattern.

There are also changes ahead for KLM passengers seated in economy on short-haul flights. After trialing buy-on-board menus on its short-haul flights within Europe, the airline has replaced its traditional complimentary beverages and snacks (often a Dutch sandwich as well as the offer for free beer and wine) for a selection of paid options from the "Grand Café." Travelers can pre-order their preferred option or decide once on the plane. Passengers can now pre-purchase or choose on board from a variety of sandwiches, salads and other snacks.

What is still free on KLM? Water, tea, coffee and orange juice, as well as a Dutch stroopwafel snack on short-haul flights. And if you’re lucky enough to travel in World Business Class on long-haul flights, the fan-favorite collectible Delft miniature house.

#211. Semiconductor Sell-Off: 5 Stocks to Buy on the Dip

Semiconductor stocks have come under pressure as investors question the durability of the AI infrastructure build-out, driven by financing concerns alongside uncertain AI utility and revenue projections. Gartner recently projected that AI revenue would not be able to support the current build-out and that the neocloud market would collapse by 2030.

However, cloud computing companies are seeing insatiable demand for AI infrastructure and seeing strong returns on their chip and networking investments. Even historically conservative companies like ASML Holding and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM +2.69%) have aggressively expanded their capacity to keep pace with surging demand for their machines and services. This would point to the current AI boom having a long, continued runway.

With the stocks under pressure, let's look at five semiconductor stocks to buy on the dip.

Nvidia (NVDA +1.87%) is the primary company fueling the AI boom with its graphics processing units (GPUs). These are the main chips used to run AI workloads, and as a result, Nvidia continues to see surging growth. Meanwhile, the company has created a wide moat in the chip market for AI training, as most original AI code was written on its CUDA software platform and optimized for its GPUs.

The stock trades at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) of just above 13.5 based on estimates for fiscal 2028 (ending January 2028), That makes it a steal at these levels if the AI infrastructure boom continues.

While Nvidia dominates the merchant AI accelerator market, Broadcom (AVGO +2.83%) is the go-to company in the custom AI chip market. Hyperscalers have been increasingly designing their own custom chips to lower costs, and one of the main companies they turn to for help in developing these AI ASICs (application-specific integrated circuits) is Broadcom. Among its customers are Alphabet, Anthropic, OpenAI, and Meta Platforms. With surging demand, Broadcom sees its custom chip revenue quadrupling to $230 billion over the next two years. With the stock trading at a forward P/E of 11 times fiscal 2028 estimates, the stock is a buy.

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD +3.56%) is riding two powerful waves in inference and agentic AI. Its chiplet GPUs, which can be packaged with more memory, are great for inference, and the company has gotten large GPU commitments from OpenAI, Meta Platforms, and Anthropic for its GPUs. At the same time, AMD is seeing demand surge for its central processing units (CPUs), given the rise of agentic AI. Given its enormous growth opportunities ahead, the stock looks like a buy on the recent dip.

Arguably the highest risk-reward name on the list is Cerebras Systems (CBRS -3.25%). Its wafer-sized SRAM-based chips provide lightning-fast speeds for inference. The company claims its systems provide 30 times the inference speeds versus GPUs and are six times faster than Nvidia's Groq-based language processing units (LPUs). However, they are also pricey and are only sold as part of a complete system due to their power consumption management and cooling requirements.

The company has signed a large deal with OpenAI and has formed a partnership with AMD on a disaggregated solution where its system handles the important decode phase of inference. If the company's systems can break into the mainstream, the stock could have huge upside. The recent dip, meanwhile, has sent the stock below its recent IPO price.

As the largest foundry in the world, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing is responsible for manufacturing the vast majority of advanced logic chips, including GPUs, custom AI ASICs, and CPUs. As such, it is riding the same trends that every other company on this list is benefiting from right now. At the same time, as the only chip manufacturer that has consistently shown it can make these advanced chips at high yields (low defect rates) at scale, it has become a vital cog in the semiconductor value chain while commanding strong pricing power.

At a forward P/E of 18 based on 2027 analyst estimates, the stock is attractively valued and a buy on this semiconductor sector pullback.

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

The average mortgage rate will climb to 7.5% in 2027, according to Fannie Mae.

Mortgage rates fell this week, breaking a seven-week streak of increases.

The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage dropped seven basis points to 7.34% APR in the week ending Oct. 15, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.) We calculate our weekly average using daily APRs recorded over the past five business days.

If you’re shopping for a mortgage and this is a rate that you could be comfortable with, you might want to lock it in. Fannie Mae now predicts that mortgage rates will average 7.4% through the end of the year, so current rates may be hard to beat in the near future.

On Oct. 12, Fannie Mae released new 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate predictions that are significantly higher than previous forecasts.

Rates are now expected to average 7.4% in the fourth quarter of 2026 before climbing to 7.5% in early 2027, and could remain there for the rest of the year. The last time that annual average mortgage rates reached these heights was 26 years ago in 2000.

Just last month Fannie Mae predicted that the average 30-year mortgage rate would be 6.8% in the fourth quarter and 6.7% in 2027. For 2027 borrowers, this is a substantial difference of 80 basis points.

To put that into perspective: Without accounting for insurance or taxes, a $400,000 30-year fixed-rate mortgage at a rate of 6.7% would cost approximately $2,581 each month. When we adjust the rate to 7.5%, the monthly payment becomes $2,797 — amounting to an additional $2,592 per year, which is more than another month’s payment at the lower rate.

While the Federal Reserve doesn’t directly set mortgage rates, it does set a target range for the rate (called the federal funds rate) that banks pay to borrow from each other overnight to fund loans like mortgages.

When inflation moves too far beyond the Fed’s goal of 2%, mortgage lenders expect that central bankers will raise the federal funds rate. Because this makes mortgages more expensive to originate, lenders proactively raise mortgage rates when they expect a Fed hike is on the horizon.

Rising oil prices sent inflation surging in September, according to the latest Consumer Price Index from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, released on Oct. 14. Inflation rose 3.7% year over year last month, with the gasoline index rocketing up 9.1%.

In the immediate aftermath of the report’s release, futures traders revised their predictions to reflect increased odds of a rate hike at the Fed’s next meeting on Oct. 27-28. By the following day, expectations had relaxed, with market analysts projecting that central bankers will vote to hold rates steady for now.

Last month, it was already a big deal when the Fed raised the overnight borrowing rate for the first time in over three years. In recent history, central bankers have preferred to take a cautious approach to monetary policy. This means waiting until they can analyze several weeks (or months) of data showing how the economy responded to the previous rate hike before making any further moves.

Back-to-back hikes would be surprising, and could be seen as too rash. Still, as of Thursday morning, traders are showing that the odds of an October rate hike are higher than they were a week ago.

If you’re looking to buy a home right now, don’t lose hope. We’re moving into what is traditionally a slow homebuying season, and rising mortgage rates may leave fewer buyers in the market. When there’s less competition for housing, you have more negotiating power on the sale price — which can help offset high rates somewhat.

You can also be strategic about how you use your budget and savings. If you were planning on making a larger down payment, you may want to shift some of that cash toward buying down your rate instead.

#218. China's third-quarter economic growth quickens to 4.5% as exports surge, beating estimates

China's economic growth accelerated to 4.5% in the third quarter from a year earlier, as robust foreign demand for the country's technological goods largely offset drags from a deepening property slump and sluggish consumer demand.

Third-quarter growth beat Reuters-polled economists' expectation of a 4.4% expansion, and was also higher than the three-year low of 4.3% in the second quarter.

"The rebound in September salvaged the lukewarm performance in July and August," said Tianchen Xu, senior economist at Economist Intelligence Unit, attributing the recovery to improved government investment that helped arrest the consistent worsening in fixed asset investment, an "ever-strong" external sector and a weak base. China's monthly trade surplus reached a record high of $133.5 billion.

Momentum from the three forces will likely extend into the fourth quarter, Xu said, forecasting a full-year growth rate of 4.7%.

The data shows an economy still leaning on factories and overseas buyers while households and private investors hold back, with growth through the first nine months averaging 4.6%, broadly in line with Beijing's official target range of 4.5% to 5%.

In September, retail sales eked out a 1.1% growth, exceeding analysts' forecast for 0.6% increase, while industrial output grew 5.5% from a year earlier, in line with the forecast of 5.5% growth. The urban unemployment rate stood at 5.2% in September.

For the first nine months this year, fixed asset investment in urban areas declined 7.2% from the same period a year earlier, compared with a 7.3% drop estimated in a Reuters poll. Investment channeled into real estate development deepened declines, falling 20.6% in the January to September period, compared with 19.9% in the first eight months.

"The prolonged housing slump will continue to limit the spillover from stronger industrial activity to the wider economy," Sheana Yue, senior economist at Oxford Economics, as Chinese households see their wealth stored in property shrink over the years.

Yue also dismissed the idea that green shoots have emerged in the property market, as home sales, construction starts, and prices offer little indication that the sector downturn is "bottoming out."

Beijing has leaned heavily on exports for growth this year, but that engine faces growing pressure as energy costs surge and its manufacturing and export surge has provoked growing anxiety among trading partners. Meanwhile, other pockets of the economy remain weak, weighed down by feeble consumption and a multiyear property slump.

"It is clear that domestic imbalances between supply and demand continue rising," Eswar Prasad, an economics professor at Cornell University, said in an emailed note after the data release on Monday. "The government might become more sanguine and maintain a passive approach, rather than infusing stimulus into the economy in tandem with much-needed reforms," he added.

Producer prices climbed at their fastest pace in over four years, rising 5% in September, while consumer inflation remains below 1%, reflecting persistent excess capacity and weak demand that are constraining businesses' pricing power. "This potentially leaves firms to absorb more of the cost shock through lower margins rather than higher selling prices," said Yue.

Economists largely expect the People's Bank of China to hold benchmark lending rates unchanged through this year, leaving fiscal measures to do most of the work.

While the decent growth pace may reduce the immediate pressure for Beijing to ramp up stimulus, Yue expects the implementation of already-announced measures to accelerate, supporting investment and activity in the coming quarters.

Chinese authorities have stepped up fiscal support in recent weeks, including a package of targeted rate cuts and mortgage subsidies in late September. Earlier this month, it also allocated 550 billion yuan of unused debt quota to help ease local government financial strains and bolster infrastructure spending.

Correction: This story has been revised to reflect that quarterly GDP growth was 4.5%.

#219. IPO postponements are accelerating in third quarter, even beyond Oura

Biometric ring maker Oura raised eyebrows on Wall Street Tuesday, postponing its initial public offering due to "uncertainty" in market conditions while also claiming there was "strong demand" for stock.

IPO delays have accelerated in 2026, even as Oura faced some company-specific pushback from the Street. Market conditions for new offerings are suddenly becoming a headwind for companies thinking about going public now, largely because of surging bonds yields, analysts say.

"The fact that we've had three or four in a row – a string of postponements – I think that does tell you something about the market," Matthew Kennedy, senior strategist at IPO specialist Renaissance Capital, told CNBC. "You can't really point to all four of them and say it's company-specific issues."

Four companies in different sectors, all aiming to raise at least $50 million, announced postponements or pulled their IPOs altogether in the past week, according to Renaissance Capital data. That makes seven in the third quarter, up from four in the second quarter and three in the first.

Before Oura's postponement on Tuesday, nuclear power component maker Holtec Nuclear withdrew its IPO last Friday; materials company Amaero postponed its IPO last Wednesday; and Bamboo Insurance postponed its IPO on Sept. 22.

"I've got a little bit of sympathy for market conditions as a rationale," said Jay Ritter, director of the IPO Initiative at the University of Florida's Warrington College of Business. "The fact that three prominent companies are doing this does indicate that it's not company-specific."

It's been a solid year for IPOs, with about $146.9 billion in proceeds coming in 110 deals, excluding special purpose acquisition companies, Renaissance Capital data shows. Those figures include mega offerings from SpaceX and South Korean memory maker SK Hynix in the second quarter.

Still, that's down 30% from this time last year. In all of 2025 there were 202 IPOs, the most since 2021 when there were close to 400. Total proceeds are up 394% this year, largely due to the SpaceX, SK Hynix and Cerebras offerings.

Health care and industrials are tied for the top sector to launch IPOs year-to-date — both accounting for 24% of the total. Technology is third, at 18% of the total.

So far this year, 59% of all of the 2026 offerings are selling at or above the IPO price although, notably, SpaceX, SK Hynix and Cerebras are all lagging.

Lately, macroeconomic factors and concern about the artificial intelligence buildout are weighing on the market for new offerings.

"IPO activity came in below expectations in the third quarter of 2026, as more concerns about AI spending, a 19-year high in bond yields and resumed rate hikes weighed on the fall pickup," Renaissance analysts wrote in a report to clients last week.

The Renaissance IPO ETF peaked in June this year when SpaceX launched.

"AI-related stuff, including the build-out of the big infrastructure, still has a lot of enthusiasm for it. Things like data centers, there's big demand there, but it's largely a commodity business," Ritter said.

Analysts said that Oura, whose business is concentrated in its biometric ring product, likely faced its own set of issues.

"I would draw a line [around] Peloton, GoPro, FitBit and Oura. Investors have been burned pretty badly by narrow consumer products, and that is the reaction Oura is getting," said Gil Luria, head of technology research at DA Davidson. "I don't think it has to do with tech or tech allocation, I think it has to do with a narrow consumer product."

Companies themselves also have more alternatives than in the past to raise capital in private markets rather than public markets, lawyers who specialize in public markets said.

"The depth of private capital and alternatives is enormous now, and much more complex and diverse," Ian Schuman, chair of capital markets and public company representation practices at Latham & Watkins, said. "You don't necessarily, absolutely need to tap the public markets, if you're not getting the value you want."
