#223. Mandates For CIOs In The Token Economy

Tiago Azevedo is CIO at OutSystems, an Agentic Systems Platform built for the enterprise.​

For the past few years, the approach to AI adoption among enterprises was more or less unanimous: More is more, and any organization lagging to adopt AI would be left behind. Token costs were a small enough line item that teams could get away with unfettered experimentation, and while AI projects were nascent, the threat of AI sprawl was just a blip on the horizon. Blindly confusing AI use with productivity gains, the industry rushed to tokenmaxxing—and then tokenminimizing, once token costs caught up.

Enterprises are quickly realizing that in the rush to adopt AI by all means necessary, they may have sleepwalked into a governance and cost-benefit crisis. The risks are real. Shadow IT is back with a vengeance: teams deploying public-facing AI apps with no authentication, credentials committed to version control through AI-assisted coding, a single user running up thousands of dollars in model costs in a single day with no guardrail in place. These aren’t hypothetical risks. They’re happening now, inside companies that think they’re doing AI well.​

The real winners aren’t the organizations exclusively using the newest or most powerful models. They’ve invested in the infrastructure and operational discipline to avoid runaway AI costs and retain control over model use. Today’s CIOs need to understand the realities of token economics and model choice, as well as the infrastructural shifts needed today, to ensure successful deployments tomorrow.

It’s not realistic to expect teams to pause and consider which model is best suited to each and every use case—sure, costs would probably even out, but such manual intervention would also negate time savings. The solution is not cultural, but infrastructural. Before scaling AI projects, organizations must invest in technology infrastructure that guarantees model flexibility and governance, and determines the model best suited for each use case, by default.

This wouldn’t be another tool, but a vendor-agnostic inference layer at the very foundation of your AI efforts: the “air traffic control” between every AI user and every AI model in your stack. Before someone at your organization uses an AI model or agent, their request is routed through this gateway, which uses MCP connections and enterprise data fabric to identify the right model for a job, route requests across models, enforce governance controls and track costs per user.

For example, this inference layer would allow organizations to automatically route a simple request to a lighter, cheaper model and reserve the heavy models for tasks that justify them. All usage is logged and attributable, and when a new model ships, teams can seamlessly evaluate and adopt it without starting from scratch. This has been incredibly valuable for our own engineering team. Not only does the inference layer allow flexibility in model choice while carrying over our governance standards, but it creates a unified source of truth for us to track usage patterns and identify missing capabilities, or promote solutions at the corporate level to mitigate duplicative work.

With this kind of control and flexibility by design, organizations like our own can, in real time, evaluate new models and capabilities as they emerge, optimize for cost and performance and adapt to changing regulatory environments without interrupting progress.

Considering what’s at stake—operational continuity, cost control and performance optimization—flexibility is no longer a nice-to-have. It’s a business imperative.

AI sprawl is the new SaaS sprawl, with an even greater financial impact, as organizations transition from isolated AI pilots to full-scale enterprise productions. It’s a three-way squeeze: The business expects the speed and cost improvements promised by AI, regulators and CFOs raise concerns about governance and runaway AI costs and most AI stacks are fragmented and messy. Still, now is not the time for CIOs and CFOs to point fingers, but rather to establish financial governance over AI.

Visibility and auditability are essential, and with the right agentic infrastructure, teams are halfway there. Your organization should have visibility into which models are being applied to specific business functions and use cases and the value those models are driving.

For a business-critical application that requires unparalleled security standards, for example, a high-cost model may still be worth the spend. The companies that build the capability to route the right model to the right task, paying frontier rates only where frontier capability is genuinely required, will have a structural cost advantage that compounds over time.

Just as organizations pay a premium for experienced, highly-skilled professionals, finance teams should understand that certain use cases will require a greater AI investment. The mindset should be far more complex than “How many tokens did we consume?” Instead, consider the ROI of each token.

At a time when cost, performance and geopolitical conditions are constantly changing, CIOs need to pair real-time visibility and governance with rigorous oversight and conditions for success. “Keeping up” with the breakneck pace of AI by layering tools on top of tools is just a new type of tech sprawl. The time is now to build AI on an infrastructure designed for long-term performance, visibility and control—or risk letting the model-of-the-week dictate all three.​

#227. China's CXMT shares fall nearly 8% as investors look past chipmaker's profit turnaround

Shares of ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, closed 7.8% lower Monday, even as the company forecast a sharp swing to profitability for the first nine months of 2026.

CXMT said in a filing Friday that it expects net profit attributable to shareholders of between 131 billion yuan ($19.58 billion) and 132.5 billion yuan for the January-to-September period, reversing a net loss of 5.28 billion yuan a year earlier, according to a Google translation of the filing.

The company expects revenue of around 265 billion yuan to 270 billion yuan, an increase of 232.9 billion yuan to 237.9 billion yuan from the same period a year earlier.

The company attributed the sharp improvement to rapidly growing demand for AI computing power since the second half of 2025, which has boosted the global DRAM market, leading to supply shortages and significant price increases, according to the filing.

CXMT has been gaining ground in the global memory chip market, challenging established players including Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Micron Technology.

The Chinese chipmaker accounted for 10% of global DRAM revenue in the third quarter of 2026, up from 5% a year earlier, according to Counterpoint Research's data last month.

Chip stocks, however, have come under pressure over the past week due to worries about artificial intelligence financing, with some experts also flagging a possible chip supply glut after a couple of years.

#230. Opinion: The Most Important Number in Taiwan Semiconductor's Earnings Report Was 68%

The third-quarter results for Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM +2.69%) are in, and investors have plenty of reasons to be excited. TSMC reported Q3 revenue of $46.72 billion, a 41.2% increase from a year ago. Net income jumped 68.7%, while the company's gross profit margin reached 66.4%.

Those are impressive numbers by any measure, particularly for a company of TSMC's size. But there's another figure buried in the company's earnings presentation that I think is even more important. High-performance computing (HPC) accounted for a whopping 68% of TSMC's quarterly revenue, with sales in that business increasing 22% from Q2.

That tells us quite a bit about where TSMC's growth is coming from -- and why its artificial intelligence (AI) business remains such an important opportunity for investors.

TSMC is the biggest chip foundry in the world, manufacturing chips for companies such as Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, and Apple. TSMC has an overwhelming 72.5% of the global market share and, in 2025, produced more than 12,600 products using 305 separate process technologies.

That business model gives TSMC an interesting advantage. It doesn't necessarily have to predict which chip designer will come out on top because it can manufacture chips for competing companies. And increasingly, those chips are being used for high-performance computing.

HPC includes processors used in AI accelerators, data centers, and other demanding computing applications. It's a broader category than artificial intelligence alone, but AI is an important driver of demand for the advanced chips that TSMC manufactures.

In Q3, HPC generated more than two-thirds of the company's revenue compared with just 21% from smartphones. And while TSMC's overall revenue increased 16.2% sequentially, HPC revenue grew even faster at 22%.

The growth also comes as major technology companies continue investing in the computing infrastructure needed to train and operate increasingly powerful AI models. Those investments create demand for advanced processors, and TSMC manufactures many of the chips used in those systems.

The growth in high-performance computing is particularly encouraging given the technology behind those chips. TSMC said that its advanced manufacturing processes, which include 7-nanometer technology and smaller, accounted for 79% of Q3 wafer revenue. Its newest 2-nanometer technology already represented 8% of wafer revenue, while 3-nanometer chips accounted for another 33%.

Here's why that's important: Smaller manufacturing processes mean that chips can be more powerful and efficient, which are important qualities for AI data centers, where computing performance and electricity consumption can have a substantial effect on operating costs.

That's one reason I've remained bullish on TSMC. Its manufacturing capabilities give the company a competitive advantage that's difficult to duplicate, while demand for advanced computing continues to expand. And the latest results suggest that customers are putting those capabilities to work.

TSMC expects Q4 revenue between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion, indicating that management anticipates another sequential increase in sales. For the full year, the company now expects revenue growth of approximately 44% in U.S. dollars.

While the current pace of AI infrastructure spending won't continue indefinitely, guidance from major chipmakers indicates an ongoing appetite for more advanced AI processors -- and that should keep profits rolling in for TSMC.

With HPC now accounting for 68% of revenue and growing faster than the rest of the business, TSMC is demonstrating just how valuable that position has become. That's the number I'd pay the most attention to in this earnings report.

Patrick Sanders has positions in Nvidia. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Advanced Micro Devices, Apple, Nvidia, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#231. Higher rates are wreaking havoc on these two ETFs. Traders see one bouncing back

The relentless surge in rates is breaking the back of two key macro trades that had been holding firm. Options traders are betting one will recover.  Gold dropped 4% to the lowest since the first week of August, as the 10-year yield climbed to 5.3% and the 30-year yield touched 5.4%. High-yield corporate bonds extended a five-day rout to the lowest since April 2025, according to the iShares iBoxx High Yield Corporate Bond ETF (HYG).Judging by options flows on Monday, traders think gold has the potential to bounce back. For high-yield bonds, they're betting things could get worse.About twice as many calls traded versus puts in the SPDR Gold Shares (GLD), with more than 68,000 calls likely bought, compared to under 32,000 puts, Cboe LiveVol data show. Net trade sentiment was bullish by almost $2.8 million with an imbalance of 105,000 "deltas" leaning bullish, according to Barchart analysis.While traders sold about as many calls as they bought in GLD, the biggest single trade of the day was a seller of 2,000 375-strike puts expiring in January 2028 worth $5.9 million. The person may have been closing out a bearish position or placing a bet the precious metal finds a floor around $375. GLD traded in roughly a 10-point range between 370 and 380 for much of this summer. When investors sell puts, they are making a bet that a security will stay above that puts strike price. In exchange for taking that risk, they collect that put's premium.

Both gold and high-yield bonds are trading with strong negative correlations to the 10-year yield – GLD's 10-day correlation is negative 0.8, HYG's is -0.99, but options trading in the high-yield HYG ETF was more lopsidedly bearish.Trading volume in HYG options was more than 2.5 times the 30-day average Monday, with more than 2.5 times as many puts trading as calls and 52,000 puts likely bought, compared to just over 15,000 calls, Cboe LiveVol data show.

About $35 million of options premium was exchanged, with $30 million of it tied to calls, SpotGamma data show. Eleven of the top 12 contracts by dollar-amount bought were puts; ranked by volume, puts accounted for 8 of the 10 most-popular contracts. The most common contract to purchase was the 78-strike put expiring Nov. 20."Sentiment in high-yield bonds has been very complacent and the risk of defaults is probably much higher than the market anticipates," Nigam Arora, founder of The Arora Report, said by phone. "A lot of these are on variable rates and debt is coming due next year. People have liked them for yield but the spread hasn't been great and I the risk-reward hasn't been favorable. I wouldn't touch them."

New tiers, one points currency and new perks arrive Jan. 1, 2027, as Southwest reshapes Rapid Rewards.

Southwest Airlines is rolling out its biggest changes to Rapid Rewards in years, many of which go into effect Jan. 1, 2027.

The biggest change in the airline’s Oct. 15, 2026, announcement affects Companion Passes, the popular perk that lets a companion fly with you for free (aside from the cost of taxes and fees) on almost any Southwest flight you book with cash or points. Starting in 2027, the unlimited Companion Pass will become part of a new elite status tier, and the rules about how you earn it will change, making it harder to attain.

The Rapid Rewards program is also renaming its elite status tiers, with more redemption options and program improvements coming later in 2027.

All of this news comes as part of a multiyear brand overhaul for Southwest, which has dropped much of what made it distinct from other airlines. In April 2025, the carrier overhauled its fare classes and loyalty benefits. Roughly a month later, it ended its free checked bag policy and introduced variable redemption rates for award flights, flight credit expiration and a new basic economy fare class.

Still, some upcoming Rapid Rewards changes could be helpful for Southwest cardholders who are heavy spenders.

New tiers and new names: The current two Southwest elite status tiers expand to three, with new names:

Two point currencies consolidate to one: Currently, you receive a Companion Pass by either taking 100 qualifying one-way flights or earning 135,000 Companion Pass Qualifying Points. Starting in 2027, you'll earn the unlimited Companion Pass by hitting Platinum elite status, which requires earning 140,000 Tier Qualifying Points (TQP) or taking 100 qualifying flights. Credit card welcome offers and other types of bonus points earned on Southwest-branded cards will no longer count toward a Companion Pass.

A brand-new Platinum tier is at the top, and comes with an unlimited Companion Pass.

A new Milestone Rewards system gives you something (e.g., points, seat certificates or a limited version of the Companion Pass) before you even reach Silver, and again between Gold and Platinum.

These changes will also take effect soon:

More redemption options: Redeem points on international partner airlines starting spring 2027, on rental cars starting November 2026, and on seat selection starting late 2027.

Southwest's entire fleet will have Starlink Wi-Fi by fall 2027, free for Rapid Rewards members.

The first Southwest Icon airport lounges are expected to open by the end of 2027, accessible through a new premium Chase-issued credit card.

Current A-List and A-List Preferred members will be automatically moved into the corresponding new tier on Jan. 1. If you already hold a Companion Pass, your current benefits will continue until your pass expires.

A-List and A-List Preferred will soon be gone, replaced with Silver, Gold and Platinum, levels commonly used in other airline elite status programs.

Southwest says it renamed the tiers for clarity, not simply to mimic competitors.

“Everybody understands Silver, Gold and Platinum,” says Nandika Suri, vice president of Rapid Rewards. “[They’re] precious metals that you know move in a certain progression.”

She adds that the old A-List naming made sense when it mapped to boarding group A, but didn't clearly signal to members how to progress from one tier to the next.

Right now, Southwest tracks two separate currencies: Tier Qualifying Points for elite status and Companion Pass Qualifying Points for Companion Pass. The two have completely separate goals — earning elite status (A-List or A-List Preferred) versus earning the Companion Pass.

That changes in 2027, when the Companion Pass becomes a Platinum status perk that can be earned through TQP.

Southwest is also expanding which cards can earn TQP. Currently, the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card, which has an annual fee of $99, does not earn TQP at all, while the other two Southwest consumer credit cards with higher annual fees earn either 1,500 or 2,500 TQP per $5,000 spent.

Starting Jan. 1, every Rapid Rewards credit card — the $99-annual-fee Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card included — will earn 1 TQP per $1 spent on purchases, making the math more straightforward.

That means all cardholders get a higher TQP earning rate on everyday spending and can potentially spend their way to elite status. Especially for Southwest flyers who are big spenders, it's another good reason to get a Southwest credit card.

Following the lead of other major airlines, Southwest is launching Milestone Rewards, which are extra goodies between status tiers, or before you’ve even reached elite status at all. Starting in 2027, there will be two Milestone Rewards:

20,000 TQP or 15 qualifying flights: Once you’ve earned 20,000 TQP or taken 15 qualifying flights (which is before you’ve accrued the 35,000 TQP/25 qualifying flights needed to hold Silver status), you’ll get your choice of either 2,000 Rapid Rewards points or two Preferred Seat Certificates (these let you sit in a standard legroom seat near the front of the cabin). NerdWallet values Southwest points at 1.4 cents apiece, making the points reward worth about $28. Prices for the Preferred Seats vary by flight, but tend to run between $20 and $40.

95,000 TQP or 75 qualifying flights: At this threshold, which sits between Gold and Platinum, you’ll receive three Companion Pass trips, which you can use on a qualifying one-way or round-trip flight. The value of this really depends on the cost of your companion's flight.

The Companion Pass is still around, but the way you earn it is changing.

On paper, the qualifying bar doesn’t look too different. Platinum's 140,000 TQP or 100 qualifying flights is close to what it already takes to earn Companion Pass currently (100 qualifying flights or 135,000 Companion Pass Qualifying Points). But with the new changes, Southwest-branded credit card welcome offers, referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus category points and points from partner spending will no longer count toward earning the perk.

Currently, a single Southwest credit card welcome offer could get you about halfway to a Companion Pass. With the new rules, that won’t be the case.

"We want the engagement to be the driver of how members are making it to the tier," Suri says.

Besides flights, Southwest is expanding what you can actually spend your points on, including:

International partner airlines (spring 2027): Members will be able to redeem Rapid Rewards points directly for flights on Icelandair, China Airlines and Etihad Airways. You won’t be able to use a Companion Pass for these flights, though.

Rental cars (starting November 2026): Points will become redeemable across all of Southwest's rental car partners directly on cars.southwest.com.

Seat selection (late 2027): Members will be able to redeem points for Preferred and Extra Legroom seats on Southwest-operated flights, after booking and before check-in.

Southwest says it expects to become the first major U.S. airline to offer Starlink across its entire fleet in 2027, which will be free for members. The airline has provided free Wi-Fi to all its Rapid Rewards members since October 2025, and it’s been slowly rolling out Starlink across its aircraft. It announced in October 2026 that it expects to finish equipping its entire fleet by fall 2027.

Other major airlines that offer Starlink include United, which is also rolling it out across its fleet. On United Airlines, Wi-Fi is free to MileagePlus members on Starlink-equipped aircraft, though it’s paid on other aircraft. American Airlines says it will begin installing Starlink in early 2027.

Southwest in September 2026 revealed the first four locations of its planned airport lounge network. In the Oct. 15 announcement, the airline said that they will be called Southwest Icon lounges. The first are expected to open at the end of 2027.

“We are not designing lounges where folks will have to wait in long lines,” Suri says. “The experience is going to be very elevated and premium, but at the same time very warm and truly Southwest.”

The biggest change: You have a steeper climb if you want to be the top dog of Southwest customers. Platinum requires 140,000 TQP or 100 qualifying flights, which is a much higher bar than the current top tier. In exchange, you’ll earn that unlimited Companion Pass, which remains one of the most distinctive offerings out of Southwest.

Here’s what you can do now:Check your progress toward a Companion Pass. You have until the end of the year to meet the current requirements — which means either taking 100 qualifying one-way flights or earning 135,000 Companion Pass Qualifying Points in a calendar year — if you intend to secure a Companion Pass through the end of 2027. For cardholders approved for a Southwest card on or before Dec. 2, 2026, the welcome offer will still count toward that requirement, so eligible flyers might want to consider applying before the year is over.

If you have a Southwest credit card, see if your spending could help you earn elite status. Even though a Southwest card's welcome offer won’t get you closer to a Companion Pass after Jan. 1, the increased rate of TQP earnings across all cards makes elite status a lot more accessible for many cardholders. Plus, you’ll get other card benefits like your first free checked bag and priority boarding. You might even want to hold off on major purchases until the new year, when the new TQP earn rates for Southwest cards take effect.

Consider a Southwest credit card. For many frequent Southwest flyers, the airline’s cards have gone from nice-to-haves to must-haves in the past few years. With this new slate of changes, they’re becoming even more valuable for earning elite status. You might also want to watch out for Southwest’s soon-to-be-launched premium card, which could get you into some of the airline’s upcoming lounges.

#237. Why Micron Stock Bounced on Monday

Last week was miserable for Micron (MU +3.75%) stock, with the maker of DRAM and NAND flash memory chips losing nearly 15% on worries that Chinese DRAM company ChangXin Memory Technologies was bringing to market "4F square" technology to increase DRAM storage density -- and begin stealing market share from Micron.

Monday morning, things are looking better for Micron, though, and the stock is up 4% as of 10:35 a.m. ET.

You can thank Michael Dell for that -- and Wall Street bankers, too.

Quoted in The Wall Street Journal Friday, the Dell founder CEO predicted the ongoing shortage of computer memory is "gonna get worse" in 2027. Perversely, that's good news for Micron because when memory supplies are too low, memory prices go higher -- and so do Micron's profit margins.

Separately this morning, analysts at Wall Street banks Mizuho and KeyBanc both chimed in to support memory stocks. Mizuho predicts demand for agentic AI will keep NAND supply tight and force prices higher throughout 2027. KeyBanc likewise predicts price increases in NAND, as reports.

Admittedly, NAND demand is more of a bull case for Sandisk than for Micron. Micron only gets about 26% of its revenue from NAND flash sales, after all; 73% of its business is in selling DRAM, and Micron is in fact the world's third-biggest supplier of DRAM.

But that's fine. Even a small boost to NAND prices, on top of the price hikes it's already enjoying, is good news for Micron. With the stock already trading under 25 times trailing earnings -- and just 7x forward earnings -- Micron stock still looks like a buy to me.

#240. Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi rejects criticism around weak yen and high interest rates

Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has rejected criticism that she was on one hand responsible for a weak yen and on the other for pushing up interest rates in the country.

Speaking in parliament, Takaichi said; "I have been repeatedly criticized for 'Takaichi's weak yen' and 'Takaichi's high interest rates,' but I clearly deny that," according to a Reuters translation of her remarks in Japanese.

She was responding to a question from an opposition party lawmaker Yoshifumi Hamano, who asked about the compilation of a second supplementary budget for the country.

Takaichi also said that her administration will increase confidence in the yen by building a strong economy.

Under her administration, yields on Japanese government bonds have risen to multi-decade highs, while the yen weakened to its lowest since 1986, prompting Tokyo and even Washington to step into the forex market to support the currency.

In January, Takaichi had reportedly said that a weak yen presented an opportunity for export industries and acted as a buffer against U.S. tariffs, though she quickly clarified that she held no specific preference for the currency's direction.

Japan's exports have been partly boosted by yen's depreciation, as a weak currency makes exports more competitive.

For bond markets, Takaichi said that "We intend to appropriately control the amount of government bond issuance," at a time when yields have been rising as Japan's central bank raises its policy rate and continues to normalize its monetary policy.

Earlier this year, Takaichi had announced a plan to cut the country's food tax and unveiled a supplementary budget earlier this year, raising the possibility that Japan might need to issue more bonds to sustain its government spending.

Takaichi has said that the total bond issuance for calendar year 2026 would remain unchanged from the original budget plan, according to Bloomberg, although experts were skeptical.

Jesper Koll, expert director at Monex Group told CNBC back in April — when the supplementary budget was announced — that "Bond markets are a lot of things, but they're not stupid. You cannot increase spending without increasing debt."

#241. ​Why Family Law Firms Need An Intelligence Layer

The amount of unstructured raw data that family law firms receive can be truly astonishing. Bank statements, income documents and asset and debt information arrive in the form of hundreds of emails and scanned documents, often named randomly, each containing multiple subdocuments. Add evidence like text messages, emails, photos and healthcare records, and a single case can easily involve thousands or tens of thousands of documents.

In some cases, sorting through that by hand is essentially impossible. Even then, attorneys still may not know what they have or what’s missing. When they talk to the client, it becomes clear the attorney doesn’t actually understand the whole picture, especially when they ask for things that were already provided. The result: The client loses confidence.

Family law is an extreme case, but not a unique one. Any practice that runs on client documents, from estate planning to bankruptcy to immigration, faces the same problem.

AI is already helping make this process more efficient, and soon virtually every firm will have this powerful technology for drafting, summarization, research, document analysis and transcription. At that point, however, simply using AI will no longer set firms apart. So what distinguishes one firm from another when everybody has similar tools?

The real divide will be between firms using AI as information tools and firms using it to build intelligence. General-purpose AI tools can understand individual pieces of information. The harder task is understanding the evolving contexts that connect all of those pieces across the life of the case.

That calls for an intelligence layer: a system that consumes and synthesizes everything into a coherent picture of the case that no individual could build. AI can consume thousands of documents and offer a summary in little time. An intelligence layer can also make sense of it all: building a timeline of critical events, generating reports on the adversarial parts of the case and mapping ownership of assets and how they could be divided.

Consider what that looks like in practice. A summary tells you a client sent 800 bank statements. An intelligence layer tells you those statements cover 15 accounts, that one account is missing three months, and that a deposit in another contradicts the client’s income disclosure. AI can do in seconds what would likely take a person days.

Intelligence compounds across the firm, the client and the case. Firms become more efficient, and clients gain confidence through better visibility. Attorneys can improve their strategy, from detecting contradictions and spotting things that are missing to stress-testing case theories against the opposing narrative. If you’re an attorney with an intelligence layer, it’s easier to find strategic openings amid the reams of data.

Employing an intelligence layer correctly starts with asking how information actually moves through the firm. I’m often surprised how little time most firms have spent understanding their own workflows. Owners should start thinking about where client and case information enters, where it lives, how it moves and where context gets lost. How many systems touch it? How many copies are there, and how often do they differ from one another? Do clients have enough visibility into the work that’s being done?

Then identify friction points: the places where attorneys and staff repeatedly search, copy, summarize, reconcile or re-request information. The biggest pain point I often hear is cleaning up the raw data clients send. Maybe that’s a zip file with 800 documents from 15 different accounts, all unhelpfully named “bank statement.”

One firm we work with received more than 1,000 documents from a client in the first week of a divorce. Within minutes they knew which accounts were represented, which statements were missing and what to ask for next. As a result, the client’s first call was a strategy conversation, not a request for documents.

Discovery and depositions create their own burdens. A request for 350 documents is more than just a search: Each one has to be found, checked for privilege and relevance, and produced on deadline. Depositions can run dozens or hundreds of hours, and someone has to comb through those transcripts to find statements that support the case. Time and costs add up fast for both sides. An intelligence layer can take on much of that work.

It’s important to keep in mind that an intelligence layer only finds and analyzes information. Consequential legal decisions still require the judgment and advocacy of experienced attorneys, and they remain responsible for accuracy and communication. The intelligence layer handles the drudgery so the people can focus on the strategic side.

Confidentiality remains crucial. Before adopting any intelligence layer, firms should know exactly how client data is stored, secured and used, because their ethical obligations remain when the work moves to software.

That’s also why firms should measure outcomes instead of just AI adoption. Track metrics like time spent searching for information, administrative hours per matter, the gap between receiving important information and acting on it, and capacity per attorney and case preparedness. Then ask whether client satisfaction, time to resolution, ideal settlement outcomes and profitability are improving as a result.

For years, the legal profession has asked which firms will adopt AI. That question is becoming obsolete. The real differentiator now is how well a firm understands and acts on everything it knows. Soon, clients will expect their attorney to know their case as well as they do, and better, and the firms that build intelligence now will be ready to meet that expectation.

#243. Nearly half the stocks in the S&P 500 are at cross purposes with the rest of the market

Nearly half of the stocks in the S&P 500 are moving against the index with a negative beta, an unusual divergence that is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.

About 45% of S&P 500 stocks have a negative three-month beta, according to a recent note from Goldman Sachs. The data closely aligns with CNBC's finding that nearly 40% of S&P 500 stocks had a negative three-month beta versus the index, while 17% have a negative one-year beta, based on weekly returns.

Beta measures how a stock moves relative to the rest of the market. A negative beta means an individual stock's returns moved in the opposite direction of the S&P 500 over the measured period.

The surge in stocks with a negative beta dovetails with other unusual market signals. The S&P rallied 1.5% last Monday. The same day 30 stocks touched a 52-week low while just 7 scored a new high. The last time the S&P 500 gained at least 1% while sitting within 1% of a new 52-week high and new lows outnumbered new highs was in December 1999, right before the very top of the dot-com boom, according to Jason Goepfert, founder of SentimenTrader.

The two indicators show that market indexes can remain at or close to records despite wide divergences among individual stocks.

The yawning gap largely reflects how concentrated the S&P 500 has become, according to Adam Turnquist, chief technical strategist at LPL Financial.

Mega-cap technology companies carry an outsized weight in the benchmark, meaning a strong performance from a small number of stocks can drive the index even when many others are moving the other way.

"It only takes a few of those mega caps names to work, and a lot of the smaller weighted stocks don't need to work," Turnquist told CNBC, pointing to unusually low correlations among S&P 500 stocks.

The same dynamic explains why the broader index can look relatively calm even when individual stocks are making large moves, said Bradley Krom, director of investing strategy at WisdomTree.

"Beta is a function of correlation and volatility," Krom said. When stocks experience large moves at different times and for different reasons, those moves can largely offset one another at the index level.

In July this year, Alliance Bernstein, using one-year trailing returns, found an unprecedented share of U.S. stocks displaying negative beta as AI winners powered market gains.

Semiconductor makers, hardware companies and other AI infrastructure beneficiaries have benefited from enormous capital spending, while companies outside the AI trade have struggled to keep up.

"But a narrow market can also distort the signal investors receive from index returns. When a handful of companies dominate performance, many financially sound businesses may lag or even decline, simply because they aren't tied directly to the most powerful market narrative," wrote Kurt Feuerman, chief investment officer of Select U.S. Equity Portfolios at AllianceBernstein.

Energy stocks with negative beta are being driven by different forces.

"Another part of the other story is energy. That's been pronounced this year: higher oil prices, higher energy stocks and then the rest of the market trades lower," said Turnquist, seeing energy as an important part of the negative-beta story, alongside more defensive sectors.

Earlier this month, Evercore ISI used a six-month measure to call out 115 S&P 500 stocks with negative beta, a list skewed toward energy, utilities and consumer staples. The investment bank called the energy sector a "synthetic S&P 500 put option" because of the way it has reacted to geopolitical pressure.

If market leadership broadens out, Turnquist believes the number of negative-beta stocks could decline. But he expects dispersion to remain elevated as investors become remain selective toward beneficiaries of AI spending and seek returns there.

Krom at WisdomTree expects the recent extreme readings to eventually revert to the mean. Similar spikes appeared around the 1999-2000 dot-com bubble, he said, when market concentration and large moves in a narrow group of stocks also triggered unusual divergences.

Turnquist pushed back on comparing today with the dot-com era, leading tech companies now are more mature businesses with established revenue and products. Krom is on the same page. He said the individual pieces driving returns don't have the same historical relationship they've had in the past.

"It is not the same market environment now versus 2000," Krom said. The negative betas seen today boil "down to the amount of market concentration."

#244. Answering Questions about Early Retirement, Roth Conversions, Closed-End Funds, and More

In this episode of Motley Fool Hidden Gems Investing, Motley Fool personal finance expert Robert Brokamp is joined by Motley Fool contributor Dan Caplinger to answer financial planning questions sent in from listeners, including:

To catch full episodes of all The Motley Fool's free podcasts, check out our podcast center. When you're ready to invest, check out this top 10 list of stocks to buy.

This podcast was recorded on Sept. 26, 2026.

Robert Brokamp: T-bills, closed-end funds, the best accounts for early retirees, and more. This week on a financial planning mailbag episode of The Motley Fool Hidden Gems Investing Podcast. I’m Robert Brokamp, AKA Bro, and it’s time for our second personal finance mailbag episode, and like the last time. I'm joined by longtime Motley Fool contributor Dan Caplinger, who is a former financial planner and trust attorney. Dan, welcome back to the show.

Dan Caplinger: Thanks again for having me. Always glad to be here.

Robert Brokamp: Like our last mailbag episode, we have chosen six questions that we've received from our wonderful listeners. I'll read each one. Dan and I will take turns, taking a first crack at it, and then the other one of us will add some thoughts. With all that said, here's the first question, and it comes from Anonymous, who asked, recently the team mentioned buying treasury bills directly through TreasuryDirect or Vanguard. Could you guys expand on how doing that compares to holding other short term options like the iShares 0-3 Month Treasury Bond ETF ticker SGOV, the Vanguard 0-3 Month Treasury Bill, ETF ticker VBIL or Vanguard Treasury Money Market Fund, ticker VUSXX.

Dan Caplinger: Anonymous, I would say that the do-it-yourself approach is to buy Treasury bills directly either through your broker or from the government's own TreasuryDirect.gov website. It's whether you decide that you want to pay the fees to an ETF that will do that for you. If you feel like saving, that depends on how much money you are investing. If you only have a couple hundred dollars, probably it’s not going to make that much of a difference. If you've got a couple hundred thousand dollars, then suddenly, even a 10th of a percentage point can make enough of a difference that take you out for a nice dinner once a year or something like that.

But with Treasury bills that you buy, you are responsible for monitoring when you buy them by participating at auctions or by buying them in the secondary market. You are responsible for knowing when they mature, and then when they mature, either if you need the money, you withdraw it. If you don't need the money, then you're responsible for then reinvesting that matured T bill into another T bill or if you want a stock or another investment, whatever that may be. With the ETFs that you're talking about, they handle most of that for you. Once the money is in the ETF, you essentially own a piece of many different Treasury bills with many different maturities.

All of the ETFs that you were talking about, as well as the money market mutual fund, all of those have maturities that are come and due probably every day, at the very least several times a week. Their management team is responsible for jumping in, reinvesting that. They'll charge a modest expense ratio. It's not that much, but it is something that if you are doing the self serve option, then you can avoid that while also customizing to your particular needs with the ETF. It's all on them to decide what they're buying when.

Robert Brokamp: I'll just point out a few stats about these. Both SGOV and VBIL are yielding about 3.6%, the Vanguard money market fund is yielding 3.8%. But if you go and buy a three month T bill straight from the government, it's yielding 4.2% right now. You'll see that in a situation where interest rates are rising, what you get from the money market funds and the ETFs will lag, what happens. Because they have older T bills. Now, the opposite will happen when interest rates go down. If you're buying a new T bill, it's going to be lower than what you're getting from these ETFs. That's just something else to think about. I'll also point out that because these are treasuries, they are free of state income taxes, so that's always something to consider.

Let's move on to our second question from Ben. I am 38 and hope to retire well before age 59.5. I have consistently maximized my available tax advantage retirement accounts, but this has left me with less than I would like in my taxable brokerage account to fund the years before traditional retirement age. Should I continue maximizing my tax advantage accounts and plan to use Rule 72t substantially equal periodic payments for early retirement income, or should I redirect some future contributions into my taxable brokerage account for greater flexibility. Ben's concern here is obviously the 10% early distribution penalty when you take money out of a tax-advantaged retirement account before age 59.5. Now, there are many exceptions to this. You can get around that 10% penalty. You should certainly know those. If you're going to retire early. The IRS website has a whole page of them.

One of them is this substantially equal periodic payment, and it can get very complicated, so I'm just going to highlight very quickly that you're basically committing to a series of payments for at least five years or until you reach age 59.5, whichever is longer. Once you start it, you cannot stop or change the payment amount outside of some approved modifications without facing not only a penalty in that year, but retroactively, so you got to make sure you stick with it. You have to choose from among the IRS's approved three methods of calculating the substantially equal periodic payment. It's all very complicated, but many people in the financial independence retire early community, follow this. It is doable. I'll just add some other thought. First of all, you certainly want to at least contribute to your 401K or employer account to get the employer match. You definitely want to do that.

Another option is to contribute to Roth accounts because with Roths, the contributions come out tax a penalty free. It's the earnings you have to worry about being taxed and penalized before age 59.5. Now, it gets a little complicated with the difference between Roth IRAs and 401Ks. With the Roth IRA, the contributions always come out first, so it's easier. With the Roth 401K, every distribution is a proportional mix of contributions and earnings. It's messier with the Roth 401K.

Final thing to think about is a health savings account if you have access to it and you have money in it, because the interesting thing about the HSA is the money comes out tax-free for qualified expenses, but they don't have to come out in that year. What many people do is, over many years, they keep the receipts for their qualified medical expenses, but they don’t take the money out until they retire, and then they get the tax-free distribution. They just have to have all those receipts ready in case the IRS comes knocking with an audit. Those are some thoughts. You could also do the taxable brokerage account as well, and that would definitely give you a lot of flexibility. Dan, do you have any thoughts on that?

Dan Caplinger: I'll just add on that last point. One of the things that using that taxable brokerage account allows that people don't necessarily think about is that in a taxable brokerage account, if you have a stock that goes up in value quite a bit, then you're going to have long-term capital gains treatment. The tax treatment on that is more favorable than a withdrawal from a traditional IRA or a traditional 401K account. If you are indeed planning to use that money before you reach age 59.5, that tax advantage in a taxable brokerage account might be a factor airing towards going ahead and putting some money in that taxable brokerage.

I know they're bet esoteric, but the yields are usually fabulous, and the risk seems to lie somewhere between bonds and equities. It seems like a decent strategy might be holding closed-end funds over bonds in your 30s-40s and then transitioning to bonds in your 50s and 60s, if one is using the traditional 60 40 portfolio. But this idea seems foreign to boast. I have held closed-end funds since the early 2000s and have found them to be wonderful for income generation, and I’m just wondering what am I missing that keeps others from singing their praises? Maybe you Fools can help me out as to why.

Dan Caplinger: Well, Scott, I have been following closed-end funds for a long time. I dabbled in them from time to time, and I share your confusion about why they get so little attention because, in many ways, they combine sort of the predecessors to modern exchange-traded funds. But you always have that lovely premium or discount question because, with these closed-end funds, what we're referring to here are funds that, unlike most ETFs and mutual funds, you cannot just go to the fund not even an institutional investor can go to the fund and say, “ You know what? I've got these shares. I want the actual assets that are held in the fund in exchange. That's why with traditional mutual funds, you almost always get net asset value with ETFs. The price generally stays pretty close to net asset value. B

ut with closed-end funds, they can vary widely. You can have some funds that trade at a discount to their actual value of the assets that they hold. You can have others that trade at a premium. I think that that may be one of the reasons why professionals have so much difficulty with them. There are certainly very popular closed-end funds that trade at huge premiums until whatever it is that they hold falls out of favor. When those assets fall out of favor, suddenly the closed-end fund declines, it loses the premium, and some investors may face losses, even if the net asset value of the shares goes up, the fact that you bought at a huge premium suddenly means that when that premium disappears, you could have a loss even when the underlying investment is doing well. The other thing that I would caution folks with a lot of closed-end funds use leverage. They borrow money in order to take leverage positions in the assets that they hold. That can be very favorable.

With bond closed-end funds, that was a winning argument for much of the first 20 years of the 21st century as interest rates were gradually coming down. You got highlighted exposure to a positive bond market. That has not been the case over the past three, four, five years, and that is something to take a look at. Always be careful with closed-end funds. Look at the nature of the distribution. Is it actually coming from income or is it a return of your own capital? Just because it looks like a dividend payment doesn't mean that the fund actually generated the income that you are getting back.

Robert Brokamp: I'll just add that if your interest is peaked, the best source on the Internet for information about close end funds is cfcnect.com, which is owned by Duvine, but they have great information on all providers of close end funds, screening tools, some education. Check that out. As I often say, when you are considering any kind of ETF, especially if it's a new asset class to you, look back at past returns, both good years and bad years just to get a sense of how the fund or asset class will perform in different environments. Let's move on to question Number 4, and it comes from Tony. For retirees with a relatively secure funding source such as a pension, in my case, or adequate Social Security, would a more aggressive investment strategy be appropriate for a discretionary fund? I stress tested it on a year 2000-2020 time frame period, and it did well, better even than a glide path scenario from 30%-60% equities over the first 15 years.

What I learned is that opportunity cost is a real thing. I would say that I think Tony is onto something, and he points out a few things that I want to highlight. First of all, pension and Social Security income or really any other source of secure income like that, maybe an annuity or a business group really be considered like a big holding in bonds. The more you get of that income, the more risk you could take with the rest of your portfolio. You can actually even value that as a holding of bonds by doing some present value calculation. If you don't know or don't want to know how to do that, visit valueyourpension.com. It was created by Professor Benjamin Bailey who wanted to basically create a present value calculation for his pension. He couldn't find one on line, so he created the website. Tony also says he's going to be more aggressive with his discretionary funds for his travel and experiences. I think that makes a lot of sense.

We've had several guests on the show recommend that you break your retirement spending into essential and discretionary expenses. You try to cover your essential expenses with a very secure sources of income, pension, Social Security, bond ladder, maybe annuity, something like that. But then you can take more risk with your non essential expenses. That sounds like that's what Soony is doing. Now, 90% stocks is pretty aggressive. But there have been studies that have looked at it, I think, inspired often by Warren Buffett, who wrote in his 2013 annual letter that in his will, he advised the person who's going to manage his wife's assets to invest 90% of it in an S&P 500 index fund and 10% in short term government bonds. The studies have found that it could definitely pay off, assuming you can stand the ups and downs of such an aggressive portfolio, and it does mean that you're going to have to cut back on your discretionary spending during bear markets.

Then my final point is, I'll just add that Tony's reference to the glide path increasing from 30%-60% over the first 15 years, I think he's referring to studies that have found it very beneficial to play it really safe around what's often called the retirement danger zone. It's like 5-10 years before retirement, 5-10 years after retirement. But then it's OK to let your stock allocation rise once you've survived that first 10 years or so of retirement. That's what he's referring to. Those studies, I think I find compelling. I personally want to play it probably pretty safe in those first few to several years of retirement. But then getting more aggressive, it turns out is perfectly fine. Dan what do you think?

Dan Caplinger: I agree 100%. I'll just add that if Tony or any listener in this situation, if you have this excess money above and beyond what your necessities are, one question always to ask is, do you have plans, hopes to leave a legacy for future generations? In that case, taking a more aggressive portfolio stance, essentially borrows that extended time horizon of the person that you're getting. You may be retired and have a relatively short time horizon, but if you're hoping to leave that money for kids or grandkids, their time horizon's much longer, justifying a more aggressive asset allocation for that portion of the portfolio above and beyond those necessities.

Robert Brokamp: Moving on to question Number 5, and it comes from Ben. I am considering going back to grad school and could cover all the tuition by selling about a third of my portfolio. I've been debating this versus taking out student loans. While current market valuations do play a role in my consideration, I'm also thinking that this type of life move is exactly what an investment portfolio can be intended to pay for. Can you help me get over my anxiety of pulling back from the market a bit to invest in my future career goals? I will only be penalized via taxes for selling from this account.

Dan Caplinger: Ben, let me applaud you for having the flexible mindset of an investor who understands the value of investing early, who understands the value of time in the market, but who also is willing to think twice before just sticking with a single-minded way of approaching money because, I'm just going to say this, one of the best investments that you can make, especially early in a career is building your human capital. It's your human capital that is going to be the source of the salary income, of the business opportunities, of so many of the things that are going to affect your financial security for the rest of your life that making an investment in that makes a lot of sense. The question often comes up. OK, yeah, well, there's student loans available. Why would you take money out of the market when you have potentially good debt available? There is some validity to that.

But one thing to keep in mind is that there's been big shifts in the way that the student loans work in recent years. You have sometimes had a federal government that seemed committed to making that funding available. At other times, now you're starting to see the federal government pull back from being as committed to making that funding available. It leaves borrowers who got in in one period of time, questioning, OK, well, things have changed. I don't have as much flexibility as I thought that I would. You are in a fortunate situation. You have the flexibility of having these assets to say, you know what? I don't even want to deal with that. I just want to take some money and invest in my immediate future to generate more career earnings over the rest of your lifetime. I applaud that. I think that that's a worthy goal. Yes, there is going to be potentially some opportunity cost to not being in the market as long, but hopefully your investment in grad school more than pays off enough to make up for that over the course of your lifetime.

Robert Brokamp: I would imagine that the rates you pay on these loans could be a factor. The rates on federal loans for grad school are ranging between eight and nine percent nowadays for private loans, it could be as low as 3% and as high as 17%. Obviously, the higher the loan interest rate, the more I would be inclined to sell some of my portfolio to pay that off. If you're going to sell some of your investments, you could always do some things to try to manage the tax consequences, maybe offset losses with gains and identify shares with lower embedded capital gains. You can manage that. The final point I would make of this is just understand that selling and realizing some taxable income may reduce at a need based aid that you could be eligible for. If you're in a higher tax bracket in the future, then it makes sense to do the Roth conversions.

That said, most people are actually in a lower tax bracket once they retire, especially since your wife is still working, this is generally because people spend less in retirement, but plus after age 65, there's a higher standard deduction. You don't take Medicare or at least aren't eligible for Medicare until age 65, but those IRMA surcharges are based on your tax return from two years prior. Then also look at what if you do it that you decide to put off doing the Roth conversions until your wife decides to retire? Maybe that's at 65. Maybe it's a couple of years one side or the other, that. But see what happens. There's a lot of daylight between age 65 and when you need to start taking required minimum distributions at age 73 or 75, depending on what your birth year is. That may make a difference in your calculation. It's worth taking a little bit of extra effort to run the numbers and see what it comes out.

Robert Brokamp: With that final answer to our final question, we've come to the end of our show. Thank you, Dan, for joining us once again and thanks to Bart Shannon, the engineer for this episode. TL;DR: Mortgage rates went up today, but not as much as they could have.

Yes, mortgage interest rates are up today, but only by a little. If anything, it’s surprising that they aren’t higher, given the spooky inflation report that dropped yesterday.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage rose to 7.32% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is two basis points higher than yesterday but five basis points lower than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.

In the coming days, the direction of mortgage rates will depend a lot on oil price fluctuations (which affect rates in the short term) and whether markets think the Fed will raise borrowing rates again later this month (which has long-term implications). For more on this, read our analysis below.

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Inflation has played a key role in driving up mortgage rates over the past several months, as the Iran war intensified price pressures. The conflict directly affects a key shipping route and oil production, and that indirectly affects the prices of all sorts of goods.

That kind of inflationary environment isn't great for bonds, and the interest rates on 30-year fixed rate mortgages are benchmarked to the yield on the 10-year Treasury note. So where bond yields go, mortgage rates go, too. (For more, here's a much deeper dive on the bond market as it pertains to mortgage rates.)

Persistent inflation also spells trouble for the Federal Reserve. Price stability is half of the Fed's dual mandate (maximum employment is the other half), and inflation has been running above the central bankers' 2% target since 2021. With the conflict in Iran making already-bad inflation worse, the Fed shifted into rate-hiking mode last month.

Raising the federal funds rate, which is the short-term borrowing rate the bankers set, is the Fed's main tool for fighting inflation. Even though the Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, changes to the funds rate ripple out through the entire economy. So a rate hike from the Federal Reserve  — or even markets having relative certainty that a hike is coming — can put upward pressure on mortgage rates.

Why do markets think a rate hike could come this month? The Bureau of Labor Statistics released the September Consumer Price Index, a major inflation report, yesterday. It showed that inflation rose 3.7% last month, largely driven by rising fuel costs.

In the hours following the report drop, futures traders initially revised their projections in favor of another rate hike on Oct. 28. Today, expectations are cooler, with traders now expecting that central bankers will probably vote to hold rates steady.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has previously expressed his wish that investors would interpret data themselves, instead of dissecting central bankers’ public statements for Easter eggs about how they’ll vote.

For now, markets are still pretty much hanging on their every word. Any time a voting member of the Federal Open Market Committee publicly voices an opinion about inflation, it has the potential to shift mortgage rates.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.82% or higher — but there just aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

#247. Forget Eli Lilly and Novo: This Biotech Could Be a Surprising Winner in the Weight Loss Market

The weight-loss market is growing rapidly, and while long-term projections differ on how large it will become, they generally agree that it will maintain its upward trajectory at least over the medium term. Investors can capitalize on this industry's growth by buying shares of those companies likely to emerge as top players. Right now, it looks likely that Eli Lilly (LLY -0.79%) and Novo (NVO -0.94%), the current market leaders, could maintain their lead over the next five years or so. However, other drugmakers are making progress in this field and are worth considering for investors. One of them is Regeneron Pharmaceuticals (REGN -0.89%).

Regeneron has at least two promising weight loss medicines in its pipeline. One of them is called olatorepatide. Regeneron licensed this medicine from a China-based company. Olatorepatide mimics the actions of the GLP-1 and GIP hormones, placing it in the same broad category as Eli Lilly's market-leading drug, Zepbound.

However, olatorepatide could be particularly attractive for one reason: It appears to display better gastrointestinal (GI) tolerability than competing medicines. In a Phase 3 study conducted in China, olatorepatide led to a mean weight loss of up to 19% over 48 weeks. That's already impressive enough.

But as Regeneron pointed out, olatorepatide also had lower rates of GI-related adverse events -- such as nausea and vomiting -- than what some competing drugs achieved in comparable Phase 3 studies. Regeneron still has to run late-stage clinical trials in the U.S. before it can earn approval in the country.

However, olatorepatide's strong performance in Chinese studies makes it a notable contender in the weight loss market. Regeneron's other leading candidate is trevogrumab. This isn't a drug designed to induce weight loss. Rather, Regeneron is developing trevogrumab to be administered alongside anti-obesity medicines to help patients preserve lean mass as they lose weight.

In a Phase 2 study, trevogrumab, administered alongside Novo's semaglutide, led to lean mass preservation of up to 42.5% compared with just 7.3% in patients receiving semaglutide plus placebo. Trevogrumab is yet another differentiated product that could help Regeneron carve out a niche in the rapidly growing weight loss market.

Of course, there is much more to Regeneron's business than its weight loss candidates. The company's main growth driver, Dupixent, a medicine for eczema that it co-markets with Sanofi (SNY -1.82%), continues to perform well.

In the second quarter, Regeneron's revenue increased by 17% year over year to $4.3 billion. Dupixent's global sales (recorded by Sanofi) increased 38% year over year to $6 billion. It is helping Regeneron overcome biosimilar competition for Eylea, a medicine approved for several eye-related conditions, including wet age-related macular degeneration.

Regeneron's newer, higher-dose (HD) formulation of Eylea is helping keep the franchise afloat, at least somewhat. Second-quarter combined U.S. revenue from Eylea and Eylea HD declined 12% year over year to $1 billion. But HD Eylea's U.S. sales came in at $596 million, up 52% year over year.

The newer version of the drug comes with fewer injections per year. More convenient dosing can attract new patients while also prompting existing Eylea patients to switch. So, this franchise, despite recent struggles, isn't exactly dead in the water. Regeneron has other products that are contributing to sales growth, particularly Libtayo, a cancer medicine.

And the biotech boasts an attractive pipeline beyond its weight-loss products, including promising anticoagulants being developed to lower the bleeding risk associated with today's anticoagulants. Regeneron has underperformed the broader market over the past two years amid competition for Eylea, but the company is bouncing back, and, given its current approved lineup and pipeline, it could perform well over the medium term. The company's weight loss products may be a key part of the business within five years.

#248. Indonesian stocks plunge to six-year low as MSCI downgrade fears mount

Indonesia's benchmark stock index plunged over 5% on Monday to its lowest level in six years, as concerns over a potential downgrade by MSCI intensified fears of further foreign investor outflows.

The Jakarta Composite Index tumbled to its lowest level since early October 2020, extending a bruising sell-off in Indonesian equities. MSCI, the index provider, on Friday proposed reclassifying Indonesia directly from an emerging market to stand-alone status, raising the prospect of the country's removal from major global equity benchmarks.

MSCI is expected to make a final decision by June, with the potential reclassification hinging on whether Indonesian authorities can demonstrate meaningful improvements in market governance and transparency.

Goldman Sachs warned in a Sunday note that a full removal from MSCI's emerging-market indexes could trigger approximately $5.6 billion in passive fund outflows, equivalent to 18 days of average daily trading volume for constituents of the MSCI Indonesia Investable Market Index.

An additional $2.7 billion could be at risk if FTSE Russell subsequently takes similar action, although the bank stressed that such a move would be a separate scenario.

Goldman estimated that active funds benchmarked to MSCI and FTSE indexes hold more than $8 billion in Indonesian equities, although any selling by these investors would be discretionary rather than automatically triggered by a downgrade.

The bank maintained its underweight rating on Indonesian equities, citing persistent index uncertainty, weak corporate earnings and macroeconomic headwinds.

"Valuations have compressed significantly, but remain above historical troughs; index, earnings, and macro risks constrain a re-rating," Goldman strategists led by Alvin So wrote.

The MSCI Indonesia Index has fallen 47% this year as of Friday, data provided by the bank showed, with foreign investors withdrawing a net $5.1 billion from Indonesian equities over the period.

Foreign ownership of Indonesian stocks has declined to 25% in October from 27% in January, while the value of foreign holdings has nearly halved to approximately $130 billion from $250 billion, the bank said.

Despite the steep declines, Goldman cautioned that Indonesian equities may not have bottomed. The MSCI Indonesia Index's 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratio has fallen to 7.3 times, its lowest level since the global financial crisis, but remains above historical troughs.

The strategists also expect Indonesia's central bank to raise interest rates twice more, by 25 basis points each in the fourth quarter of 2026 and first quarter of 2027, potentially adding further pressure to economic growth and equity valuations.

#249. Meta's Muse reignites AI disruption fears. Traders are targeting this brokerage stock as next casualty

Meta's latest consumer AI product is sending such big shockwaves through the market that it's even inflaming a long-time rivalry in the brokerage business between 55-year old investing giant Charles Schwab, and Robinhood, an icon of the post-Covid trading boom among young investors.Shares of Schwab fell 6% Tuesday, touching the lowest since early July and the stock is now down more than 8% since Meta announced Muse. Meanwhile, Robinhood's stock was higher, notching anotheryear-to-date high. In May, the company launched AI agents that can now trade and manage portfolios on behalf of users.Shares of sprawling wealth management business LPL Financial Holdings dropped 7% Tuesday, financial services firm Raymond James Financial shed 3.5 percent, and Interactive Brokers slipped 1% as the State Street Financial Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLF) lost 2% and is now down 6 percent from highs made earlier this month. Higher interest rates may not be helping.It's not the first time an AI product has jostled the group – in February, the same group of stocks dropped when tech platform Altruist said its platform `Hazel' can create tax-planning strategies for individuals and advisors. Schwab stock recovered some in the months after – LPL has not."Schwab's an interesting animal," said Jimmy Lee, founder and CEO of The Wealth Consulting Group, a Las Vegas-based advisor that oversees $8 billion in assets. "To us in the advisor space they're kind of neutral and figuring out how best to protect their market share. I don't think Meta brings a lot of competition from the custodian perspective because it's not like Altruist's platform, but there is a lot of disruption that's going to happen among financial middle-men that charge fees for billing, reporting, trading, etc."Meta's AI assistant says it won't trade for users or give financial advice, but when queried with how it might mimic the work of a financial advisor or broker, lists abilities including tracking investments and progress towards goals, as well as analyzing how portfolio holdings fit together.

Last week, Schwab Advisor Services, the company's platform for registered investment advisors, announced it is working with Anthropic to create Claude for Financial Advisors. In May, the company launched an AI tool that includes tailored analysis from the company's research arm. Representatives from Schwab did not respond to a request for comment. Robinhood reps declined to add to this story.Robinhood's bounce on Tuesday brings its stock to a 10% rally on the year after dropping more than 40% in the first three months. The retail-focused brokerage, which also offers digital banking and advisory services, is up 1200 percent the past three years. Schwab stock is up 83 percent and the XLF is up 65 percent."AI and tokenization threaten to dismantle the frictions that legacy financial intermediaries have historically monetized," Piper Sandler analyst Patrick Moley wrote in a note in April. "Schwab's reliance on low-yielding sweep cash puts it squarely in the crosshairs."

Judging by options-market flows around the stocks on Tuesday, the threat to Schwab may be a lasting one.Options volume in Schwab was more than five times the average, with nearly twice as many puts bought vs. calls, Cboe LiveVol data show. The most popular contract to buy was the 90-strike put expiring mid-January, a bet the stock drops another 13% the next three months. To be sure, there was one big counter-trade sale of the Oct. 16 95-strike puts.

What's arguably most notable is in Robinhood options, sentiment was the opposite – traders bought twice as many calls as puts with more than 80 percent of the $95 million in premium traded tied to calls. The most heavily traded contract was the 125-strike call expiring on Friday."Gen Z and millennials gravitate towards platforms like Robinhood and Public which is why those platforms ship products so quickly," Gav Blaxberg, founder of Wolf Financial, a popular online trader enclave, said in a call. "Robinhood has built enough trust rebuilding its brand since GameStop and they're allowing agents to trade literally everything."
