#250. Don’t Kill The Golden Goose: Rectifying AI Cost Without Stifling Innovation

Mark Williamson, CTO at Undo, builds agentic debugging to fix complex non-deterministic bugs — likes to remind computers who’s in charge.

​For two years, the AI story in software engineering has been simple: adopt fast, spend freely and trust the returns will follow. Engineering leaders were rewarded for getting developers onto AI tools, token spend became a badge of progress and the question of what it was producing was set aside.

That story is running out of road. According to TechCrunch, Uber exhausted its entire 2026 AI budget by April, primarily on Claude Code. Axios reported that an AI consultant’s unnamed client spent roughly $500 million on Claude in a month after failing to set usage limits.

CFOs are asking what the business got for that spend. Over the next 12 to 24 months, that scrutiny is going to turn into budget pressure for most engineering organizations. But there’s a danger in how companies respond.

On the way up, the mistake was treating token consumption as progress. Companies built dashboards tracking prompts, tokens and active users. Some ran leaderboards ranking teams by usage.

​Google’s own usage figures illustrate how dramatically AI token consumption has grown: The company reported processing more than 3.2 quadrillion tokens per month in May 2026, compared with 9.7 trillion two years earlier. But usage volume alone doesn’t establish business or engineering value.​

For many companies, all those AI tokens don’t necessarily translate into better productivity. In fact, Gartner found that over half of developers say AI has improved team output by 10% or less. A team can double its AI usage without shipping any faster.​

Now the emerging mistake is treating token cost as the thing to control. Cap the spend, mandate cheaper models, push budgets onto individual teams and let them ration.​

These look like opposite strategies, but they’re really two sides of the same coin. Both treat the token as the unit that matters. Neither asks what a token actually buys. The better measure is the cost of solving the problem. And once you price things that way, some of the “obvious” cost savings turn out to be nothing of the sort.​

Many companies now have an internal mandate that amounts to using the cheaper model wherever possible, and saving the frontier model for special occasions. On paper this is sensible. The workflows look identical and one model costs a fraction of the other per token.​

Engineers, meanwhile, are grumbling that the cheaper model isn’t up to the harder problems. It’s tempting for leadership to hear that as engineers wanting the shiniest toy. But model choice can miss the bigger variable. What makes a model effective on a given task often has less to do with the model than the context it’s given.​

On a complex debugging task, for example, even the most expensive AI models can struggle to identify the root cause of a bug if they only have the source code. Context on the runtime behavior of the software is also essential.​

Taking issue #20086 in DuckDB (a widely used open-source database) as an example, testing across different models and contexts, my company discovered:

• Claude Sonnet, source code only spent $4.35 and gave a confident wrong diagnosis.

• Claude Fable 5, source code only spent over an hour and $37.60 and still hallucinated the root cause.

• Claude Fable 5 with runtime context found the real root cause in 12 minutes, for $2.88 to $6.31 across runs.

• Claude Opus 4.8 with runtime context found it in 14 minutes, for $8.06.​

First, this wasn’t a cheap-model problem. With source code alone, both Sonnet and Fable 5 confidently got the root cause wrong. The real variable was context rather than model.

Second, with runtime context, the model gap nearly disappeared. The cheaper model performed close to the more capable one and beat that same model running on source alone.

Third, better context changed the economics completely. Fable 5 went from $37.60 and wrong to $2.88 and correct—a six- to 13-times cost reduction.

That’s why token price is the wrong metric. A cheap failed run still leaves the bug unsolved. What’s important is cost per solved problem or, put differently, token ROI.

There are two levers engineering leaders can pull to optimize the ROI of AI, and neither is as simple as buying cheaper tokens.​

1. The first lever is matching the model to the task. Cheaper models are genuinely the right choice for a lot of engineering work, such as boilerplate code and mechanical refactors. Frontier models are better suited for harder reasoning tasks where a wrong answer is expensive, like debugging unexpected system behavior. A blanket “use the cheap one” mandate eliminates the judgment call that makes spend efficient.

2. The second lever is engineering the context so the model succeeds first time. An AI agent with the right context behaves like a smarter model. Feed it a full recording of everything the code did at runtime, rather than asking it to guess dynamic behavior from logs and static source code, and it stops hallucinating plausible-but-wrong causes and starts finding real ones.​

Even with both levers pulled, engineering leaders need to know whether AI spend is working, and the answer will never be on a token dashboard. The questions worth asking are the boring ones. Has MTTR for customer issues come down? Are features shipping faster? Have escaped defects dropped? If those numbers haven’t moved, the spend isn’t working, regardless of how much AI is nominally in the process. If they have, defend the budget with them.​

The budget crunch is coming, and there are two ways to respond. Organizations that ration tokens could pay twice: once for cheap tokens, and again for the wrong answers and the engineer-hours spent chasing them. Those that respond by pricing the solved problem, matching models to tasks and giving agents the context to succeed first time will get the productivity gains everyone signed up for, at a bill their CFO can live with.​

The golden goose doesn’t need a bigger feed budget, but to stop being judged by how much it eats.

#251. How to Tailgate on a Budget

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Hosting a pregame party doesn’t have to be expensive with a little extra planning.

It’s football season, which also means tailgating. If you love to throw a pregame party at your home or in a stadium parking lot, then you know hosting can be expensive.

But you don’t have to let cost get in the way of a good celebration, because we have plenty of ideas for how to save money.

As a regular party host myself, I make planning ahead my guiding principle to control costs. I set the menu well in advance so I have more time to hunt for sales.

Amy Webb, an accredited financial counselor (AFC) based near Galveston, Texas, agrees. Planning makes it easier to invite other people to contribute and decide what you need to buy, she says.

Check your team’s schedule to get a leg up.

“Pick the games you want to go all out for. Sometimes people will plan to host last minute or every Sunday, and that’s when it can get pricey,” she says. Circling the date of a big rivalry game can give you more time.

Here are four more ways to save on tailgating.

Perfecting one go-to dish can make a party feel festive without racking up a big expense, Webb says. She makes a kind of Cincinnati-style chili that features cinnamon, chocolate and other sweeter flavors to serve while she cheers on the Cincinnati Bengals.

“To me, that’s something cheap that I can make at home, and it makes everyone feel like they are in Cincinnati,” she says.

A ham-and-cheese slider platter is my go-to for tailgates. It’s relatively inexpensive to buy sweet buns, ham, cheese, butter and honey. Plus, sliders are easy to make in the oven and serve in a grab-and-go style for large groups.

When you know what you're making ahead of time, you can schedule your grocery shopping trips around sales.

Katie Ubelhor, an AFC in Cincinnati, buys the meat she needs on Tuesdays, when her local store marks it down by 50% to 75%.

That can work well even if your party isn’t until Sunday. “I freeze it and thaw it right before I need it,” she says.

Writing down your shopping list before hitting the store can also help, says Lynn McHann, an AFC in Bozeman, Montana.

“Apply the meal-planning mindset. Pick the main event — like wings or burgers, but not both — then use cheaper sides to fill everything else in,” she says. Otherwise, you might overbuy.

Don’t forget to apply your grocery store’s loyalty account at checkout, if you have one.

Turning the tailgate into a potluck can spread out the costs, and guests are often happy to contribute. Your mission is to make it easy for everyone to know what to bring.

Webb suggests circulating a virtual sign-up sheet for people to select which type of item they want to bring. “It helps everybody,” she says, because otherwise guests might have no idea what to bring, or you could end up with too many desserts.

Drinks can also turn into a “bring your own beverage” invitation, says Amanda Christensen, AFC and extension professor at Utah State University Extension. She suggests that the host provide a cooler of ice and guests bring their own favorite beverage.

“Not only does this share in the community-building experience, but it also helps share the cost,” she adds.

Ubelhor says if you’re concerned friends can’t afford to purchase items to bring, you can invite them to share what they already own.

Maybe they have a canopy or a cooler at home that would help out, or they could find supplies to borrow from friends or neighbors. “There’s no need to buy something new,” she adds. Some library systems also allow users to check out equipment for gatherings.

NFL-branded decor can be pricey, but color-themed tablecloths and signs can feel just as festive, McHann says.

“Don’t pay a Pinterest tax and think we have to make an elaborate event for people,” she says.

Instead, make decorating an activity during the party. Guests can make their own signs with a few supplies. You can also encourage them to wear their team colors.

“It gives you the festive feeling but on the cheap,” she says. “No one’s ever left a great tailgating party saying, ‘I wish they had football-shaped napkins.’”

You can also look out for decor throughout the year, when it might be on sale. Webb picks up any tiger decor she sees at dollar stores. Because … Bengals fan.

“If it’s on clearance and a tiger, I will get it,” she says.

Another piece of hosting advice: Don’t do up your whole house for a pregame party. “Just pick a table or a spot. You don’t need to go overboard,” Webb says.

#252. Not Nvidia. Not Micron. This Artificial Intelligence (AI) Chip Stock Has the Most Upside Through 2030.

As the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution evolves, investors face an increasingly difficult question: Which chipmakers stand to dominate five years from now?

Nvidia (NVDA +1.87%) faces growing competition from custom silicon developed by its own customers. Meanwhile, Micron Technology (MU +3.75%) could face less favorable memory market dynamics as manufacturers expand production.

This is why I see Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM +2.69%), otherwise known as TSMC, as a more attractive long-term opportunity. Taiwan Semi's latest earnings report displayed how its business is becoming more valuable than ever to the AI infrastructure era.

Image source: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing.

Nvidia is the undisputed king in the AI accelerator market thanks to its graphics processing units (GPUs), networking technology, and CUDA software ecosystem. However, the company's largest customers are developing alternatives. Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, and Meta Platforms are investing in application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) optimized for their own AI workloads. While these chips won't replace Nvidia's GPUs entirely, they should reduce dependence on Nvidia while giving the hyperscalers more control over infrastructure costs and model performance.

Meanwhile, Nvidia is also exploring agentic AI, autonomous vehicles, and robotics. Indeed, these opportunities could be enormous. But commercial adoption may take longer than the next four years.

Micron is looking at a different challenge. The company's memory solutions are essential for AI computing, particularly high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and advanced DRAM. Memory manufacturing has historically been a cyclical industry, meaning today's shortages and elevated prices will lead producers to expand capacity. By next decade, more supply should come online, leading to pricing pressure and eroding profit margins.

Moreover, competition from China's ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) also deserves attention. Although CXMT is not yet an equivalent competitor across every advanced memory category, its progress could affect the industry's supply dynamics over time.

Here's what makes TSMC different: Whether AI hyperscalers buy Nvidia GPUs, develop custom silicon, or adopt entirely new architectures, many of those chips will require Taiwan Semi's advanced foundry capabilities. In turn, Taiwan Semi doesn't need Nvidia to defeat Alphabet's custom chip strategy. It can manufacture chips for both companies.

Taiwan Semi's third-quarter earnings report put the company's competitive position on full display. The company generated $46.7 billion in revenue, representing 41% growth year over year. Meanwhile, TSMC delivered a gross margin of 66.4% and an operating margin of 58.7%. This underscores the pricing power commanded by the company's advanced manufacturing technology.

Management expects AI-driven momentum to continue. For Q4, revenue is projected to reach between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion as the company's next-generation, 2-nanometer technology continues ramping.

Building a semiconductor foundry requires significant upfront capital, years of engineering development, and the ability to manufacture complex chips at commercially viable yields. This creates substantial barriers to entry. As demand for AI compute grows, TSMC should benefit from higher production volumes, more sophisticated manufacturing processes, and additional opportunities in advanced packaging.

Furthermore, the company's opportunities extend beyond today's AI hardware. Consider what could happen between now and 2030. AI workloads are going to shift from training large language models (LLMs) toward inference deployments across autonomous systems, robotics, and applications that have not yet been commercialized at scale. Some of these will require more GPUs, while others will depend on custom accelerators, central processing units (CPUs), or specialized processors.

While TSMC doesn't manufacture DRAM or HBM, it does produce advanced logic chips that operate alongside these memory types. In other words, Taiwan Semi stands to benefit from the broader evolution of AI rather than relying on one particular semiconductor category.

That versatility potentially supports more valuation expansion for Taiwan Semi relative to other semiconductor stocks. Historically, chip manufacturers traded at discounts relative to other designers due to their capital-intensive business models. However, TSMC's dominant position in leading-edge manufacturing, growing profitability, and indispensable role in the AI infrastructure value chain could justify a higher earnings multiple in the long-run.

To me, Taiwan Semi offers a unique proposition: exposure to a broad range of advanced chip architectures regardless of which designers are in demand. Combined with its manufacturing capabilities, robust profitability, and potential for long-term upside, I see TSMC as a compelling buy-and-hold AI chip stock through 2030.

#255. U.S. presses China on Mastercard, Citigroup market access in bilateral Bangkok talks, official says

BANGKOK – U.S. officials pressed Beijing on market access issues for Mastercard Inc and Citigroup Inc during at least two bilateral meetings with Chinese counterparts in Bangkok this week, according to a U.S. Treasury official.

The Treasury delegation, led by Deputy Secretary Francis Brooke, held bilateral meetings with officials from the People's Bank of China and the finance ministry on the sidelines of the Group of 20 finance meetings and the IMF-World Bank annual gathering this week, the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss the closed-door meetings.

The talks included market access for U.S. companies, including Mastercard, Visa and Citigroup, the official said, adding that regulatory approval was part of the agreement reached during the meeting between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping during the latter's state visit in Washington last month.

The sideline meetings in Bangkok continued discussions on implementing these deals, the official said.

The PBOC, China's National Financial Regulatory Administration, China Securities Regulatory Commission, Chinese embassies in Singapore and Thailand, the U.S. Treasury Department press office and Visa did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. Citigroup and Mastercard declined to comment.

The progress follows China's Oct. 13 approval for Visa Inc. to begin preparing a wholly owned domestic card-clearing business. Visa has up to a year to prepare before it applies for an operating license, the PBOC has said.

China has opened much of its financial sector to foreign firms since 2018, gradually lifting foreign ownership caps on services such as securities, futures and fund management. It still limits cross-border capital flows and has kept state-backed domestic players dominant in payments.

Mastercard currently operates yuan card payments in China through a local joint venture with NetsUnion Clearing Corp., which began operating in 2024. The pending approval would allow it to operate as an independent entity, the person said.

Citigroup — which has hired several dozen employees for its China unit — is seeking a wholly owned securities license to conduct A-share brokerage, underwriting, research and principal trading businesses in the onshore market, two people familiar with the industry said, requesting anonymity for discussing private matters.

One of the two people close to Citigroup said the bank planned to increase its China securities staff to about 100.

The bank applied in late 2021, and Reuters reported last month that approval could come soon.

Trump and Xi are expected to meet in person for the third time this year in Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November.

"The move suggests the US-China trade environment remains benign, and Beijing is keen to keep up the momentum," said Dan Wang, China director at Eurasia Group.

Licensing U.S. financial firms is a "limited concession" on market access, she said, though it signals China is continuing to open up, and "this should marginally bolster investor confidence in Chinese assets."

#257. Lennar shares pop as Berkshire builds almost a 10% stake in beleaguered homebuilder

Berkshire Hathaway has gone on a buying spree in beleaguered homebuilder Lennar, accumulating almost a 10% stake.

The position is a "classic" value play, according to a CFRA analyst.

Berkshire Hathaway bought almost 2.7 million Class A shares of Lennar over three trading days ended Monday, bringing the position to 23.7 million shares worth $1.8 billion, according to a securities filing late Monday. The Omaha-based conglomerate also owns 528,000 of Lennar's Class B shares, each of which carries 10 times the votes of a Class A share.

Lennar surged as much as 6.6% at one point Tuesday, to a high of $83.24. The Miami-based company has plunged more than 32% in the past year.

Berkshire's latest purchases have come as interest rates rise, which hurt homebuilders by raising the rate on 30-year mortgages and dimming affordability. The nationwide average 30-year fixed mortgage rate reached 6.95% last week, up from the prior week's average of 6.76% and last year's 6.26%, according to Freddie Mac. The State Street SPDR S&P Homebuilders ETF (XHB) is down almost 16% since the end of June.

"Berkshire likes to buy undervalued assets," said Catherine Seifert, an analyst at CFRA Research. Betting on Lennar is a "classic Berkshire value play."

The move isn't a stretch for current Berkshire CEO Greg Abel, who took over last year from Warren Buffett.

Berkshire has "a pretty significant presence" in the homebuilding market, Seifert said, after its acquisition of Taylor Morrison. Berkshire also owns building material companies, including paint manufacturer Benjamin Moore and Johns Manville, a maker of roof tiles. In 2003, Berkshire bought Clayton Homes, a maker of manufactured and modular homes, for almost $2 billion.

Lennar last week reported weak results in the fiscal third quarter ended Aug. 31. Earnings per share totaled $1.23, missing Wall Street analysts' consensus estimate of $1.29, while revenue slumped 8% from the same period a year ago.

Even more importantly, Lennar forecast fourth-quarter guidance below expectations, citing affordability challenges from rising interest rates. On management's conference call with analysts, CEO Stuart Millar said 30-year mortgage rates at 7% constrain affordability and reduce the pool of qualified buyers.

Plagued by a mismatch between supply and demand, the housing sector has helped dampen consumer confidence. A shortage of new housing supply is pushing up the price of existing homes and making new homes harder to afford. Higher mortgage rates have priced millions of first-time buyers out of the market altogether.

Steeped in a deep value investment philosophy that often veers toward the contrarian, the tough housing environment could provide rich targets for Berkshire, which sat on a war chest of some $367 billion at the end of June.

On Friday, Buffett officially stepped down as chairman effective immediately, succeeded by his son Howard Buffett.

#259. India’s finance minister says market liquidity makes it easier for investors to exit

The high degree of liquidity in India's equity market has provided easier exits to foreign portfolio investors, according to Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman.

"Because of the ease of liquidity, ease of availability, people are even exiting easily," Sitharaman told CNBC in an exclusive interview on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok on Friday. However, the fundamentals of the Indian economy are "fine," she said.

Since January, India's key benchmark indexes have slipped nearly 12%, as per LSEG data, even though the country's economic growth has been resilient amid trade uncertainty and geopolitical shocks. India has been hit with record outflows by foreign investors from its equity markets.

Still, domestic capital continues to flood the market. Indian equity mutual funds have recorded net inflows every month since March 2021, according to data released by industry body Association of Mutual Funds in India earlier this month.

Multinational companies, private equity funds and foreign investors have been able to make partial or full exits from their investments at a premium. Between 2021 and 2025, Indian initial public offerings collectively raised $60.4 billion, of which "a staggering" $37.7 billion, or 63% of total proceeds, went to existing holders who sold their shares to the public, an EY report in August said.

The flight of capital toward AI and the U.S., which otherwise moves toward different countries for different sectoral investments, is "a concern," Sitharaman said. When asked about the biggest risks for the Indian economy in 2027, the finance minister underscored fuel, fertilizer, and "flow of capital."

The global AI rally is showing cracks, but Sitharaman said India wouldn't be "hurt" from any spillover if the bubble burst. India has not received the "AI kind of investments coming into different jurisdictions," she said.

Sitharaman, who is India's longest-serving finance minister to hold the office continuously, added that the South Asian country was "no longer a laggard" in the frontier tech space and investment was being made to set up semiconductor manufacturing.

Foreign portfolio investors have sold direct Indian equities of over $33 billion so far this year, as per Indian depository firm NSDL. India is seen by some portfolio managers as an anti-AI trade, while markets like Taiwan and Korea, with AI champions, have attracted strong investment flows.

Taiwan now has the largest market weighting in the MSCI Asia Pacific ex-Japan index at 29%, while Korea has moved into second place at 22%, as per a report by Goldman Sachs on Oct. 8. India's share has compressed from 19% a few years ago to 10%, it added.

-Correction: This article has been updated to clarify that Sitharaman was discussing ease of exit from India's equity market, rather than attributing stock market underperformance to excess liquidity.

#261. Beyond Price Hikes: Turning Pricing Into A Long-Term Value Strategy

Vasudeva Akula, VOZIQ AI cofounder and head of data science. Helps recurring revenue businesses improve customer retention using ML.

​Strategically executed price hikes are one of the most powerful levers a business can pull to improve profitability. According to McKinsey, even a 1% price increase can translate into an 8.7% increase in operating profits, assuming there is no loss of volume. This is a significant gain for a growth-minded business.

However, if not targeted correctly, the same price increase can produce completely different outcomes for different customers. While some may absorb the price increase, those who are more price-sensitive may end up downgrading to a lower-priced plan or even reconsider the relationship altogether. This attrition driven by a price increase is easily the worst outcome a business may want.

So, the real pricing challenge is understanding where an increase is likely to create value and where it could put existing value at risk.

In my experience, that boils down to three questions: Who can absorb the increase? How much can they absorb? And when is the right time to make it? ​

Customers do not respond to price changes uniformly. Some are highly sensitive to price, while others may barely react. But price sensitivity alone does not tell us who can absorb an increase.

In order to gain a more complete view, leaders should combine price sensitivity with the future value of a customer (predictive CLV) and the satisfaction level of the customer (predictive NPS). Predictive CLV can bring future value and risk into the decision, while predictive NPS can show how healthy the customer relationship is today.

Consider two hypothetical customers who both show low price sensitivity. One has high predictive CLV and high predictive NPS. The customer is valuable, the relationship is healthy and there is little evidence of price-driven risk. The other may show the same price sensitivity but have lower predictive value, higher risk or weaker relationship health. The two customers may look identical through a price-sensitivity lens, but they are not equally suitable for a price increase.

Leaders must shift from identifying customers who are unlikely to react to identifying customers for whom a price increase makes economic sense. Price sensitivity tells you how a customer may respond. CLV and NPS tell you what is at stake and how healthy the relationship is.

A uniform increase may be easier to execute, but it assumes every customer has the same capacity to absorb the increase. They do not.

Assume the plan is to raise prices by 5%. Now consider a customer paying $35 with a low price-sensitivity score, when the average price for the service is $50. In this case, the customer could have absorbed a higher price hike than 5%. By contrast, another customer who is paying $65, which is already above the average price, and showing high price sensitivity may be better served with a smaller-than-5% increase or no increase in the current cycle.

The amount of the increase should, therefore, reflect where the customer’s current price stands relative to the average, their current engagement and satisfaction levels, their future value to the business and how they have responded to previous price increases. This allows the business to move beyond a single percentage applied across the customer base. ​

A customer who can absorb an increase today may not be the right candidate tomorrow. The right time to increase the price is when recent changes in the customer relationship do not indicate elevated risk.

Those changes can show up in everyday customer interactions. A complaint, service issue, reservice request or contract interaction can indicate that something has shifted. A cancellation discussion, a competitor mention or collections activity can also signal that the timing of an increase may be wrong.

The challenge is making these signals visible before the decision is made. Frontline teams are closest to many of these interactions, so they need the right customer intelligence to understand what is happening in the relationship and how it should influence the pricing decision. ​

That intelligence should give frontline teams a current view of the customer relationship, bringing together recent interactions and changes in behavior that may affect the decision. When evaluating these solutions, be sure to look for intelligence that explains why a customer’s risk or relationship health has changed, rather than simply providing a score without the context behind it. This context can help frontline teams recognize when the conditions that once supported a price increase have changed.​

Leaders don’t necessarily need to say, “Don’t increase this customer’s price.” They might instead say, “Don’t increase this customer’s price now.” When the relationship signals indicate higher risk, the better decision may be to wait until those signals change. ​

A price increase can create an immediate revenue increase, but that is only the beginning of the economic outcome. What matters is whether that increase creates value that lasts.

A customer who stays for the next 24 months can be worth far more to the business than the incremental revenue from a single price increase. That is why the objective cannot be limited to increasing revenue per customer. It has to be focused on increasing the lifetime value of the customer relationship.

Who receives the increase, how much they receive and when they receive it all influence that outcome. A decision that seems positive after one billing cycle may look very different when viewed over the life of the customer relationship.

The question is not how much more revenue a price increase can generate today. It is how much long-term value that decision can create.​

#263. KFC to switch to Coca-Cola beverages in U.S. restaurants for the first time in decades

KFC's U.S. restaurants will ditch PepsiCo and switch to Coca-Cola beverages next year, marking the first time in decades that the Yum Brands chain has changed its drink supplier, the restaurant company said Thursday.

Some of KFC's international markets serve Coke products, but the chain's U.S. restaurants have stuck with PepsiCo drinks ever since Pepsi bought KFC in 1986. At the time of the acquisition, KFC was Coke's second-largest fountain account, trailing only McDonald's. Pepsi later spun off KFC, along with sister chains Pizza Hut and Taco Bell — but even as the combined Yum Brands, the company stayed loyal to its previous owner. Without Pepsi, Taco Bell would not serve its iconic Mountain Dew Baja Blast.

The change comes as KFC aims to win back U.S. diners, who have ditched the fried chicken chain for rivals such as Chick-fil-A or Popeyes.

"This decision is a critical step in the Kentucky Fried Comeback," KFC U.S. President Catherine Tan-Gillespie wrote in a memo to franchisees and employees obtained by CNBC. "A new beverage offering, with a new partner in Coca-Cola, gives us a platform to innovate, meet changing tastes and give customers more reasons to choose us."

For many fast-food chains, beverages have become a critical way to attract consumers. A number of restaurants, including McDonald's and Taco Bell, have broadened their drink offerings with options such as refreshers or "dirty soda." For its part, KFC recently unveiled new drinks, including iced coffees and shakes, at Open House, its innovation restaurant in McKinney, Texas.

Coke told CNBC earlier this year that the company has helped many of its restaurant partners create new drinks.

KFC expects to be pouring Coke beverages in all of its U.S. restaurants by the end of the first quarter of 2027, Tan-Gillespie said.

Tan-Gillespie also said that Pepsi remains an important partner for KFC's parent company and the chain's international markets.

For decades, Coke and Pepsi have tussled over important restaurant partners, which represent both a sales opportunity and the chance to grow the visibility of their beverage brands.

It is unusual for large restaurant chains to switch beverage providers, but not unprecedented. In 2024, Pepsi poached Subway, the largest U.S. restaurant chain by number of locations, from Coke. Besides KFC, Coke has wooed away a number of notable Pepsi customers in recent years, including Culver's, Arby's and Panda Express.

#265. 3 Dividend ETFs That Deliver More Power as a Combined Portfolio

As a general rule, more stocks or ETFs doesn't necessarily make a portfolio diversified. With so much of the S&P 500 being top-heavy and overweight in mega-cap tech companies, adding a growth or semiconductor ETF to a core S&P 500 fund doesn't do much to actually spread out risk or exposure.

The same principle applies to dividend ETFs. You shouldn't choose only higher yielding funds, nor should you just load up on the latest top performers. You need to understand what the fund's target market is before matching it up with different strategies to give you a more comprehensive and diversified portfolio.

With so many choices in this space, it's actually pretty easy to cover all three dividend investing pillars -- dividend growth, dividend quality, and high yield -- with just a few ETFs. If you're building out the dividend equity segment of your portfolio, here are three solid dividend ETFs that actually work better together than they do individually.

The Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF (SCHD -0.41%) is one of the most popular funds in this category and for good reason. It's enjoyed a renaissance in 2026 by gaining more than 27% year-to-date and has an average annual return of more than 13% over the past decade.

But it's the portfolio construction process that makes it so appealing. It considers the dividend growth, dividend quality, and yield factors in choosing the roughly 100 stocks it targets. You don't end up getting most of the popular tech stocks of the moment but you do end up getting a portfolio of high quality, durable companies that can withstand challenging economic conditions and continuing growing over time.

Its 3.3% yield is more than triple that of the S&P 500 right now and it's managed to increase its annual dividend every year since its inception in 2011. If you were to own only one dividend ETF in your portfolio, this one might be it. But there are still ways to add around it.

The Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF (VIG -0.14%) is built like a traditional dividend growth fund. It includes U.S. large-cap stocks with at least 10 consecutive years of annual dividend growth and then market cap weights those stocks that qualify. But it's unique in that it unintentionally has pretty strong growth profile too.

Since there's no yield qualifier for inclusion (outside of the fact that the top 25% of yields are excluded off the top), low-yielding stocks can receive large weightings. Take, for instance, the fact that Microsoft, Apple, and Broadcom are the top three holdings with a combined weight of around 14%. Roughly 27% of the fund overall is tech stocks, so the fund becomes much more of a balance between growth and income.

That's why it pairs well with the Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF. If you combine its defensive profile with a growth-tilted Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF, you cover more of the full dividend stock universe.

You can often find higher dividend yields overseas than you can here in the United States. The Vanguard International High Dividend Yield ETF (VYMI -0.53%), for example, has a dividend yield of 3.2%. That's a full 1% higher than the 2.2% yield of its U.S. counterpart, the Vanguard High Dividend Yield ETF, that uses substantially the same strategy.

This fund is a pure high yield strategy, but it's the international diversification that's also a key feature. On the high yield side specifically, international dividend payers have outperformed U.S. dividend stocks over the past five years with comparable risk levels. The sector compositions are also fairly different, especially the 40%+ allocation to financials in the Vanguard International High Dividend Yield ETF.

The bottom line is that diversifying internationally has delivered better risk-adjusted returns overall over the past several years.

With just these three ETFs, you cover each important segment of the dividend stock universe multiple times. The Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF gives you quality and yield. The Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF gives you quality and dividend growth. The Vanguard International High Dividend Yield ETF gives you yield and overseas diversification.

It's a trio where the sum total really is greater than its individual parts.

#266. The bloated workweek is coming for Sundays—as some embrace flexibility, others worry about job security

Alessia Montanaro is just about to close her second busy season of the year. Since September she's been logging up to 60 hours of work per week, sometimes going as late as 11 p.m., and making a habit of working Sundays from her home office.

The 30-year-old works in public accounting in Austin, Texas, and has gotten used to these sprints around tax season. She's not the only weekend work warrior.

For many office workers, Sundays have become the unofficial new start to their workweek: Nearly half of workers often clock in on Sundays, according to a recent report from Owl Labs, the video-conferencing technology company, which surveyed 2,000 people in July with a margin of error of 2%. Some 21% of people surveyed say they work the whole or nearly the whole day, and another 24% say they often do a few hours of work.

Of the remaining set of workers, 11% say they quickly check messages but don't really work, 18% say they rarely do any work on Sundays, and 26% say they never do.

It's been six years since work for many moved home during the Covid-19 pandemic, opening the possibilities of logging hours anytime and anywhere there's Wi-Fi. While some people deprioritized work and put up strict boundaries to protect their personal time, tech use data shows that many years later, working time has bled into every hour of every day. Chat messages sent outside of the standard Monday through Friday 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. workweek rose 15% year-over-year, now up to an average 58 messages per user, according to Microsoft's 2025 research on what it calls the rise of the "infinite workday."

Among those working on the weekends, nearly 20% check their email before noon on a Saturday and Sunday, and over 5% are in their inboxes on Sunday nights, per Microsoft.

As far as these online habits show, the sanctity of Sundays off may be vanishing as an always-on work culture takes over.

Some Sunday workers say working weekends or after hours is the only way to get focused work done. During the workweek, "I get pulled in five different directions" with messages or requests from associates and higher-ups, Montanaro of Austin says.

Working a distraction-free Sunday can help workers get more done, says Frank Weishaupt, CEO of Owl Labs. But it can also be a signal that the typical Monday-through-Friday is overloaded with busywork.

The work of getting work done can be disruptive: Employees are interrupted roughly every two minutes during core work hours with meetings, emails or chat messages, according to Microsoft data. Some 38% of workers say they have meeting fatigue, with the most common gripes being that meetings are too long and there are too many of them, according to Owl Labs.

Weishaupt says Sunday work periods could be seen as a good thing "as it relates to the employee's desire for flexibility" and a growing interest in "microshifting," a term Owl Labs coined to mean working outside of a traditional Monday through Friday 9-to-5 time block.

Microshifting can be especially helpful to moms, caregivers and anyone who might need to duck out for a few hours on workdays. Kylie Gonzalez, 29, says she'll clock into her account manager job from home on a Sunday if she took some time during the week for doctor's appointments, school pickup for her kids or other events.

But she's wary of spending more than an hour or so working on the weekend, or making a habit of it. "Some companies may take advantage of that fact and add more to your plate because they see so much is being done," she says.

In 2019, the norm was going into the office on a Monday and getting settled for the week ahead, Weishaupt says. That prep work is now shifting to Sundays.

"My Sunday evening feels awful because I'm just thinking about Monday and all the work that I didn't finish on Friday," says Tobi Collins, 28, a strategy consultant in Dallas. Her weekend work helps her curb the Sunday scaries, she says: "If I just get ahead of it, I'm not as nervous about the week."

Dina Otero, 42, of Philadelphia, says she used to regularly log weekend hours, even spending her Sundays back from vacation catching up on emails before her actual return to work. Working a little extra at the start of the week would help her get ahead, she told herself. Really, it was just anxiety and "my own way of thinking that I had control over things that I really did not," she says.

In the current tough job market, when companies are signaling layoffs before they happen, hiring less and raising expectations around artificial intelligence, Weishaupt says Sunday work could also be a sign of overworking when people are worried about job security. Workers are "doing anything they can to hug that job, and that may mean that they're just working a lot more, Sunday included," he says.

That can become a big problem if unchecked. "If 40 hours become 60 hours, you know you're going to have burnout, you're going to have frustration, and then when that pendulum swings the other way, you're going to have a lot of churn," Weishaupt says.

LaToya Allen, 45, in Washington, D.C., isn't sure the extra work hours are always worth it. She found herself in a burn-and-churn cycle in 2020, when she became disillusioned by her corporate tech job and what she saw as a false promise of success and security.

She now runs her own boutique tech consultancy and says working "pretty much seven days a week" comes with the territory of entrepreneurship. For 9-to-5 workers, though, "I don't see how working on a Sunday is going to save your job," she says. "Just because your manager sees you working on Slack on a Sunday, what does that matter?"

#269. Post-Quantum Cryptography In The Financial Sector: Protecting Trust In The Quantum Era

Dr. Najwa Aaraj, Chief Executive Officer, Technology Innovation Institute (TII) and QuantumGate.

​The financial sector runs on trust, and that trust runs on mathematics. The encryption protecting banking, payments, insurance and capital markets today runs on mathematical problems that classical computers cannot solve in any practical timeframe.

A cryptographically relevant quantum computer, however, is on the horizon, with industry estimates pointing to this technology being only 10 years out, according to NIST in 2024. When one arrives, the cryptographic foundations of the financial system suddenly become very breakable. Financial institutions cannot delay post-quantum cryptography (PQC).

Preparing for exposure to cryptographically relevant quantum computers can’t be deferred until those machines exist. Encrypted information captured today can be stored and decrypted later, an approach known as “harvest now, decrypt later.”

Financial records, transaction data, customer information and regulatory archives may need to remain confidential for years or decades, so information intercepted today could still be valuable by the time the capability to decrypt it exists.

Digital signatures and authentication infrastructure face a related challenge: They, too, depend heavily on public-key cryptography that must eventually be replaced.

​The replacement algorithms already exist. NIST published the first post-quantum standards in 2024.

Meanwhile, in January 2026, the G7 Cyber Expert Group issued a coordinated roadmap for the financial sector, in particular, identifying 2035 as a useful overall planning target and suggesting that the most critical systems may warrant earlier migration, for example during 2030 to 2032.

The roadmap is deliberately non-prescriptive, but its message is clear: Migration planning needs to begin well before the threat materializes, and it needs to be done across systems that cannot be taken offline.​

​​Migration begins with an inventory, but that’s also where, in my experience, many programs stall.

My company, QuantumGate, re​cently surveyed organizations to assess the state of post-quantum readiness in Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) markets. The survey found a majority use a combination of manual and automated tools to keep track of their cryptography, with more than a quarter relying on spreadsheets. A third use purpose-built automated discovery tools, and only 2% reported having no formal cryptographic tracking process at all.

​A first pass at inventorying usually returns the certificate estate because certificates are the most visible cryptographic assets, and many existing tools were built to manage them.

What it tends to miss is cryptography nobody ever recorded as cryptography: algorithms written a decade ago that are hard-coded into applications, key material sitting in hardware security modules with no current owner and dependencies inside third-party products where the institution has no visibility into the vendor’s own stack.

The G7 roadmap similarly identifies limited vendor transparency and access to detailed supplier roadmaps as barriers to effective planning and prioritization.

Companies also struggle because they treat inventorying as a one-and-done exercise. Remember: A discovery snapshot decays the moment it is taken. Organizations will need to turn one-time discovery into continuous governance for continued agility and control.

Nothing about this transition requires replacing everything at once, and trying to do so is usually a mistake. A risk-based prioritization plan, on the other hand, ranks systems by how long the data they protect stays sensitive and how central they are to operational resilience.

Europol and its partners, including FS-ISAC, published a prioritization methodology for financial services in January 2026 that is a reasonable starting point. Long-lived customer data, payment infrastructure and signing keys sit at one end; systems whose data is worthless within months sit at the other.​

When making these updates, one of the most important lessons I can share is to remember that this will not be the last algorithm change. Systems designed so that cryptographic algorithms and protocols can be changed without rebuilding the underlying technology will be far more resilient to future threats.

Our survey mentioned above found that cryptography is rarely reviewed, with only 27% of respondents auditing on a fixed schedule and 22% only when a major system is already being rebuilt.

Post-quantum readiness must move from a one-time migration project into an operational capability. Various technologies, such as continuous discovery, can help make agility sustainable. (Disclosure: My company is one of a few providers that offer a continuous discovery feature.)

Beyond integrating technology, three moves can help jumpstart a PQC strategy:

1. Build a cryptographic inventory scoped to include vendor dependencies, not only your own code.

2. Ask your most critical suppliers for their post-quantum roadmap in writing and note which of them cannot produce one.

3. Name a single accountable executive owner for cryptographic transition because programs otherwise risk stalling between security, infrastructure, architecture, procurement and third-party management.

The financial system has always depended on cryptographic trust. Preserving that trust in the quantum era starts long before a quantum computer arrives with knowing where today’s cryptography lives, which systems matter most and whether they are built to change.​​​​

#270. I've studied over 200 kids—parents who raise resilient, successful children teach them these 6 lessons early on

When we talk about raising successful kids, we tend to talk about what they can do.

Are they getting good grades? Are they going to basketball practices and winning games? Did they clean their rooms and set the table? Are they motivated? Responsible? Social? Can they solve problems, make good choices and eventually become independent adults?

But after years spent working with more than 200 families, I've seen that some of the most important lessons children need to live successful, happy and fulfilling lives — and to build healthy relationships — have very little to do with action or achievement.

Children absorb crucial messages in ordinary moments based on how we respond when they struggle, fail, disagree with us, disappoint us or simply become someone different from who we imagined they would be.

In my experience, there are six things parents of the most successful, confident, resilient and well-adjusted kids teach them early on that have nothing to do with accomplishments.

Children notice what happens between you when something goes wrong. They see your face when the grade comes back. They notice whether you seem prouder after the win and more distant after the loss.

A child should be able to fail without feeling they have fallen in your eyes. For example, instead of immediately asking "Why didn't you study more?" try "I know you wanted a different result. How are you feeling about it?"

When children know a bad result won't change how we see them, they don't have to be so afraid of getting things wrong. Failure can become something they learn from instead of something they feel they need to hide.

If being "good" means pleasing other people, someone else's disappointment can start to feel like proof a child did something wrong. They may learn to read the room before they learn to read themselves.

We can show them a different way. You might say: "Someone else can be disappointed in your choice, and it can still be the right choice for you."

Your child needs to know that you can disagree with them and they can still trust themselves. That matters later, too, with friends, partners and bosses.

Even positive labels can feel like pressure. If adults keep saying:

A child can quietly start to hear: This is who I have to keep being. Then a B isn't just a B. Getting cut from the team isn't just disappointing. Struggling can start to feel like losing a piece of who they are.

Instead of making the achievement their identity, notice what went into it. You might say: "You kept going even when that got difficult."

When we separate what children accomplish from who they are, we give them room to become more than whatever they happen to be good at today.

Children need to disagree with us sometimes and discover that the relationship is still okay.

That doesn't mean they make every decision. We are still the parents. We can hold a boundary with our kids and stay connected to them at the same time. You might say: "You're allowed to be angry with my decision. The answer is still no, and we're still okay."

A child shouldn't have to choose between having a voice and feeling close to us. If they feel like they have to give up their voice to stay connected at home, saying no can become much harder everywhere else too.

Our instinct as parents is often to make our children feel better. We fix, reassure, distract or tell them everything will be fine.

Sometimes they need something simpler: "This is hard. I'm here."

Children need to learn that feeling bad doesn't mean something has gone wrong. They can be embarrassed and get through it. They can be nervous and still walk into the room.

We don't have to rescue children from every uncomfortable feeling. Sometimes staying beside them as they experience those feelings is how they discover: I can handle this.

Children already live in a world that measures them: grades, teams, rankings, likes and eventually college admissions, job offers and performance reviews.

The outside world will keep asking: "What can you do?" Home should answer a different question with an emphatic yes: Do I still matter when there's nothing to celebrate?

Sometimes it helps to say it directly: "I love watching you succeed. But you never have to impress me to belong here."

Achievement should add to a child's life. It should never become the only reason they feel worthy.

Reem Raouda is a certified conscious parenting coach, speaker and author dedicated to one core idea: that loving your child and making them feel safe are not the same thing. She is the founder of The Safe Mom and creator of The Safe Mom Masterclass, helping parents raise emotionally healthy children through emotional safety, connection and self-awareness. Find her on Instagram.

#272. Rule Breakers Analysts Hunt AI’s Invisible Winners

At FoolFest 2026, The Motley Fool's annual gathering for members, co-founder David Gardner was asked what has attracted his curiosity right now that most investors might be missing. His answer began with AI.

"Well, I think we're all paying attention to artificial intelligence for very obvious reasons. It is a general technology."

Later in the same answer, he added, "So I don't feel any stress or anxiety that I don't have enough AI in my portfolio."

That kind of calm takes imagination, perhaps the most underrated skill in investing. The AI winners David has in mind aren't household names yet, and some probably don't exist.

His reasoning starts about a century ago, with an idea he credits to Vasant Dhar, an NYU professor and author of Thinking With Machines. Dhar traces AI's lineage back through the internet and the computer to electricity.

Most of today's attention goes to the builders of AI, such as Nvidia (NVDA +1.87%) and Alphabet (GOOGL +1.39%)(GOOG +1.31%). David calls them "amazing stocks," and Nvidia has been one of the defining picks of his career. He thinks the overlooked opportunity lies a layer farther out.

The internet followed the same sequence. Amazon (AMZN +5.12%) was in investors' sights early. "But then along came Uber, and then along came Airbnb. Ten years later, things that used the internet and enabled us to do things that didn't exist before."

Uber (UBER +0.06%) and Airbnb (ABNB +0.37%) were founded more than a decade after Amazon went public. Nobody booking a ride or a spare room thinks about the networks underneath.

David is looking for that kind of company, one whose customers may never notice the AI at all. The wait could be shorter this time. As Chapter 7 of Rule Breaker Investing notes, AI is catching on even faster than the internet did, so more Rule Breakers are likely headed our way than ever.

Palantir (PLTR +5.10%) shows what an early start can look like. David, a shareholder, credits it with deploying AI at scale "way earlier than a lot of other companies." In 2025, The Economist asked whether Palantir might be the most overvalued firm of all time. David's response: "There you go. What a Rule Breaker."

Two things have to go right. AI has to keep spreading the way electricity did, getting cheaper and more general. And the companies that use it most creatively have to come public while they still have room to run. If either one falls short, the builders could prove the best AI investments after all.

David, for his part, is sticking with the innovators.

The Chief Rule Breaker no longer picks stocks for members himself, but the analysts on Team Rule Breakers who do carry the same outlook. We're optimists by nature, and we invest for a future we expect to be bigger than today. We welcome a compelling story, and then we test it against the numbers. Like venture capitalists, we invest with a long horizon and accept that some picks will miss, because that's the trade-off of Rule Breaking. A single great winner can more than make up for those misses, and we're always looking for the next one.

#273. Historic lawsuit sparks flurry of option activity in this stock

While President Donald Trump's war with the networks dominates the headlines, a far more consequential fight is unfolding in a Lower Manhattan courthouse. At stake? The economics of journalism itself, and the war is sparking options traders' interest.

On Friday, newly unsealed statements from Microsoft and OpenAI executives threatened the "fair-use" defense in the New York Times lawsuit. The defense rests on showing that the accused product is neither a substitute for nor a direct competitor to the source work.

According to the unsealed material, an OpenAI executive allegedly acknowledged their chatbots were exactly that: an "existential threat" to journalism, delivering the information directly and sparing the reader the click-through, per the Wall Street Journal.

OpenAI allegedly copied millions of copyrighted articles for training, possibly exploiting hacks to retrieve them, and Microsoft's own director of applied science, Brent Hecht, reportedly described the training as "the largest theft of labor in human history," according to the Washington Post, while the companies' own data showed Times' click-through rates dropping precipitously.

OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman, meanwhile, reportedly wrote in 2017 that he was "deeply motivated by the gazillions" he hoped to earn commercializing the technology, according to the Financial Times, and allegedly replied "ah nice" when told an employee had found a hack around the Times' paywall.

These findings meaningfully raise the odds of either a massive settlement and licensing deal or, failing that, a Times victory at trial that would be catastrophic for the defendants and enormously remunerative for the plaintiff.

The one wrinkle for the Times was the September 1st statement of interest from the Department of Justice asking the court to hold that training AI models on copyrighted work is fair use, citing national security. If foreign adversaries will train on anything they can access by any means, the argument goes, restricting U.S. systems risks ceding an insurmountable lead.

Given the enormity of what's at stake, you would think this would garner more investor attention, but New York Times shares have been flat year-to-date and barely moved on Friday.

But options activity has heated up. The meat of the flow was a purchase of roughly 4,400 October 72.5/77.5 call spreads for a $0.925 debit — risking just 1.3% of Friday's close to win at least 4.6% by October expiration, and potentially 10% or more on a move to the $77.73 average analyst target. Concurrent volume in the October 62.5 and 65 puts suggests the trader may have trimmed the outlay further by selling downside puts, just below the August lows.

The October expiration implies an expectation that a summary judgment ruling, or a settlement, could potentially land within weeks, a likelihood the unsealed emails just increased.

But if the risk is a negative surprise driving new lows, and the near-term target coincides with the analyst consensus anyway, why not go in the money as a stock substitute with a defined risk and reward and lower capital use rather than trying to establish whether options premia are too hot, too cold, or "just right." A 65/77.5 call spread offers more than $7 of upside against just over $5 of downside, with a de minimis outlay of extrinsic premium.

Put differently: less capital, defined risk, asymmetric payout.

#275. Berkshire Hathaway CEO Greg Abel Just Took a Page Out of Warren Buffett's Playbook, Plowing $930 Million Into a 'Wonderful Company at a Fair Price'

Greg Abel has been CEO of Berkshire Hathaway for only about 10 months. But he's been at the company since 1999, so he's been able to learn from the Great Warren Buffett for decades.

While Buffett has always loved to buy value stocks trading at bargain prices, he learned from his right-hand man, Charlie Munger, who served as Berkshire's vice chair until his passing in 2023, that value doesn't always look like a beaten-down stock the market has abandoned.

He took this advice to heart. In a 1989 letter to shareholders, Buffett wrote: "It's far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price." The lesson seems to have stuck with Abel, too, who in recent months has plowed $930 million into a stock that embodies just that.

In July, Berkshire invested $600 million in Bending Spoons' (BSP -1.87%) initial public offering (IPO). Bending Spoons acquires or rolls up digital businesses, optimizes them, and then reinvests the earnings to buy more digital businesses.

Recently, another securities filing revealed that Berkshire has invested an additional $330 million, bringing its total stake in the company to about 4%.

Since Bending Spoons' inception in 2013, the company has acquired 50 businesses, including notable names like AOL, Eventbrite, and Vimeo, all three of which were acquired within the past two years. Results have been great. For the second quarter, Bending Spoons grew revenue 126% year over year to over $704 million. Diluted earnings per share surged 163% to $0.28. Adjusted operating margins were 54%.

While the company has taken on debt to fund acquisitions, Bending Spoons' net leverage ratio was 2.4x, which is manageable and not a cause for concern.

Another interesting thing about Bending Spoons is that while naysayers may view many of the companies it is purchasing as legacy technology or as companies that couldn't compete with peers, management is clearly bullish on the potential to layer artificial intelligence into these businesses.

For instance, at one of Bending Spoons' companies, Brightcove, a cloud-based video platform, AI was used to enable auto-translations, audio-track dubbing, and live captions in over 50 languages.

Ultimately, Bending Spoons' strategy aligns closely with Buffett and Berkshire's value philosophy, in which they seek out businesses the market may have abandoned but that have solid underlying fundamentals and good stewards of capital who can unlock shareholder value.

Now, investors should understand that Berkshire bought shares at significantly more attractive levels than where the stock trades today. The company was priced at $29 per share in the IPO, and Berkshire's recent $330 million purchase was at $33 per share.

As of this writing, the stock trades at nearly $54.50 and has a market capitalization of nearly $35 billion. Even though revenue and profits are growing quite nicely, the stock now trades at nearly 39 times forward earnings and 11.6 times forward sales.

Whether that valuation is reasonable is debatable, but the stock is by no means a bargain right now. Still, it's a good business with strong long-term prospects, so investors can consider whether to start nibbling, practice dollar-cost averaging, or add it to their watch list and wait for better entry points.

Overall, I think Berkshire's purchase of Bending Spoons is a good lesson that Buffett, Munger, and now Abel have been teaching for decades. Just because a business isn't in the hottest sector or is an old name doesn't mean there isn't good value there.

It depends on management, how the business is run, and ultimately, the financials. Abel and his team saw a good opportunity and have already been rewarded. There's always value to be had in every market, regardless of the environment.

#279. M&T Bank: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 16, 2026, M&T Bank (MTB -1.15%) reported that year-to-date net operating earnings per share increased 17% over the prior year. The bank continues to expand its deposit base to fund loan growth. That internal capital generation gives it flexibility to absorb regulatory shifts without diluting shareholder value. Three takeaways from management's presentation highlight how the business is positioning itself for long-term compounding.

Management transferred $8.3 billion of residential mortgage-backed securities from available-for-sale, which are investments sold before maturity, to held-to-maturity to insulate tangible capital from accumulated other comprehensive income, or unrealized paper losses. That move shields regulatory capital ratios if proposed bank rules begin counting paper portfolio losses against equity reserves.

Expanding customer deposits allowed M&T Bank to lower its reliance on average short-term wholesale borrowings by $2.8 billion during the quarter. Funding loan growth through primary operating accounts keeps deposit costs manageable while preserving net interest margin, which measures the profit spread on lending.

Despite competitive pressures in commercial real estate and business lending, management refuses to compromise on credit deal terms to chase volume. Maintaining strict loan covenants and structural protections ensures credit quality remains durable across economic cycles, even if loan growth might slow.

Asset repricing across fixed-rate loans and the investment portfolio provides ongoing revenue support. Strong customer relationships and deep market roots enable the bank to maintain underwriting standards without sacrificing market share.

Long-term performance hinges on maintaining pricing discipline and optimizing funding costs across economic shifts. Management remains committed to generating attractive returns through prudent capital deployment.

#281. 3 Wall Street Analysts See Intuitive Surgical Hitting $500. Here's the Bull Case.

Intuitive Surgical (ISRG +1.43%) has built a leading position in robot-assisted surgery, and three Wall Street analysts see its shares reaching $500. Oppenheimer upgraded the stock to Outperform in August with a $500 price target. Meanwhile, Citigroup and Baird lowered their targets to $500 in July but kept their Buy and Outperform ratings.

As more hospitals adopt its technology, the company is finding new ways to accelerate growth. Here's why the bull case may have more room to run.

Intuitive Surgical's bull case is straightforward: it isn't just selling surgical robots; it's building a whole ecosystem that hospitals and surgeons can rely on for years. Its flagship da Vinci surgical system allows surgeons to perform minimally invasive procedures using robotic tools through a console.

But the bigger revenue driver is what happens after a hospital purchases a robot.

Intuitive can generate recurring revenue from instruments, accessories, and servicing as hospitals continue to use its systems. That creates a business model with both a sales component for equipment and an ongoing revenue stream from surgical procedures.

The company's next major opportunity comes from Intuitive's latest platform, da Vinci 5. The system builds on established technology with features such as improved imaging, enhanced computing capabilities, and tools to support surgical workflows. If it succeeds, da Vinci 5 could encourage new purchases, upgrades, and broader adoption across hospitals.

The new rollout is already underway. In the second quarter of 2026, Intuitive placed 246 da Vinci 5 systems, up from 180 in the previous year. That suggests that the new platform is already contributing to more overall sales.

But of course, the bull case doesn't depend entirely on selling new robots. As the installed base expands, Intuitive has more opportunities to generate recurring revenue from the tools and accessories used in procedures.

Beyond intelligent surgical robots, Intuitive also benefits when hospitals use its systems more frequently. Each additional procedure can create demand for accessories and related services. And so far, the trend has been encouraging. Compared with the same quarter last year, procedures done by surgeons using da Vinci systems grew 15%, while revenue from instruments and accessories climbed 18% to roughly $1.7 billion.

These figures demonstrate why Intuitive's business model is so compelling. The company doesn't need every dollar of growth to come from selling another robot. It can also grow by making greater use of the systems already installed in hospitals.

The opportunity extends beyond the U.S., too. Intuitive reported strong international procedure growth, supported by broader adoption across surgical specialties. Continued expansion into new markets could help the company reach hospitals and surgeons that have yet to adopt robot-assisted surgery.

On top of that, Intuitive's Ion platform adds another opportunity beyond da Vinci and surgical robotics. Ion provides robot-assisted bronchoscopy, which helps physicians perform biopsies on lung nodules that may be difficult to access using traditional techniques. That matters because finding lung cancer earlier can be important for treatment decisions. Ion gives Intuitive exposure to the broader push toward earlier diagnosis rather than focusing only on growth in surgical procedures.

Still, the bull case is not without risks. Some of these risks include slower procedure growth, limited hospital budgets, and stronger competition from other surgical robotics companies. But if the company successfully navigates these risks, the upside could be compelling.

A consensus among 31 Wall Street analysts rates Intuitive Surgical a Strong Buy, with target prices indicating potential upside of between 12% and 60% over the next 12 months. However, the biggest challenge today is valuation. The stock trades at a price-to-earnings ratio (P/E) of about 49, which leaves less room for disappointment if procedure growth slows or new system sales fall short of expectations.

Looking ahead, third-quarter results, expected on or around Oct. 20, will show whether procedure growth and da Vinci 5 placements are holding up. Still, for investors who believe robot-assisted surgery will only become more common, today's stock price might make sense. If Intuitive Surgical accelerates earnings growth and exceeds those high expectations, the stock has a realistic path to $500.

#282. Caruso-Cabrera: The investing tailwinds for Latin America are the best in decades

As measured by the iShares Latin America 40 ETF (ILF), the region is handily beating the S&P 500 year to date, up 15% compared to the S&P's 11% move. It's up more than 70% since late 2024.

In a new report from Citi, Chief Latin America Economist Ernesto Revilla answers with a qualified yes — only if the countries seize the moment.

"Latin America is poised for take-off. Or to be more precise: the conditions for Latin America to achieve a higher rate of growth are the best they have been in decades, and it is time to capitalize on the opportunity," wrote Revilla.

The tailwinds helping the region are the best in decades: a weak dollar, strong commodities, favorable geo-politics, and a wave of elections that have brought pro-business and pro-reform leaders to power. The most important factor in the region's success is the weaker dollar, said Revilla.

Investors seek out "stronger currencies and returns, debt repayment is cheaper (because they borrow in dollars) and commodity prices move higher." Add modern and mature central banking which is far better at controlling inflation than in decades past.

Real rates in Latin America are some of the highest in the world leading to carry levels as high as 10% in Brazil, the report highlights. That attracts fixed income and foreign exchange inflows. At the same time, it also leaves room for cuts, which in turn would help stocks.

Beyond the macroeconomic tailwinds, there are country-specific reasons to be optimistic according to the report, whether its Mexico benefitting from the AI boom through the export of CPUs assembled there, or Argentina undergoing the "most market friendly shift in a generation."

Danny Osorio, CEO of Andean Capital Advisors, said private capital flows into Latin America "have been reenergized" as "the region is on more stable footing than it has been in a while." An advisor to asset managers, family offices, and sovereign wealth funds, Osorio said he is seeing repatriation of capital back to Colombia, Peru, Ecuador and Argentina.

Also helping is the recent strengthening of ties between the U.S. and Latin America. This month, Secretary of State Marco Rubio visited Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, which are closely aligned with the current U.S. administration. His visit reflects the White House's focus on the Western Hemisphere as articulated in both the National Security Strategy and National Defense Strategy, which called for a renewal of the Monroe Doctrine — leading to the portmanteau of "Donroe Doctrine."

This aligns with numerous elections leading to leaders who want stable currencies, increased trade, more open economies, and closer ties with the United States.

The region is not without risks and headwinds. The greatest potential threat — a continued rise in U.S. interest rates.

"If the US sneezes interest rate wise, that's full-on pneumonia for Latin America," said Osorio. Both Revilla and Osorio also point to El Nino, which is leading to both droughts and flash floods, hurting the important agriculture sector in countries such as Colombia and Peru.

Cit's Latin American equity analysts acknowledge the regions' markets have been on a strong run and "part of the opportunity has already been reflected in valuations." For it to continue, earnings will have to improve, which they believe could lead investors to increase their allocation to the region.

"Even a modest reallocation of global capital toward the region could have a meaningful impact," wrote Andres Cardona, director, LatAm Equity Research for Citi.

Investors in Europe have put more money into Latin America stocks already in 2026 than they have the last 16 years, according to The Financial Times, citing Morningstar figures.

The most liquid play in Latin American equities is the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (EWZ) with $8.6 billion assets under management and average daily volume of 23 million shares. The ETF is up 18% so far this year.

The fund has heavy exposure to mining with Vale S.A., oil via Petroleo Brasileiro SA Petrobras, and financials through Itau Unibanco and Nu Holdings.

The region is underbanked and Osorio says the expansion of financial services is a strong trend with lots of opportunity as mortgages and car loans are becoming more available than ever before.

Nu, a digital bank started in Brazil that has since expanded to Colombia and Mexico, is rated an overweight by Morgan Stanley with a price target of $21, up from its current price just under $14. The company announced this month it will expand into the United States.

Brazil also has a key near-term catalyst and/or risk. The country's presidential election is just weeks away. New polling shows Flavio Bolsonaro, the more business friendly candidate neck and neck with current President Lula da Silva. That poll, the first to show Bolsonaro within reach of becoming president, led to a sharp rally in the Bovespa. The first round will be October 4 with a runoff scheduled for October 25.
