#283. We Don't Fear Market Corrections. Nor Should You.

In January 2022, Team Rule Breakers recommended Spotify(SPOT -3.04%) to Stock Advisor members at about $209 a share. By November, with the S&P 500 deep in a bear market, it had fallen to about $69, a drop of roughly two-thirds.

Drops like that are hard to sit through, and with economic headwinds possibly ahead, plenty of investors are wondering how to prepare for the next one. Our answer comes from the philosophy by which every analyst on Team Rule Breakers invests. It starts with accepting that bad years will come, and it ends with a portfolio built to hold through them.

Spotify's story didn't end in November 2022, of course, and we'll come back to it.

Down years are common. Depending on how you count, the market has fallen in somewhere between one year in four and one year in three. Some of those stretches have been brutal, from the dot-com bust to the financial crisis and the COVID-19 crash. Each one also turned out to be a stop on the way to the stock market's long-run gains.

So, at The Motley Fool, we don't try to call the next downturn. Nobody knows whether it will arrive next year or a decade from now, but history suggests it will show up regardless. We spend that energy studying businesses instead. A falling market sometimes offers great companies at better prices, and that's where our attention goes.

The Rule Breakers' habits and principles are built with these stretches in mind. The third habit of a Rule Breaker investor -- Invest. For At Least Three Years. -- sets three years as the bare minimum for holding a stock, and we'd happily hold our best companies for decades.

The fifth habit -- 5% Max Initial Position -- helps keep a single stock's fall from doing lasting damage to a portfolio. The sixth principle of a Rule Breakers portfolio -- Review Quarterly, Manage Accordingly -- has us checking in on each business when it reports results so that a rough week in the market doesn't drive our decisions.

Members who held Spotify through 2022 have since watched it recover. As of Friday's close, it's up around 156% since the recommendation, about 71 percentage points ahead of the S&P 500.

Not every dollar necessarily belongs in stocks. The Motley Fool has said from the start that money in the market should be money you'd be comfortable leaving there for at least five years. That's the thinking behind the second portfolio principle -- Know and Name Its Purpose. A portfolio meant to fund a house deposit next spring has a different job from one meant to compound for 20 years.

The fourth principle -- Establish Your Sleep Number -- adds a personal limit: how large a single holding can grow before it keeps you up at night. Investors nearer to retirement have fewer years to recover from a bad stretch, so it may make sense for that number to come down over time.

Chief Rule Breaker David Gardner likes to say the market always goes down faster "than it goes up, but it always goes up more than it goes down, and you have to hold both of those thoughts in your mind."

Both Team Rule Breakers and Team Hidden Gems hold both. We invest with a long horizon, and we plan to stay invested through the bad years because, historically, the good ones have more than made up for them, much as Spotify's recovery has more than made up for its 2022 slide. Fool on!

#284. Buffett takes next step in plan to keep Berkshire from straying

(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)

Warren Buffett is taking a third major step in his multi-year plan to gradually step away from Berkshire Hathaway, the formerly troubled Massachusetts textile manufacturer he took control of in 1965 and lovingly built over six decades into one of the world's most valuable companies.

But even after just turning 96, he is still not leaving altogether, as he continues to do everything he can to make sure Berkshire retains the core values he built into it even after he does say goodbye for good.

First, over many years, he allowed Berkshire veteran Greg Abel, the CEO-designate, to handle Berkshire's many operating companies.

Then, in May of 2025, he announced he would step down as CEO at the end of the year but remain chairman, with Abel taking over as chief executive.

Now, as we reported in a special edition of the newsletter Friday morning, he is stepping down as chairman but will remain on the company's board of directors as "chairman emeritus" to "continue to offer his valued judgment and perspective."

And, very importantly, "consistent with the company's long-standing succession plan," his son, Howard, will become chairman.

As Buffett wrote in a letter to shareholders, Howard's primary responsibility will be to "guard [Berkshire's] culture and values – both worth more than anything on our balance sheet."

Both the company's news release, and Buffett's attached letter to shareholders, stress the continuity represented by having Buffett's son as chairman of the board.

Abel is quoted as saying, "The culture Warren built and the values he championed will remain at the heart of Berkshire, and Howard will be their guardian."

Buffett notes his son has been a director for 33 years. "Think of Howard as a policy the shareholders own and hope never to claim against."

As CNBC's Becky Quick put it in her "Squawk Box" breaking news report Friday morning, Buffett "has always talked about Berkshire Hathaway like another one of his children, and making sure it's in the right hands has been one of the most important decisions I think he's ever made."

Since Abel took over as CEO, both he and Buffett have made of point of saying Buffett still comes into the office five days a week and the two talk with each other at least every few days.

Many on Wall Street believed Abel was responsible for Berkshire's now $37 billion investment in Alphabet's AI ambitions, but in July, Buffett told CNBC he was the one who initiated it, with Abel's approval.

"I am not doing anything that [Abel] doesn't approve of. He's not doing anything I don't approve of. We talk all the time... but he is the decider."

We don't yet know whether today's announcement signals a change in that relationship, with Buffett taking an even more passive role, or if he will still be as active, just with a different title.

Buffett did say in his letter he still has "the best job in the world" and has "never felt better about what comes next."

"It was always a matter of when, not if. Buffett has made a graceful exit," Annex Wealth Management's Brian Jacobsen tells Reuters.

"This feels more like the completion of a carefully planned succession than a sudden changing of the guard."

While we've long known Warren Buffett planned to have his son, Howard, who prefers to be known as "Howie," succeed him as Berkshire Hathaway's chairman, he is not nearly as well-known as his father.

That prompted several major news organizations to run profiles of him and his "eclectic background," as Bloomberg describes it.

The New York Times says he attended three colleges without graduating from any of them before he started running a 400-acre farm north of Omaha in 1986 that he continues to operate, along with a 1500-acre farm in Illinois.

He has been involved with law enforcement, serving as a county sheriff for over a year starting in 2017 after completing what Reuters described at the time as "more than 3,300 hours of patrol and training, [with] 76 weapons qualifications including Tasers, handguns, rifles and shotguns."

Howard Buffett, like his father, is a major philanthropist. His foundation, which receives a donation each year from Warren Buffett, gave away $700 million last year, focusing on food security, conflict mitigation, and countering human trafficking, Barron's reports quoting the group's annual report.

Ukraine has been a major beneficiary, receiving around $350 million in 2025 and a total of $1.1 billion since Russia's invasion in 2022.

He has traveled to the country, telling CNBC in 2022 he had "never quite seen anything like this in my lifetime."

While Howard is not a typical businessperson, The Wall Street Journal notes he is "no stranger to corporate boards," having served as a director for Coca-Cola, Coca-Cola Enterprises, and ConAgra Foods, among others.

But, says the Journal, his main qualification to be Berkshire's chairman is that "his father is Warren Buffett."

It quotes Buffett telling the newspaper in 2025, "He is getting it because he is my son."

In that article, Howard said of eventually becoming chairman, "I feel I'm prepared for it because [Warren] prepared me. That's a lot of years of influence and a lot of years of teaching."

"When the time comes, I'm ready to do it. But that's how I am. I've gone through most of my life doing things that I wasn't sure exactly how to do."

Wall Street apparently does not anticipate the announcement will have a major effect on the company's prospects, at least for now.

Both the Class A and Class B shares initially fell in early trading Friday but then recovered to end nearly unchanged on the day.

That may be because what's been called the "Buffett Premium" has already faded.

Berkshire shares are down more than 5% since his announcement in May of last year that he planned to step down as CEO at the end of 2025. That's well behind the S&P 500's gain of more than 34%.

And since the beginning of this year, Berkshire's B shares are underperforming the benchmark by more than 10 percentage points.

Warren Buffett explains why he's confident that Berkshire's culture is so "deeply embedded" that it will continue long after he and Charlie Munger are gone.

AUDIENCE MEMBER: How can we, as outside investors, judge the state of Berkshire's culture long after you depart from the company?

WARREN BUFFETT: Well, I think it's fair that you do, you know, come with a questioning mind to the culture, post-me and Charlie, but I think you're going to be very — I don't think you should be surprised, but I think you will be very pleased with the outcome...

It's a vital part of Berkshire to have a clearly defined, deeply embedded culture that pervades the parent company, the subsidiary companies. It's even reflected in our shareholders.

And, you know, when you have 97 percent of the shareholders vote and say we don't want a dividend, I don't think there's another company like that in the world.

So we have a — our directors sign on for it and, there again, we behave consistently. Instead of having a bunch of directors who are — love to be a director because they'd like to get $2- or $300,000 a year for showing up four times a year, we have directors who look at it as a great opportunity for stewardship, and who want their ownership, and have their ownership, represented by buying stock in the market, exactly like you do.

So we — it's — we try to make clear and define that culture in every way possible, and it's gotten reinforced over the years to an extreme degree.

People who join us believe in it; people who shun us don't believe in it, so we — it's self-reinforcing.

And I think it's a virtual certainty to continue and to become even stronger, because once Charlie and I aren't around, it will be so clear that it's not the force of personality, but it's the — it's institutionalized that, you know, nobody will doubt that it will really continue for decades and decades and decades to come.

#287. Three words from Kevin Warsh have Wall Street wondering how far the Fed will go with rate hikes

With a few carefully chosen words, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh both explained this week's decision to hike interest rates and raised vexing questions about what comes next.

Warsh described Wednesday's decision to lift the central bank's benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point not specifically as a tightening of policy but rather as removing "a dose of accommodation." Further, he said the move was possible because of a U.S. economy that appears to have "strengthened" and financial conditions that have become less restrictive.

While the language may sound like central bank semantics, it gets to the heart of what markets are debating now: How far will the Warsh Fed go if it has only removed a "dose" of help, and what are the guidelines it will be using to formulate policy?

The phrase was "the one stand-out hawkish element" of Warsh's post-meeting commentary to the press, Krishna Guha, head of economics and central bank strategy at Evercore ISI, said in a client note.

"This was not a mistake; it was a phrase he repeated several times and looked very much a deliberate choice to frame policy in this way," Guha added, noting that "the framing is substantively different to that used by the Fed in recent years, and raises the possibility of a more open-ended approach to the number of hikes that might be required."

That framework has included a calibration of where policy should sit relative to the so-called neutral rate, one that neither boosts nor holds back growth. By extension, benchmark rates that sit well above the neutral rate are considered restrictive, while those closer to or below neutral are regarded as accommodative.

Warsh's framing of the hike as removing "a dose" of accommodation could be seen as the first of multiple steps toward withdrawing support the Fed no longer feels is necessary. The Fed is looking to return inflation to 2%, and policymakers generally consider raising rates as a way to tamp down demand and control price pressures.

"Warsh's framing, if taken literally, raises the possibility that rates might have to keep going up until financial conditions facing the private sector are no longer 'accommodative' — however that is defined," Guha said. "This is a relatively open-ended prospect."

Warsh had the chance to clarify what benchmark he was using to determine how much accommodation remains in policy.

Asked by CNBC's Steve Liesman to explain how far he sees the current rate — in a target range of 3.75%-4% — sitting above neutral, Warsh essentially rejected the framing, in a statement that runs counter to how central bank policy has operated for more than a decade.

Warsh said measuring the benchmark rate relative to neutral is "useful academically. It's a discussion to help us think about policy. Do I think it has any operational effect of decisions that we make today? No, I don't."

The answer helped add a layer of mystery to a Fed chairman already developing a reputation for being cryptic when it comes to how he views the wheels of policy needing to be tuned.

A round of post-meeting speculation on Wall Street about what's to come has ensued.

One of the initial reactions was pricing in higher odds for another hike when the Fed next meets in October. Goldman Sachs added an October increase to its forecast, as does Bank of America, which also expects another move in December. The market-implied odds of an October increase were near 58% Friday morning, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge. A week ago, the probability was 42%.

"The word 'accommodation' means 'stimulus' at the Fed; this comment implies that the current monetary policy stance is meaningfully stimulative," wrote James Egelhof, chief U.S. economist at BNP Paribas Securities.

"With policy starting at a stimulative stance, a strong cyclical impulse, and persistent inflation, we think significant rate increases, perhaps more than the three we expect, may be necessary to stabilize the unemployment rate from below and prevent overheating next year," he added.

Egelhof agreed that the "dose of accommodation" remark was "the most striking feature" of Warsh's abbreviated news conference.

Markets are pricing in the likelihood that the Warsh Fed removes a few more "doses" before it is finished. Futures are implying a fed funds rate of 4.635% near the end of 2027, which would argue for three or four more hikes ahead.

If that's the case, the Fed at the very least will undo many of the FOMC rate cuts approved under Warsh's predecessor, Jerome Powell, who now sits on the committee as a governor.

The "dose of accommodation" remarks "seemingly helped to underscore this hawkish tone, implying that [the] committee no longer views policy as modestly restrictive," said Jack Janasiewicz, portfolio manager and lead portfolio strategist at Natixis Investment Managers Solutions.

"We remain unconvinced that this is the start of an aggressive new tightening cycle," he said. "Rather, we see this as a removal of the insurance cuts the Fed delivered in the fall of 2025."

#288. Will the Fed Raise Rates This Month? Here's What Markets Say.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics released the latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) report last week, showing that inflation was significantly higher than expected in September.

Headline inflation, which includes food and energy prices, showed the CPI rose 3.7% year over year in September, and climbed 0.6% from the previous month. When food and fuel are excluded -- so-called core inflation -- prices rose 2.6% year over year and 0.3% over August. Those numbers were above general forecasts, and September's numbers were higher than August's, suggesting that inflation is heating up, not cooling down. This means it's moving in the wrong direction.

That inflation data suggests that the Federal Reserve will implement a second consecutive rate hike when its monetary policy committee meets on Oct. 27-28. The Fed hiked its benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point in September, and most Fed watchers expected that to be the first of a series of rate hikes intended to bring inflation closer to the Fed's 2% goal.

Bond and futures markets, however, are not convinced the hotter-than-expected September inflation reading will prompt a rate hike by the Fed -- at least not yet. Futures traders are pricing in an 85.1% likelihood that the Fed will leave the federal funds rate unchanged at a range of 3.75% to 4% at the October meeting. Futures markets assign a 74.1% likelihood that the Fed will resume hiking that rate when it meets for the final time this year, in early December.

Bond markets seem to agree with futures traders. The yield on the two-year Treasury note, which climbed in September to 4.93%, has since backed off to 4.73%. That's significant, as the two-year yield is most sensitive to changes in the federal funds rate, so when it falls, it indicates lower expectations for rate hikes. That said, the two-year yield remains well above the Fed's current rate, suggesting bond investors expect that rate to rise eventually.

Futures traders do, too. They're pricing in a 65% chance of at least three quarter-point hikes by the end of 2027, taking the federal funds rate to a range of 4.5% to 4.75%, exactly where the two-year yield stands right now.

This matters to equity markets. Research by Charles Schwab and others shows that when the Fed goes slow on rate hikes, the stock market performs much better than when it hurries its rate-hiking schedule. I've been watching and listening closely to new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh since he took the helm of the central bank back in May of this year, and he looks like an incrementalist to me. That's a good thing for investors.

#290. I've Covered Netflix for 24 Years. Here's Whether the Stock Is Overvalued Right Now.

I'm not one to typically celebrate investing anniversaries, but this month marks 24 years since I became a Netflix (NFLX -1.32%) shareholder. It's been largely ups along the way, but lately there's been a hard road down.

Shares of the company behind the world's leading premium streaming video service have plummeted more than 40% over the past year. I got in early, a few months after Netflix began trading and it was a broken IPO. Today's pullback isn't the same ground-floor opportunity, but is the stock a smart buy now or still overvalued? Let's take a closer look.

If you bought Netflix the day that article came out, you would have a 1,400-bagger on your hands today. I would unfortunately sell nearly all of my own shares along the way. The 1% of the original stake I still own is my largest personal holding. Imagine where I would be with the other 99%.

Netflix has still come a long way in the 24 years that I've been following the company since its 2002 springtime IPO. Netflix was losing money the year it went public, generating $153 million in revenue. Trailing revenue is now more than $48 billion at a record net margin.

The valuation math may change by the time that Netflix reports third-quarter results after the market close on Wednesday. Right now, it's easy to make a compelling bullish case for the out-of-favor growth stock.

Even though Netflix staged a near-term retreat following each of its last few reports, the valuation is compelling. Netflix is trading for less than 19 times next year's analyst profit target and just 15 times the following year's profit forecast.

With its top rivals consolidating and pushing out price increases in recent months, the near-term outlook for the industry is more favorable than you might expect. Netflix has scalability and the pricing flexibility to keep growing even at this stage of its life cycle.

I've suffered through all of the downturns. The current pullback isn't as bad as the Qwikster aftermath of 2011 or the growth stock sell-off in 2022. The stock was cheaper coming out of those two bear turns, but Netflix is a premium business trading at a discount to the market. This is the kind of story that usually plays out well for the believers.

#293. Arm vs. Lumentum: Which Tech Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?

As artificial intelligence (AI) pushes computing power and data transmission to new limits, investors are weighing different paths to growth. Is Arm Holdings (ARM +2.09%) or Lumentum Holdings (LITE +4.69%) the better choice today?

Arm creates the foundational blueprints for the world's most energy-efficient processors. Lumentum provides the optical components that allow data centers to communicate at lightning speeds. Both companies are central to the infrastructure of modern computing, but they operate with vastly different business models and financial profiles.

Arm designs and licenses central processing units (CPUs) and other systems used in everything from smartphones to high-performance data centers. Rather than manufacturing chips, the company earns revenue through licensing fees and royalties on every chip sold. This model enables high scalability and profit margins in the semiconductor industry.

In fiscal 2026 (ending in March), Arm's revenue reached $4.9 billion. This represents growth of nearly 23% compared to the prior year. Net income was roughly $698 million, though the net margin decreased slightly from roughly 16% in the previous year to about 14%.

As of its June 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.1x, indicating the company has very little debt relative to its net equity. The current ratio is roughly 5.3x, suggesting a strong ability to meet short-term financial obligations.

Trailing-12-month (TTM) free cash flow was $1.5 billion through the June quarter, but note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 69% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Lumentum manufactures optical and photonic products essential to cloud data centers and telecommunications networks. In its latest fiscal year ended June 27, 2026, Lumentum revealed that Customer A accounted for approximately 26.6% of revenue while Customer B accounted for roughly 15%. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, as the loss of either client would be significant.

For fiscal 2026, the company reported revenue of $3 billion, which was an increase of about 83% over the prior year. Despite this massive top-line growth, the company reported a net loss of approximately $6.9 billion, although its operating profit (earnings before interest and taxes) was $525 million. The $6.9 billion net loss was due to a $7.7 billion non-recurring loss on debt extinguishment.

According to its June 2026 balance sheet, the company has a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 0.4x. The current ratio is nearly 1.7x, indicating about $1.70 in short-term assets for every $1.00 of short-term debt.

TTM free cash flow for the period was roughly $300 million. However, stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 22.7% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Arm faces intense competition from established rivals and open-source alternatives. If major tech companies decide to design their own architectures rather than paying licensing fees, the company could see its market share erode. Additionally, the business relies on continued growth in the mobile and data center markets, and any slowdown in hardware upgrades would impact its royalty income.

Lumentum is highly dependent on a small number of customers for a significant portion of its sales, and many relationships lack long-term volume commitments. The company is also subject to complex trade policies and export controls, specifically regarding operations in China. Competition from global firms such as IPG Photonics and Viavi Solutions exerts constant pressure on pricing and operating margins.

Lumentum appears to be the more value-oriented choice as it trades at a significant discount to its peer across both sales and future earnings estimates.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

Arm is a great business that generates high margins from royalties and licensing fees. It would be a solid chip stock to own, but Lumentum offers better value right now.

Analysts expect Arm to grow earnings at a 25% annualized rate in the coming years. However, Lumentum is expected to deliver 132% annualized growth, as the business scales and expands margins. Relative to their forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratios, Arm looks expensive, trading at a forward P/E-to-growth (PEG) ratio of 4.3x, while Lumentum trades at an attractive 0.29x.

Lumentum is benefiting from data centers shifting to optical connectivity for AI workloads. Revenue surged 109% year over year in the recent quarter, marking the eighth consecutive quarter of growth and signaling strong momentum that may not be fully reflected in the stock's valuation right now.

Arm is benefiting from the growing demand for CPUs, and its expertise in designing power-efficient chips could help it gain market share in the data center market.

Both companies are meeting demand at crucial chokepoints for AI, and they both face comparable risks. But it's difficult for me to pass up the huge discrepancy between each stock's PEG ratios. I would buy Lumentum since it's growing much faster than Arm and commands a much lower premium for future earnings growth.

#294. Prediction: This Will Be Micron's Stock Price By the End of 2027

Micron Technologies (MU +3.81%) has long been a relatively boring investment. After it peaked during the dot-com bubble in 2000, the company faced a long-lasting slump as modest demand and intense competition eroded its growth prospects relative to other tech giants. However, everything changed in 2022 when the release of ChatGPT sparked an entirely new industry: generative artificial intelligence (AI).

Micron's shares have risen by an eye-popping 333% over the last 12 months alone as data center clients scramble to purchase its advanced memory hardware. But even though demand shows no signs of slowing any time soon, there is reason to be nervous. Let's dig into Micron's pros and cons to decide how much shares might be worth by the end of 2027.

The early phases of the generative AI boom were driven by chipmakers like Nvidia, which supplied graphics processing units (GPUs) and other types of compute hardware needed to run and train large language models. However, as these chips became more powerful, a bottleneck emerged in the supply of memory hardware capable of keeping up. Micron is in the right place at the right time to cash in on the windfall.

Fourth-quarter revenue skyrocketed by a jaw-dropping 379% year over year to $54.23 billion. This is the type of growth you typically see in a small penny stock, not a 48-year-old behemoth. And it wasn't only driven by data center and cloud computing-related sales. Micron is enjoying strength across all its segments as memory shortages have led to higher margins in less-glamorous opportunities like mobile and automotive.

Micron's profitability growth is even more breathtaking, with fourth-quarter net income surging more than 10-fold to $37.7 billion. The company will likely return some of this to investors through a buyback program with $35.7 billion in share repurchases authorized.

But if Micron's business is doing so great, why is its stock so cheap at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) of just 7 compared to the S&P 500 average of 19? To answer that question, we need to look at what is happening in South Korea, home to Micron's biggest rivals, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, both of which also produce high bandwidth memory.

The country's KOSPI Index is dominated by chipmakers, and it has cratered by over 40% since its peak in June, erasing more than $2 trillion in value. This crisis resembles the scale of crashes like the dot-com bubble burst, and it is being driven by fears that rising bond yields will make it more expensive for AI companies to buy memory chips. Investors are also worried about rising Chinese capabilities.

This month, Chinese memory producer CXMT announced plans to roll out new server memory products based on breakthrough designs. It is becoming clear that the upstart could soon become a bona fide competitor to the established giants, raising fears of margin-eroding competition and a race to the bottom -- similar to what happened to other industries China has taken over, like electric cars and solar panels.

The Korean stock market crash may be an early warning of what high-flying American chip stocks might soon face. And Micron is particularly exposed because it operates on a business model similar to that of South Korea's giants.

Some South Korean experts are now predicting a memory chip supply glut by 2029. And if this happens, Micron could easily find itself facing years of stagnant performance, similar to what happened after the dot-com bubble. These uncertainties will likely be priced into Micron's stock price over the next few months, and investors shouldn't expect the stock to exceed its current price of $879 by the end of 2027.

#295. If a Market Correction Is Coming, Warren Buffett Says This 1 Move Is Key to Building Wealth

The market has seen an uptick in bearish pressure recently, and it's not unreasonable to think that bigger contractions could be on the way. Inflation is proving stubbornly sticky, and dynamics connected to the Iran war could cause energy prices to remain higher for longer and create trickle-down inflationary impacts. As a result, investors, analysts, and economists now believe that it's highly likely that the Federal Reserve will implement at least one more benchmark interest rate hike this year -- and higher rates typically create a less favorable backdrop for the stock market.

Concerns about inflation and higher interest rates aren't the only factors driving fears of a potential market correction as of late. High bond yields are also creating bearish market pressures and making it increasingly expensive to service interest payments on the U.S.'s rapidly expanding national debt. Meanwhile, there are concerns about valuations for artificial intelligence (AI) stocks, which have been the driving force in pushing major indexes higher this year.

With rising fears that a substantial market contraction could be on the horizon, here's one key bit of advice from legendary investor Warren Buffett that could help investors build wealth through volatility.

Warren Buffett. Image source: The Motley Fool.

Warren Buffett stepped down as chairman at Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA -0.24%) (BRKB -0.27%) last month after stepping down as the company's CEO at the beginning of the year. While Buffett remains on the company's board of directors, there's no doubt that the famous moneymaker's career is winding down -- and what a career it's been.

To put things in perspective, Berkshire Hathaway stock was valued at roughly $19 per share when Buffett purchased a majority stake in the company and became its CEO in 1965. Today, a single share of the company's class A stock is valued at roughly $798,000.

Over more than six decades at the helm of the investment conglomerate, Buffett executed successfully through market corrections and crashes -- and one core piece of wisdom could provide investors with the foundational grounding needed to build wealth amid volatility. As the Oracle of Omaha famously said, "The stock market is a device for transferring money from the active to the patient."

At its core, this piece of wisdom stresses the importance of not overreacting to market moves and viewing investments as long-term opportunities. Buffett repeatedly advised investors that attempting to time short-term market moves with regularity was virtually impossible, and he also cautioned against trying to time the bottom of a contraction.

Additionally, he also stressed the importance of having funds available to take advantage of opportunities created by pullbacks and of analyzing stocks based on the fundamentals of the underlying companies. Doing so gives investors a better chance to determine whether things have materially changed for a business -- or if pricing swings are mostly just noise.

#296. Truist: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 16, 2026, Truist (TFC -1.13%) announced a strategic plan to exit non-core lending businesses and reallocate capital toward relationship banking. For long-term investors, the shift aims to improve return on capital, lower credit risk, and boost earnings quality across its Sun Belt branch network.

Three takeaways from management explain how the strategy unfolds.

Truist agreed to sell $7.7 billion in LightStream unsecured loans after closing its Regional Acceptance Corp. subprime auto loan portfolio sale. Exiting stand-alone lending units will lower credit risk and free up capital for higher-return relationship banking.

Management is reinvesting proceeds from portfolio sales to shift securities out of low-yielding mortgage-backed securities, which are pools of residential mortgages, into potentially shorter-duration U.S. Treasuries. The bank is also paying down high-cost wholesale borrowings, which are short-term corporate funding obligations.

Management is reviewing every business and process to cut low-priority overhead expenses. The savings will fund branch renovations, technology upgrades, and commercial banker hires to win daily demand deposit accounts, which are low-cost checking accounts.

A dense branch network across Southeastern markets and full-service commercial banking provide a strong operational foundation. Long-term strategy focuses on deposit growth, expense discipline, and capital efficiency.

Future value hinges on disciplined resource allocation to boost profitability without expanding risk. Management remains focused on meeting return on tangible common equity, a key bank profitability metric.
